News.title: Disturbing internet searches of teen, 17, accused of killing mom & younger brother leaving them with ‘obvious trauma’
News.content:
A TEEN accused of killing his mom and younger brother allegedly made disturbing internet searches about murdering his own family before the bloodshed.

Cops say the two victims were found dead with “obvious trauma” inside their home after the 17-year-old allegedly fled in his mother’s car.



Arjun Aravind has been charged with two counts of murder over the deaths of his mom, Sudha Venkatesan, 45, and 14-year-old brother Siddharth Aravind in Acton, Massachusetts.

Prosecutors claim the high school student had displayed “concerning behavior” in the months before the alleged killings – including chilling online activity involving his family.



Middlesex District Attorney Marian Ryan said Arjun had allegedly used the internet and ChatGPT to explore “theoretical ideas or fantasy stories regarding the killing of his family.”

He allegedly used the AI chatbot to create “Gothic novel-kind of stories” involving characters and questions that authorities believe appeared to relate to threats against his family.



Ryan said the teen was allegedly “engaged in the use of ChatGPT, in creating fantasies, stories, gothic novel kind of stories” and “asking questions, creating characters.”

She said the material appeared to “relate to threats to his family not surviving.”

The horror unfolded after Arjun’s dad asked cops to carry out a wellbeing check at the family’s home on Tuesday evening.

A tutor had arrived at the Martha Lane property for a scheduled appointment shortly after 6.30pm but was reportedly unable to get inside.



Arjun’s father, who had last seen his wife before leaving for work at around 7am, then tried unsuccessfully to contact his family before calling the police.

Officers who entered the home discovered Venkatesan dead in a finished basement.

Siddarth was found dead on the first floor.

Both had suffered “obvious trauma”, according to Ryan, although officials have not yet revealed exactly how they died.



The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner is working to determine their causes of death, while investigators are also probing whether a weapon was used.

Arjun was nowhere to be found when cops arrived – and his mother’s 2014 green Honda Accord was also missing.

An overnight manhunt was launched before cops in nearby Wayland stumbled across the car while responding to an unrelated alarm call at a business early Wednesday.

The Honda was spotted in a nearby parking lot with Arjun inside, authorities said.



He was arrested without incident.

Investigators are still working to piece together exactly when the mother and son were allegedly killed.

Venkatesan was last seen alive by her husband at around 7am Tuesday, while Siddharth had visited a recreational facility that morning before returning home shortly after noon.

Arjun had previously been reported missing around a year ago before being found with the help of Acton cops, Police Chief Douglas Sturniolo said.

But the chief said he was not aware of the teenager making any public threats before this week’s horror.



Ryan said: “This is an unspeakable tragedy.

“It is an incredibly dark day. Obviously an insurmountable tragedy for the dad in this case. It is a very dark day for this community, for this school system.”

Arjun faces two counts of murder, two counts of assault and battery on a household or family member and two counts of assault and battery.

He has also been charged with use of a vehicle without authority and theft of a motor vehicle.

He was due to face the murder and related assault charges in Concord District Court after appearing in juvenile court over the vehicle allegations.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ryan said: “We are at the beginning of a very dark and long process.”

Authorities said the investigation remains ongoing but stressed there is no threat to the wider public.

News.title: Nigel Farage heads to the polls to cast his vote in the Clacton by-election against Count Binface
News.content:
POLL POSITION Nigel Farage heads to the polls to cast his vote in the Clacton by-election against Count Binface

NIGEL Farage has been spotted heading to the polls to cast his vote in the Clacton by-election.

The Reform UK leader is one of a staggering 34 candidates standing in the constituency – a record number of wannabe MPs.



Mr Farage quit as an MP to trigger the by-election in protest at media and parliamentary scrutiny of donations from his backers.

He now faces the threat of Count Binface, a joke candidate, taking his seat from him.



Mr Farage wanted it to be a “people versus the establishment” showdown but Labour and the Conservatives did not chose to stand candidates.

The two parties left the Reform UK leader facing down the likes of actor-turned-politician Laurence Fox.

Mr Farage will also have to battle it out with three candidates from the Official Monster Raving Loony Party and an array of independents.

Speaking ahead of the election Mr Farage said: “At the beginning of summer we called this by-election to give the people of Clacton the chance to have their say on the endless political attacks on me, my family and those around me.

“It’s given us the opportunity to knock on tens of thousands of doors, making the affirmative case for what I’ve done for the area, and what Reform will do for Britain.”

He added: “It’s not just about me, it’s about the people versus the establishment.”



The 34 candidates in Clacton beat the previous record of 26 candidates, set at the Haltemprice and Howden by-election in July 2008.

Haltemprice and Howden’s by-election was triggered by Tory Sir David Davis in his own seat and similarly ignored by the main Westminster parties.

In the 2024 general election, Mr Farage won Clacton with 46.2% of the vote and a majority of 8,405 over his Conservative rival.

News.title: Watch terrifying rare ‘mud volcano’ erupt sending sludge flying into the air and trapping cattle in quake-hit Colombia
News.content:
THIS is the harrowing moment a mud volcano erupted in Colombia – just 24 hours after a 7.4-magnitude earthquake killed more than 265 people.

Footage shows thick streams of mud, water and gas being spewed in the air before descending down the slopes of the volcano.



Cattle were seen struggling in the sludge after being caught in the fast-moving flow, while people were warned not to approach them.

One local resident can be heard saying: “The problem is that you cannot go in because look at how the mud is moving, it is carrying it towards the stream; there are two cows trapped.”



The eruption happened in the rural village of Molinillo, in the Antioquia region, on Tuesday morning.

An alarm was sounded and people living near the volcano were evacuated as a precaution.



Meanwhile, access from the affected area was also restricted because of the unstable terrain and fears of further eruptions.

Authorities said no people had been injured, while local reports indicated that livestock and farmland had been affected by the eruption.



Mud volcanoes are an unusual geological phenomenon in which pressure underground forces a mixture of mud, water and gases to the surface through cracks in the ground.

Unlike conventional volcanoes, they do not erupt molten rock or lava. But they can also catch fire.

Colombia has more than 100 mud volcanoes, most concentrated along the Caribbean fold belt in the north-western part of the country.



The eruption comes as more than 2,500 people were wounded and over 4,000 have been reported missing since the powerful earthquake.

Cali and Pereira remain among the worst-affected cities, with widespread building collapses and extensive damage to homes, businesses and public infrastructure.

Rescue teams sent from across the country, supported by police, soldiers, volunteers and international aid, continue working around the clock.

What is a mud volcano? MUD volcanos are an unusual geological phenomenon in which pressure underground forces a mixture of mud, water and gases to the surface through cracks in the ground. Also known as mud diapirs, they don’t have any lava flowing through them unlike a normal volcano. They range from tiny, bubbling mud pots only a few centimetres tall to massive domes up to 700 metres high and 10km wide. While most are found on land, mud volcanoes can form underwater in the sea as well. Most ooze gently and safely, but trapped methane can occasionally ignite or explode. Azerbaijan is the country with the most mud volcanoes globally. It is widely recognized as the mud volcano capital of the world.

They are racing against a critical 72-hour window to find survivors alive.

“We are entering the final phase,” Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said, adding that survivors could still be found afterward but that the odds grow steadily worse.



He said crews were still detecting signs of life underneath the rubble and urged speed, saying that “every minute is vital.”

Meanwhile, Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said: “Our efforts are focused on the disappeared.”

The government has declared a national disaster and an economic state of emergency to speed up relief and recovery efforts, while officials continue structural assessments and urge residents to avoid entering damaged buildings until they have been declared safe.

News.title: Man in his 60s dies after bungalow destroyed in huge ‘gas explosion’
News.content:
BLAST HORROR Man in his 60s dies after bungalow destroyed in huge ‘gas explosion’

A MAN has tragically died after a bungalow was destroyed in a huge gas explosion.

The victim, in his 60s, was fatally injured after the property in Newton Longville, Buckinghamshire, was blown apart on Sunday morning.



Cops were scrambled to the home on Cobb Hall Road, near Milton Keynes, at around 9.45am – as nearby properties were evacuated.

Horrified eyewitnesses described seeing bricks and tiles flying hundreds of feet into the air during the horror.



The victim was urgently rushed to hospital where he was receiving treatment for his injuries.

However, despite the best efforts of medical teams, the man has since tragically died, Thames Valley Police confirmed today.

DI Philip Turner-Robson said the investigation into the explosion was still ongoing following the “tragic development”.

Issuing a statement, he said: “Our thoughts are with the man’s family and friends at this extremely difficult time.



“Thames Valley Police is managing a coronial investigation into the circumstances surrounding the explosion and collapse of the property, working jointly with the Health and Safety Executive.

“Our enquiries remain ongoing as we seek to establish the full circumstances of what happened.”

Shocking footage captured the roof of the bungalow rocketing into the sky, before debris rained down on cars below.

Further clips showed the home completely gutted with bricks, planks of wood and furniture scattered around it as a fire continues to burn.

A neighbouring bungalow also appears to have its roof severely damaged, with tiles dangling off it.



Locals told how they could smell smoke and gas following the explosion, but the fire department are yet to confirm the cause.

Residents were evacuated from their homes as engineers from SGN, a gas distribution company, carried out safety checks.

Graham Fuller who lives on the road, told the BBC he heard his wife scream, before running outside to an “Armageddon” scene.

He said: “Debris everywhere, I ran out into the street and my neighbour had already managed to grab hold of the occupant of the property…

“We’ve been kicked out of our homes at the moment – we don’t know when we’re going back.”



Another neighbour, Marc Betts, was just about to leave his house when the “big bang” occurred.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

He said: “The great big bang can only be described as World War Three in the street.

“I wouldn’t wish it on my worst enemies, to be quite honest with you.”

News.title: Pilot and passenger, 26 & 24, killed after small plane crashed into field during ‘flight experience’ are pictured
News.content:
FLIGHT TRAGEDY Pilot and passenger, 26 & 24, killed after small plane crashed into field during ‘flight experience’ are pictured

A PILOT and his passenger who died when a small plane crashed during a “flight experience” have been pictured.

Investigators confirmed 26-year-old pilot Dylan Patel from Harlow and his 24-year-old passenger Vamshi Mandala from India passed away in the deadly smash.



The horror collision happened on June 30, when the pair’s light aircraft came down in a field near Ongar, Essex.

Dylan and Vamshi’s two-seater Cessna plane had taken off from North Weald Airfield a short time before the plane plunged to the ground.



The fatal accident happened amid what was supposed to be a short “flying experience”, investigators said.

Cops said that the families of the victims “will be supported” and treated with “dignity and respect.”



The Air Accidents Investigation Branch led the probe into the terrifying accident.

Detective Chief Superintendent Morgan Cronin said: “My thoughts, and those of my officers, are with the family and friends of Vamshi and Dylan as they continue to grieve.



“The process of formal identification has been a complex one and one we have carried out with utmost sensitivity.

“I want to thank those who responded to the incident and who have continued to investigate for the way they’ve carried out their work, ensuring the dignity of Vamshi and Dylan.

“We continue to work in parallel with the Air Accident Investigation Bureau so we can give their families the answers they need about what happened.”

“If you have any information or footage in relation to this incident, then please get in contact with us.

“You can let us know by submitting a report on our website or by using our online Live Chat service which is available 24 hours-a-day, seven days-a-week.”

News.title: Man, 102, was ‘pushed from stage as band were playing’ at pub and left fighting for his life – as man, 56, arrested
News.content:
PUB 'ATTACK' Man, 102, was ‘pushed from stage as band were playing’ at pub and left fighting for his life – as man, 56, arrested

A PENSIONER, 102, who was allegedly pushed from a stage while a band was playing has been left fighting for his life, with a man, 56, arrested in connection with the incident.

Emergency services were called to The Crow’s Nest in Cwbran, South Wales, at around 10.25pm on August 1.



The 102-year-old, who was a regular at the local pub, suffered critical injuries after tumbling backwards and hitting the floor.

A 56-year-old from Llanelli has since been arrested in connection with the incident.



Gwent Police said he was taken to hospital and remains in critical condition.

Onlookers said the centenarian wandered onto the stage where Llanelli-based band SuperHans were playing when he was knocked over.

One witness said: “My understanding from the police and staff at the time was that the 102-year-old, who lived independently and was a regular at the pub, went onto the stage, which was up three steps, to ask for the music to be turned down.

“He was pushed, causing him to fall down the three steps and broke his hip.

“At 102, this will cause life-changing, if not life-shortening, injuries.”

Locals described the elderly man as “lovely” but “confused”.



Another pubgoer said: “It’s believed the 102-year-old was pushed hard enough that he did not fall down the steps, but cleared them and landed on the floor below.”

The force said: “We’re appealing for witnesses following a report of an assault at The Crow’s Nest pub in Cwmbran at around 10.25pm on Saturday 1 August.

“Officers attended along with crews from the Welsh Ambulance Service and a 102-year-old man was taken to hospital for treatment. He remains in critical condition.

“A 56-year-old man from Llanelli was arrested on suspicion of section 20 assault and has since been released under investigation.

“Enquiries are ongoing and we are asking anyone who was in the pub between 10pm and 11pm on Saturday 1 August to contact us.”



The Crow’s Nest shared the police appeal, adding: “If anyone was in the pub that night and witnessed this please get in contact with the police.”

News.title: Terrifying moment octopus latches onto fisherman’s face forcing him to club creature in suffocating tug-of-war
News.content:
THIS is the terrifying moment an octopus clamped its tentacles onto a fisherman’s face forcing him to club the creature in a bizarre battle.

Angler Jesser Cervantes was fishing off Puerto Princesa Island in Palawan, the Philippines, when he reeled in the feisty sea creature.



Shocking footage appears to shows Angler sitting in a small wooden dinghy as he desperately tries to prise the writhing octopus from his face on July 10.

The clip shows the determined creature spread its tentacles around his head, with its powerful suction cups gripping his skin.



At one point the eight-arm beast can be seen latching onto the fisherman’s mouth gluing it shut.

The clip shows Angler frantically trying to peel away the gripping discs one by one.

But the relentless octopus refuses to release its grip, forcing Angler to grab a cut bamboo stem and repeatedly tap the creature in a bid to loosen it.

After several tense moments wrestling with the marine monster, he finally manages to tear it from his face.

Angler then lowers the octopus back into the cold water and catches his breath after the exhausting struggle.

He said: “The Octopus I caught was very hard to handle. It almost ripped my face.”



The experienced fisherman said encounters like this are surprisingly common during his fishing trips.

He added that many octopuses react in the same way after they’ve been caught.

Octopuses are known for their remarkable intelligence, powerful suction cups and flexible bodies, allowing them to cling tightly to rocks, prey and almost any surface.



Their formidable suction cups can generate a surprisingly powerful grip, making the creatures notoriously difficult to remove without carefully peeling away each arm.

It comes after a horrific incident involving an aggressive octopus nearly strangling a diver after its home was disturbed.

The eight-limbed creature shot a cloud of ink and latched onto the divers hands near Primorsky Krai, Russia, last year.

Realising he could not detach from the tough marine mollusc, the frightened man then tried to rip the octopus off himself, which had stuck on using its extremely strong suction cups.

He then started to swim upwards for air eventually reaching the surface where he gasped desperately for air.



But even then, the creature was latched on, using its whole body to cover the man’s upper torso and lower half of his face.

According to local media, he was able to release the octopus from his body several minutes later.

It is unclear however, whether the diver sustained any serious injuries.

The octopus in the video is believed to be a common octopus, which is not known to be dangerous to humans.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

They can grow up to 1.3 metres in length, and can weigh between 6.6 to 22 lbs, according to National Geographic.



The mollusc does classify as poisonous, but its venom is not lethal.

News.title: Do you think it’s right that Burnham wants to move migrants to middle-class areas? VOTE NOW

POLL OF THE DAY Do you think it’s right that Burnham wants to move migrants to middle-class areas? VOTE NOW

NEW Prime Minister Andy Burnham said more middle-class areas should take in migrants.

On Tuesday the PM suggested that wealthier areas should take more people into dispersal accommodation.

He told GB News: “We cannot have a situation where it’s only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers.”

Mr Burnham was responding to protests in Piddington, Oxfordshire, where the village of 350 people held a mock independence referendum over plans to house 1,000 asylum seekers at a MoD base.

Migrants are more likely to be housed in areas with higher deprivation scores, a Government metric used to track poverty.

News.title: Students celebrate A-Level results day after record number accepted on degree courses
News.content:
Students celebrate A-Level results day after record number accepted on degree courses

A total of 262,820 UK 18-year-olds gained a place at university or college according to Ucas, with the number from the most disadvantaged backgrounds also soaring

View 3 Images Students celebrate their results in Liverpool (Image: Colin Lane/Liverpool Echo)

The number of students getting into university has risen to a record high.

‌



A total of 262,820 UK 18-year-olds gained a place at university or college according to Ucas, with the number from the most disadvantaged backgrounds also soaring.

‌



The university admissions service said it is the highest number of placed students on results day on record, driven by a rising number of 18-year-olds in the population.

‌



International student numbers also increased 2%, with, 53,740 applicants accepted onto undergraduate courses. Accepted applicants from China rose to 13,870 from 12,380 last year.

The proportion of candidates earning top grades rose for the third year in a row, and remains higher than before the world was hit by the Covid-19 pandemic.

Are you smarter than an A Level student? Put yourself to test with tricky maths question READ MORE :

View 3 Images Two friends embrace after receiving their results in Ebbw Vale, Wales (Image: Getty Images)

‌



More than a quarter (28.5%) of UK entries were awarded an A or A* grade, up by 0.2% percentage points on last year, when 28.3% achieved the top grades.

Boys outperformed girls in terms of top grades again, having doing so for the first time in seven years last year.

Overall 28.9% of boys’ A-level entries scored an A* or A this summer, compared to 28.0% of their female classmates.

‌



The most popular subject for this academic year was maths, for the 13th year in a row. It had 115,380 entries, up 3.9% from 111,033 in 2025. About one in eight of all A-level entries this year were for maths.

It is the highest proportion of entries scoring top grades outside the pandemic-affected years of 2020-22, according to the figures from the Joint Council for Qualifications for England, Wales and Northern Ireland.

View 3 Images Skills minister Baroness Jacqui Smith (second left) meeting students at Bury College as they get their results (Image: Gary Oakley/PA Wire)

‌



Jo Saxton, chief executive of Ucas, said: “Today’s school leavers were just starting secondary school when the pandemic interrupted their education.

“Given the significant disruption they faced at such a formative stage of their learning, it is wonderful to see so many young people getting a place at university or college.”

New PM Andy Burnham added: "I want to congratulate everyone receiving their results today.

Article continues below

“I know there will have been a mix of excitement, nerves and relief this morning, but you should all be proud of the hard work that got you here."

Mr Burnham pledged in a speech during his bid for the Labour leadership that the “days of a school system configured entirely around the university route will be brought to an end”.

The Met Office has warned people living in 47 areas that they should brace for 'adverse health effects' with power cuts also possible as temperatures reach 38C

‌



There are now 47 places covered by the weather alert, which warns "adverse health effects are likely to be experienced" in the coming hours.

‌



The alert came into force at 9am this morning and runs until midnight. It covers areas of the East Midlands, East of England, London and the South East, North West England, South West England, West Midlands, and Yorkshire and the Humber.

‌



The Met Office warning added: "The highest temperatures will be in parts of the the Midlands and western England, where 37 or even 38 Celsius could be reached."

Some changes in working practices and daily routines are also likely to be required in the affected areas and some heat sensitive systems and equipment may fail, with the potential for some power cuts and the loss of other services too, the forecaster warned today.

News.title: Woman who hid husband given 465 years to pay back £28k she claimed in benefits
News.content:
Woman who hid husband given 465 years to pay back £28k she claimed in benefits

Lesleyann McLean has been given 500 years to repay nearly £28k in fraudulently obtained money from the DWP - it would take 465 years for her to pay it back

View 2 Images Lesleyann McLean has been given 500 years to repay £28k

A woman who pocketed nearly £28,000 after hiding her husband from the authorities has been given nearly 500 years to repay to stolen cash.

Lesleyann McLean, 44, didn't update the Department of Work and Pensions when she married her husband and kept her status a secret for three years. The woman, from Scone, outside of Perth, Scotland, admitted to stating she was single and lived alone on universal credit claim forms, when the truth was she was living with Barry McLean. She illegally claimed £27,908 between July 27, 2020, and November 4, 2023.

Perth Sheriff Court was told that the benefits agency is now taking the money back from McLean's benefits at a rate of £5 per month.

DWP to revoke driving licences over benefits debt for 2 years from October - 56 day rule READ MORE :

Fraudster who swindled £300K from grandma before fleeing to Tenerife is jailed READ MORE :

View 2 Images Lesleyann McLean did not tell the DWP she was living with her husband

At this rate, it would take the 44-year-old more than 465 years to pay back - and the debt will not be paid until McLean turns 510 years old, reports the Daily Record.

Sheriff William Wood placed McLean on a curfew for 12 months as a direct alternative to a prison sentence, after she admitted to failing to notify the DWP of a material change in her circumstances.

Sheriff Wood, in court, said: "What is beyond doubt is that fraud of this kind affects all of us because it means there is more money for you that you are not entitled to - and less for the other people who are entitled to it. It could be used for other services or things the Government provides. There was a change of circumstances you ought to have told them about and you ignored that."

Solicitor Kirsty Watson, defending, said her client was "not funding a lavish lifestyle" but had been using the fraudulently obtained cash to support her drug addict son's debts.

Watson told the court: "The claim was not fraudulent from the outset. She and her husband had separated. Once she made the universal credit claim the relationship resumed and she failed to notify DWP of that change.

"The money was not funding a lavish lifestyle. It was largely used for household bills and ordinary living expenses. Her husband was working full-time, but she was carrying a disproportionate share of the household expenditure.

"There was further pressure from her adult son, struggling with drug addiction and debts, and she was giving money to him that she simply could not afford.

"She is remorseful and recovery of the over-payment has commenced at £5 per month. That is modest and she accepts that. There was no sophistication, significant planning or abuse of trust involving others. I accept the duration of the offending is an aggravating factor.

Article continues below

"Against that is a completely clean record, remorse, significant health difficulties, financial pressure and domestic abuse. She is a first offender."

News.title: Should Brits be expected to work during heatwaves? Take our poll and have your say
News.content:
Should Brits be expected to work during heatwaves? Take our poll and have your say

The Climate Change Committee has urged the government to introduce maximum working temperature laws in the UK, as heatwave conditions grip Britain with temperatures set to soar

View 2 Images Should workers be expected to graft in scorching conditions? (Image: Getty Images)

With Britain bracing itself for potentially sweltering temperatures of up to 38C, the question on everyone's lips is - should workers be expected to graft in scorching conditions?

‌



It's no secret that hot weather can leave you feeling exhausted, dehydrated and lethargic, meaning productivity could take a serious hit, yet there is currently no maximum temperature threshold for workers.

‌



The Met Office warns that the soaring temperatures are a stark indicator of just how swiftly our climate is shifting, while The Climate Change Committee has cautioned that the UK was "built for a climate that no longer exists". It is now urging the government to introduce maximum temperature legislation to protect workers' wellbeing.

‌



Rare amber “extreme heat” warnings have been issued by the Met Office for London and parts of the South East, East Midlands, East of England, West Midlands and South Yorkshire from 9am to midnight on Thursday. The scorching highs are expected after Prime Minister Andy Burnham chaired a meeting of the Government’s emergency Cobra committee on Wednesday in response to the prolonged spell of exceptionally hot and dry weather.

Do you think there should be tighter regulations around working in a heatwave? Take our poll and let us know!

‌



The UK is currently experiencing its fifth heatwave of the year and the CCC has previously called on the government to roll out air conditioning and other cooling technologies in schools and hospitals, arguing it should be among the top priorities.

"It's a very sensible thing to do because we know that productivity drops very significantly when the weather gets very hot and we know that people become more prone to making mistakes and to having accidents," said Baroness Brown, chair of the CCC's Adaptation Committee. "It's not rocket science - we know what to do but we haven't yet seen a government that's prepared to prioritise adapting to the change of climate, protecting the people and the places that we love."

She lambasted the "woeful" track record of successive governments in tackling the present and future risks the UK faces from climate change.

‌



She added: "We need to recognise that there are aspects of our British way of life which are now really under threat from climate."

View 2 Images A worker cools off with water in a construction site (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The government stated it would thoroughly examine and respond to the committee's guidance. The CCC stops short of recommending a maximum temperature but draws attention to Spain's example, where the highest permitted indoor working temperature stands at 27C for sedentary work and 25C for light physical work.

‌



Labour Party Environment Secretary Emma Reynolds said: "We are acting to protect people and places from the impacts of climate change that are already being felt across the UK - from flooding to extreme heat and drought.

"Robust, independent science is essential and we will carefully consider the Climate Change Committee's latest recommendations to drive further action."

This comes on the heels of a report by the Autonomy Institute, which found that two-thirds of the UK workforce could be toiling in heatwaves surpassing 35C before the end of the decade. The organisation points out that despite a string of record-breaking summers, there is still no legislation or official guidance on a maximum working temperature.

‌



It estimates that roughly six million workers — particularly those in construction, agriculture and logistics — are already being exposed to dangerously high levels of heat.

It recommends that ministers set a threshold of 27C as the maximum acceptable working temperature for employees. This is in line with guidance from the Trades Union Congress (TUC) for those undertaking "strenuous work".

The TUC has previously called for a maximum temperature of 30C in indoor working environments, while urging employers to make every effort to reduce temperatures should they climb above 24C.

Article continues below

Autonomy also contends that workers should have a legal right to down tools during periods of extreme heat, alongside provisions for shelter and rest breaks for all staff.

TUC general secretary Paul Nowak said: "Everyone deserves to be safe and comfortable at work. Setting a legal limit is a simple, common-sense step to protect people from dangerous conditions – especially as extreme temperatures become more frequent. It's time the law caught up."

The Health and Safety Executive's website notes: "There's no law for maximum working temperature, or when it's too hot to work, because every workplace is different. No meaningful upper limit can be imposed because in many indoor workplaces high temperatures are not seasonal but created by work activity, for example in bakeries or foundries."

News.title: Saddleworth Moor fire: Emergency crews battle moorland blaze as road closed
News.content:
The blaze has broken out at Saddleworth Moor in Greater Manchester

Residents have been told to avoid Saddleworth Moor in Greater Manchester as fire crews have been tackling the huge fire which has broken out overnight

Firefighters are tackling a massive blaze in Greater Manchester which has engulfed a huge area of moorland.

In a statement issued on Thursday, a spokesperson for Greater Manchester Fire and Rescue Service confirmed: "Our crews have been tackling a moorland fire near Holmfirth Road in Oldham through the night. Please avoid the area while emergency services respond to the incident."

The blaze at Saddleworth Moor comes after wildfires have ravaged Greater Manchester and sections of the UK over the summer. Major blazes erupted at Dovestone and Tintwistle earlier this summer, with the fires damaging nearly 1,000 acres of land.

News.title: First chocolate bar made from entirely British-grown ingredients since 1932
News.content:
First chocolate bar made from entirely British-grown ingredients since 1932

A student has created the second ever 100% British chocolate bar but only a handful have been made - Maha Khan revealed how and why she set out on the challenge

View 5 Images Maha Khan created a 100% British chocolate bar (Image: University of Reading / SWNS)

The first chocolate bar made entirely with 100% British ingredients for the first time in nearly 100 years has been created.

‌



A student from the University of Reading has crafted the sweet treat with cocoa from Berkshire and not from Ghana or Ecuador. The only other 100% British chocolate bar to be created was back in 1932 - and it was gifted to the then six-year-old Princess Elizabeth – who later became Queen Elizabeth II.

‌



This time around Maha Khan, a food security master's student, incredibly used sugar, milk and cocoa all grown in the UK for her creation.

‌



Super El Nino enters 'historic' second phase as UK weather dealt massive setback READ MORE :

View 5 Images Only six bars have been produced (Image: University of Reading / SWNS)

Maha said: "It has been amazing to follow the entire chocolate-making process, from pod to bean to bar, without leaving Reading."

The student described the chocolate as "delicious", adding: "It's incredible to taste the complexity of the flavour profiles as the cocoa is made from plants originating from over 300 varieties grown here."

‌



View 5 Images Maha created the chocolate at the University of Reading (Image: University of Reading / SWNS)

The British-grown cocoa was cultivated at the University of Reading's International Cocoa Quarantine Centre – a collection of more than 300 varieties of cocoa plant, which handles 97% of the world's international movement of cocoa plants.

The climate-controlled facility in Berkshire is carefully managed to prevent the spread of pests and diseases between different cocoa-growing regions of the world. Cocoa pods from the centre's collection are usually discarded unused, but this time were harvested as the source of beans for the new chocolate bar.

‌



View 5 Images Maha used cocoa grown in Reading (Image: University of Reading / SWNS)

The first stage involves cracking open the pods and extracting the beans, fermenting them, before they are laid out and dried in the sun, and subsequently roasted.

Maha then crushed and ground the beans to a consistent cocoa powder then combined it with British-grown sugar and milk to produce a chocolate mixture. This was then heated, shaped and formed into a ready-to-eat, entirely British chocolate bar.

‌



The student said: "It has been amazing to follow the entire chocolate-making process, from pod to bean to bar, without leaving Reading."

View 5 Images Maha pouring out the chocolate into the mould (Image: University of Reading / SWNS)

Confectionary giant Rowntrees created the 1932 British chocolate bar but Maha revealed she set out to create this bar to shed light on the impact of the climate crisis on cocoa plants.

‌



The student said: "This British bar of chocolate highlights the precarious nature of our food supplies. Cocoa plants are very sensitive to changes in temperature and rainfall, and climate change is already causing problems in countries that produce most of the world's cocoa.

"Protecting different varieties is vital if farmers need hardier plants that can cope with a changing climate. I hope this shows people just how much work goes into the chocolate we enjoy, and how important it is to protect cocoa farmers and communities around the world."

While the UK's chocolate market is valued at £10.4 billion, it is entirely dependent on imported cocoa, underlining the significance of internationally traded food to global farmers, UK consumers and the wider economy.

Article continues below

Only six limited edition bars have been made so far, but Maha hopes to make more. Rowntree's sole previous bar of UK-grown chocolate was crafted from a glasshouse-grown cocoa plant at the Rowntree headquarters in York.

Professor Carol Wagstaff, director of AgriFood Futures at the University of Reading, said: "The UK chocolate industry rests on a supply chain that starts thousands of miles away in the tropics of Africa, South America and Asia.

"A resilient global market is crucial to the many smallholder farmers who underpin the industry and find themselves farming in some of the regions most exposed to risks from climate change, as well as to chocolate makers and chocolate lovers in the UK."

News.title: Benidorm holidaymaker films crowd queuing for 90 minutes before sunbed surge
News.content:
Benidorm holidaymaker films crowd queuing for 90 minutes before sunbed surge

Hayley Newland says after the crowd settled down, she was easily able to walk up to the pool and find a bed with no wait

Benidorm holiday films huge crowd queuing for 90 minutes before sunbed surge

A British holidaymaker has captured the moment hundreds of guests queued from 7.30am before racing for sunbeds when a hotel pool opened in Benidorm. Teaching assistant Hayley Newland, 39, from Brighton, was staying with her family at a hotel when she witnessed the scramble.

‌



Hayley said she had never experienced anything like it, despite being familiar with the infamous holiday sunbed rush. The footage shows a large crowd waiting behind a barrier before security guards open the pool area at 9am.

‌



As soon as the barrier lifts, guests stream through in a bid to claim their spot. Hayley said the same thing happened every morning during her 10-day stay, with some holidaymakers beginning to queue as early as 7.30am. She said: “It was madness, I have never experienced anything like this before. I would watch this all happening from the breakfast hall."

‌



View Image Hayley Newland

Article continues below

Despite the dramatic scenes, Hayley said the rush was ultimately unnecessary – as she had no trouble finding sunbeds once the crowds had dispersed. She said: “Once the chaos was over, I would go and find some beds for my family with no problem.”

She described it as “chaos for no reason”, but admitted it was also entertaining to watch. The footage is likely to reignite the debate among holidaymakers over whether it is ever worth getting up at the crack of dawn to bag a sunbed.

News.title: 'I dismissed cancer symptoms like Lucy Davis and thought I was too young'
News.content:
'I dismissed cancer symptoms like Lucy Davis and thought I was too young'

Alex Cheshire-Round, 29, was pregnant when she noticed something

View 4 Images Alex Cheshire-Round in hospital (Image: Alex Cheshire-Round/SWNS)

A mum who initially dismissed her breast cancer symptoms, like The Office star Lucy Davis, has urged women to get checked.

‌



Alex Cheshire-Round, 29, was expecting her second child when she noticed a hardness in her right breast when she rolled over in bed in May. She thought her hard breast tissue at 24 weeks was a sign her milk was coming in early - but it turned out to be breast cancer.

‌



She started leaking milk at 18 weeks pregnant with her firstborn, Ronnie, now 10 months old, so she thought it was happening again. But her husband, Tom Cheshire-Round, 31, urged her to have it checked out and a biopsy and scans revealed she had stage two breast cancer.

‌



Alex had a 5cm lump cut away from her breast and lymph nodes taken from under her right arm on July 14 at University Hospital Coventry. Five minutes after she woke from the operation, her baby was distressed.

Alex was put under again and her daughter, Lexi, was born at 1.57pm, weighing 4lb 13oz at 33 weeks. Both Alex and her baby are now safely home after the birth, but Alex is waiting to see what further treatment she will need for the cancer. She thinks chemotherapy is likely.

View 4 Images Alex Cheshire-Round with her daughter Lexi (Image: Alex Cheshire-Round/SWNS)

‌



Lucy Davis, who played receptionist Dawn Tinsley in The Office, revealed her terminal cancer diagnosis earlier this week after nearly missing a small lump that felt like a "hard spot".

Alex, from Nuneaton, who works in sales, said: "It was very scary and it was a huge shock. I just shrugged it off at first - you go through so many changes when you're pregnant.

"It's so rare for someone my age to get breast cancer. I just thought it must be something to do with pregnancy and hormonal changes.

‌



"My milk came in early in my pregnancy with Ronnie, I reassured myself it was just that happening again. I got really worried when my GP said they don't give mammograms for under-40s, but then offered me one after inspecting it.

"We're lucky we decided to have our children close in age, because the treatment might affect my fertility. Women feel insecure enough about our looks after having a baby, this is much worse for me now, as I'm also worrying about hair loss and being tired from chemotherapy."

View 4 Images Lucy Davis has shared the 'really tiny' cancer symptom she almost ignored (Image: Noam Galai/Getty Images for New York Comic Con)

‌



Last week, Alex, who spoke to Talk to the Press, went for an MRI and further full body scans now she is no longer pregnant. Lucy Davis recently found out she has been diagnosed with "incurable" stage four breast cancer.

In response to the news she said on Instagram: "As of now, I'm trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can. The initial lump that I felt, wasn’t a ‘lump’ as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny.

“I almost didn’t bother getting it checked. So I guess I’m saying don’t ignore anything – get everything checked out.”

‌



Like Lucy, Alex explained that she does not let herself get “depressed” about her diagnosis.

Alex said: “I never thought I’d have to say that I am praying that it is curable cancer. If it is stage four cancer I will be on treatment until it basically kills me, it will depend on how effective the treatment is.

View 4 Images Tom Cheshire-Round with his daughter Lexi (Image: Alex Cheshire-Round/SWNS)

Article continues below

“I am awaiting the results of all the tests now. I have two little babies and in a way that is good because I have to get on with it, I can’t sit and be depressed, I have to get up.

“It is scary to know that my son’s first birthday is next month and I am thinking to myself will I be there for the next one. Accidents and tragedies happen all the time around us and you do not know if you are going to make it to the following day anyway, you can't look at it and feel sorry for yourself because you won't be able to get out of bed."

News.title: Met chief accepts mistakes made over Simon Levy but defends investigation into murders
News.content:
The head of the Metropolitan Police has defended the force's investigation into double murderer Simon Levy, saying public debate needed to be "better informed".

Sir Mark Rowley acknowledged mistakes over the force's handling of Levy, but said suggestions it had not tried to build a case over his first murder were "just not true", following criticism including from Labour MP Jess Phillips.

He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that detectives had done "serious" work but "didn't have enough evidence" for a charge.

Levy was on bail and being monitored by police when he murdered Carmenza Valencia-Trujillo in March 2025 and Sheryl Wilkins five months later, as well as violently raping a third woman.

The police and Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) has apologised over a series of decisions that left the convicted sex offender free to attack the women.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) is currently examining how Levy, 40, was managed over the four-year period from his first conviction in September 2021 for sexual assault up to his final arrest in September 2025.

At the Old Bailey on Wednesday, he was given a whole life prison sentence, meaning he will never be released.

Timeline of Simon Levy's crimes, external

Speaking on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, Sir Mark - who on Wednesday called the case a "whole system failing" - said he had already apologised for what the Met had got wrong.

It emerged after Levy's conviction that the Met did not class Valencia-Trujillo's death in March 2025 as a murder, or pass the case to specialist homicide detectives, until after he had killed again.

But Sir Mark said "the public debate needs to be better informed" because "the facts on that are much more complex than people want to acknowledge".

He said that while Valencia-Trujillo's death was "clearly very suspicious and concerning", a pathologist was unable to determine a cause of death and the force "didn't have enough evidence to get to a charge".

Sir Mark added it was only after the murder of Wilkins that the Met had the "combined evidence" to move forward.

"So the inference that the Met didn't try on that case is just not true, the Met tried," he said.

Sir Mark acknowledged mistakes were made in the management of the case. He said the force was "too slow" to act when it waited five months to question Levy over the sexual assault of a female prison officer in HMP Brixton in April 2022.

He also said it was a mistake to downgrade Levy from a high-risk sex offender to a medium one in August 2024, meaning a lower level of monitoring and contact was required.

"Those are mistakes and those are our mistakes, that is part of what is being investigated and that is part of what we've apologised for," he said.

But the Met chief also emphasised failures by other government agencies: "[Levy] was released on licence by the prison service having sexually assaulted in prison one its people. I don't understand that decision either."

"We take our accountability seriously, the rest of the system is not doing that," he said.

News.title: Once-in-a-generation solar eclipse wows millions in UK and Europe
News.content:
The UK and Europe have enjoyed their most dramatic solar eclipse for nearly 30 years, with millions thought to have witnessed the once-in-a-generation event.

Those watching the astronomical phenomenon from the UK were treated to a partial eclipse, which peaked shortly after 19:00 BST, when most saw more than 90% of the Sun covered by the Moon.

But parts of Greenland, Iceland and Spain experienced the complete darkness and spectacle of a total eclipse.

Large crowds at viewing sites across the UK and Europe reacted with gasps and cheers, with astronomy enthusiasts saying it served as a reminder of how "amazing" the Universe is.

News.title: Watch: Moment 'surreal' solar eclipse witnessed in UK and Europe
News.content:
Millions of people across Europe and the UK witnessed the most significant solar eclipse since 1999 on Wednesday.

For the UK, more than 90% of the Sun was covered by the Moon, whereas in some parts of Europe, a rare total eclipse could be seen.

BBC science correspondent Pallab Ghosh was in Burgos, Spain, and said he got goosebumps from the spectacle.

News.title: UK defends seizing shadow fleet tanker after Putin threat
News.content:
The UK government has defended its seizure of a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel, after Russian President Vladimir Putin threatened to "respond in kind".

The Smyrtos was taken to be anchored off Weymouth after Royal Marines Commandos intercepted and boarded it in a first-of-its-kind operation to disrupt the sanctioned tanker in June.

The vessel's captain, Ajay Pant, has been charged with breaching Russian sanctions, accused of directly or indirectly supplying or delivering prohibited Russian oil.

Overseeing Russian navy drills in the Pacific Ocean, Putin scolded Western countries for "seizing our vessels", branding such action "nothing other than piracy and banditry".

"If these plans are put into practice, we will have to respond in kind," Putin warned on Wednesday.

"And not necessarily in the waters where raids on our ships and vessels are planned, but wherever we deem it necessary and appropriate, anywhere."

Viktor Liina, commander of Russia's Pacific Fleet, accused Western countries such as Britain and France of operating their own "shadow fleets".

"We have the capacity to inspect and detain vessels of unfriendly states and their shadow fleets, and interagency cooperation is in place, ready to begin addressing these challenges," Liina said.

In response to Putin's comments, the UK government said Britain's armed forces and law-enforcement officers had boarded the Smyrtos "in full accordance with international law".

"The UK is disrupting and deterring shadow fleet vessels and their harmful maritime activity which is fuelling Russia's war with Ukraine," a government spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said unlike Russia's shadow fleet, "UK armed forces and commercial vessels operate firmly in line with international maritime law".

News.title: UK economy grows but experts warn of challenging months ahead
News.content:
Summer sun and sports fixtures helped the UK economy grow between April and June, according to official data, but some economists warned the outlook for the rest of the year was weaker.

The economy expanded by 0.4%, in line with market expectations but below a 0.6% increase in the first three months of this year.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said growth had "remained relatively robust", with the UK ahead of other G7 countries for growth this year so far.

Experts questioned whether this resilience would be maintained, however, given growth was fuelled by some temporary factors and energy prices could remain volatile if the Middle East conflict continues.

The British economy is now 1.2% bigger than a year ago, the ONS said, despite fears that the Iran war, which started at the end of February, and politically uncertainty around Sir Keir Starmer's resignation as prime minister would hold back growth.

Between April and June, sectors including computer programming, advertising and the pharmaceutical industry lifted growth. That was offset by falls in power generation and sewerage.

The ONS said some businesses reported that "good weather and sporting events may have had a positive effect" in June, boosting month-on-month growth to 0.3%.

The men's football World Cup, which kicked off mid-June, increased customers at hospitality venues showing the matches.

June also saw several of summer's heatwaves. However, May's growth was revised down from 0.1% to zero growth.

News.title: Leading doctor rebukes NHS chiefs over transplant failings
News.content:
While NHS Blood and Transplant manages organ donations and supports transplant centres, services are commissioned and paid for by NHS England.

But in a letter to NHS England and a small group of patient advocates, Manas said the central body had created a "fragmented" system "with poor accountability".

There is a "mismatch", he said, between each hospital's waiting lists, organ availability, capacity to carry out surgeries and the availability of operating theatres.

This is "leading to last-minute cancellations [and] unpredictable utilisation of donated organs," he warned.

The BBC reported in March that the UK, once a world leader, had fallen behind major Western nations in heart and lung transplantation, though it fares better in other areas such as kidney transplantation.

The NHS transplants one in 10 lungs and one in seven hearts that are donated - half the proportions seen in some other countries.

It has not invested in modern technology at the same rate as other countries, and suffers from a lack of theatre space, intensive care beds and staff.

Wales and Northern Ireland do not have a heart and lung transplant centre, so patients commonly travel to England for surgery. There is one heart transplant centre in Scotland.

News.title: Trump says White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt to leave post
News.content:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt will step down from her position at the end of the month, President Donald Trump has announced.

Leavitt, whom the president called one of his "most trusted aides", will depart from her role to spend time with her young children and family - "a decision I totally understand and respect", Trump wrote in a social media post.

"Karoline will now be one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party," he added.

Leavitt, 28, took the job as White House Press Secretary last year - becoming the youngest person to ever have the role. It was not immediately clear who will replace her.

News.title: Polls open in Clacton by-election
News.content:
The polls have opened in Clacton-on-Sea as a record number of candidates vie to become the town's next MP.

An electorate of 79,785 registered voters have the chance to vote for one of 34 candidates standing in the Essex resort - the most ever to stand in a British election.

Fifty-one polling stations have opened, covering Clacton and the surrounding towns of Jaywick, Frinton and Walton-on-the-Naze. The constituency also has rural villages including St Osyth, Weeley and Great Bentley.

Voters will need to show a form of acceptable ID - such as a driving licence or passport - to be able to cast their ballot.

They will receive the longest ballot paper in British electoral history at 90cm - about 3ft long - to choose their candidate and cast their vote.

There are 12 political parties and 20 independents standing.

Polling stations will remain open to anyone registered to vote until 22:00, with the count taking place overnight.

News.title: Man dies days after explosion at bungalow
News.content:
A man has died in hospital days after a suspected gas explosion at a bungalow.

The explosion, which happened at 09:45 BST on Sunday, destroyed the home in Cobb Hall Road in Newton Longville, a village near Milton Keynes.

Thames Valley Police said a man in his 60s was taken to hospital where he was receiving treatment for his injuries. His death was announced on Thursday.

Det Insp Philip Turner-Robson said: "This is a tragic development and our thoughts are with the man's family and friends at this extremely difficult time."

He added: "Thames Valley Police is managing a coronial investigation into the circumstances surrounding the explosion and collapse of the property, working jointly with the Health and Safety Executive.

"Our inquiries remain ongoing as we seek to establish the full circumstances of what happened."

Witnesses in the village described how the blast sounded like "a bomb just dropped in the village".

The gas distribution firm SGN said an engineer arrived within 16 minutes of receiving a call from a member of public just after midnight on Sunday.

A company spokesperson said it had been "advised by the HSE that they are no longer looking at our physical network as part of their investigation. The gas network remains safe and secure".

The added: "We're also continuing to work alongside the local authority to support the local community."

News.title: I lost my lovely home to road scheme that got shelved
News.content:
Roberts moved into her four-bedroom house in 2011 and spent two years renovating the property with her husband.

In 2012, the couple first heard about the A38 proposals and were given a compulsory purchase order in 2021.

Many of her neighbours accepted it and moved out, leaving her "stuck in a lovely house in a derelict street".

She said the two-year dispute over the value of the house was "absolutely infuriating", with Roberts eventually accepting Â£40,000 less than an independent valuation she had been given.

"I've lost so many years of my life to this, to the point where I was in hospital," she said.

Roberts has multiple sclerosis and collapsed in January 2023, temporarily losing the use of her legs. She said two neurologists linked her decline in health to stress.

"I think on the surface I handled it well, but clearly underneath, it was there constantly," she said.

In autumn 2023, Roberts and her husband temporarily moved into a bungalow in Ockbrook, Derbyshire, where they continue to search for a new home.

In late June 2026, the A38 project was put on hold in order to fund new defence plans.

Roberts told the BBC she was "appalled but not surprised" by the decision.

"I always had an inkling that it wouldn't actually go through, because the public consultations have gone on and on and on," she said.

"I think the indecision is disgusting. How long can it go on like this?"

Roberts said it had been "painful" to see her old home boarded-up for the past three years, and for months she "diverted halfway around Derby" to avoid passing by it.

"Those are all unique, individually, architecturally designed houses, and they're empty," she said.

"There's so many homeless people. If they're going to leave them alone, why don't they do something with them?"

The Stop the A38 Expansion Group has called for the properties to be restored and returned to use should the scheme be officially scrapped.

Roberts said she would continue to search for a home suited to her disability needs, but recognised she had probably lived in the "best house" she would ever live in - on Queensway.

National Highways said the potential cancellation of the A38 scheme remained under consultation.

It added no final decision had yet been made and an update would be shared in due course.

News.title: Streets evacuated after massive fire destroys homes
News.content:
Homes have been destroyed and 20 people had to spent the night in a leisure centre after a massive fire in south Wales.

There are no reports of casualties, but six bungalows were evacuated near Hazelwood Road, Newbridge, in Caerphilly county, on Wednesday.

"The houses were absolutely gutted. Their cars were damaged too," said councillor Adrian Hussey.

He said residents tried to put the fire out but could not because it was so severe.

It is still not clear how the fire started, but First Minister Rhun ap Iorwerth said fire services in Wales were "at full stretch" due the heatwave and wildfires this summer.

News.title: First 100% British chocolate bar made since 1932
News.content:
A chocolate bar has been made using entirely British ingredients for the first time in nearly a century, with cocoa from not Brazil or Bali, but Berkshire.

Created at the University of Reading, it was named the Reading 100 Chocolate Bar to mark the university's 100th anniversary.

It is the first of its kind since 1932, when Rowntree's gifted a six-year-old Princess Elizabeth the only other bar of UK-grown chocolate ever made.

Food security master's student Maha Khan created the chocolate bar by harvesting, fermenting and processing the Reading-grown cocoa.

While the UK's chocolate market is worth Â£10.4bn, it is entirely reliant on imported cocoa.

Maha told the Today programme she made the bar to highlight the challenges facing the cocoa growing industry.

She said: "It is incredible that we can make 100% British chocolate â but in the context of climate change, pests and diseases, there are estimates that 30 to 40% is lost.

"And we've seen with these heatwaves, climate change, these problems and challenges are only going to get exacerbated."

News.title: Arrest in Thetford migrant address sharing investigation
News.content:
Police have arrested a man as part of an inquiry into how the addresses of asylum seekers were shared during disorder linked to anti-immigration protests in a town, the BBC can reveal.

Properties in St John's Way, Bracken Road, Clover Way, Elm Road and Chester Way in Thetford, Norfolk, were recently targeted by crowds over three nights.

The man, in his 60s, was arrested on Friday on suspicion of assisting an offender and inciting racial hatred and has been released on bail until 14 October.

The houses are believed to have been used by Serco, a firm contracted to accommodate migrants, which said it was investigating allegations "relating to how address information has been made public".

The firm added it was working with the Home Office and Norfolk Police "to ensure that appropriate safeguarding measures are in place".

After his arrest, the man in his 60s was taken to Wymondham Police Investigation Centre for questioning.

News.title: Scottish Labour leader hopefuls warn against party divisions
News.content:
Scottish Labour leadership contenders have warned about the dangers of internal feuds and briefings at their first party hustings in Glasgow.

Monica Lennon, Joe Fagan and Michael Marra made their cases to succeed Anas Sarwar as they pitched to rebuild Scottish Labour after May's crushing electoral defeat.

Those attending the hour-long event were met by a handful of pro-Palestine protesters, whose shouts were heard during the first part of the event.

All three candidates promised to change, rebuild and unite the party following its worst Holyrood election defeat since devolution.

News.title: 'Online trolls who target me are bored and jealous'
News.content:
A woman who posts food reviews on social media has spoken out against the level of online abuse she receives after some trolls have urged her to take her own life.

Gloucestershire's Becca Stock, who has millions of followers on TikTok, said while "bored" and "jealous" people do target her online, they are in the minority.

She has shared her experience of online bullying following the University of Gloucestershire publishing new research into what drives digital abuse.

Dr Amy Grubb, associate professor of forensic psychology at the University, said posting comments online creates the "perfect storm" for abuse as the "digital environments reduce normal social restraints".

The research comes as mental health charities are reporting that online harms are having a growing impact on young people's wellbeing.

News.title: GB's Hudson-Smith wins historic 400m gold on home track
News.content:
On his childhood track, in front of a stand named in his honour, hometown hero Matthew Hudson-Smith was not going to be denied.

A full-circle moment, completed by writing his name in history.

More than two decades after stepping foot inside Alexander Stadium for the first time aged nine, Hudson-Smith delivered Great Britain's latest gold in Birmingham to become the joint-most decorated man of all-time at European Championships.

The 31-year-old celebrated the third European 400m title of his illustrious career by making his way into the crowd and placing a hand on the banner bearing his name.

Moments before, Hudson-Smith had stormed down the home straight, just as he had countless times before as a member of local club Birchfield Harriers.

This time, though, the Olympic and world silver medallist did so to rapturous cheers inside the arena which fostered his love for the sport.

With his eighth podium at the championships, Hudson-Smith equalled French sprinter Christophe Lemaitre's men's record medal tally - with the relays still to come.

"Honestly, words can't describe how much that meant to me," he told BBC Sport.

"Nobody was going to beat me on this track. This is my home. I know this track like the back of my hand. I have my stand. Now I'm going to go for Mayor of Birmingham and Wolverhampton!

"I knew I was the best in the world. I knew that, on paper, I was a second faster than every single one of these guys. It was about me and the clock."

The fate of Barbie 2 seems more uncertain than ever, as new reports claim that the film’s cast has rejected Warner Bros’ “highest offer ever”, despite director Greta Gerwig allegedly having an idea for a sequel.

Warner Bros is said to be racing against the clock to secure a deal for Barbie 2. If the studio does not reach an agreement with talent by December, the rights will reportedly revert to toy manufacturer Mattel.

Insiders claim that, if the deal isn’t sorted, Mattel will have to reboot the franchise with a film unlinked to Gerwig’s 2023 blockbuster. The film starring (and co-produced by) Margot Robbie, with Ryan Gosling as Ken, was a huge hit, earning rave reviews and making an eye-watering $1.448bn (£1.072bn) at the global box office.

open image in gallery Six rounds of offers from Warner Bros have allegedly been rejected ( Warner Bros Pictures )

While suggestions of a sequel were shut down by Gerwig and the cast at the time, recent reports have claimed that Robbie, Gosling, Gerwig, and her co-writer husband Noah Baumbach, are now in talks about bringing the characters back in another film.

According to a new report by Variety, discussions are said to have stalled as CEO David Zaslav is reportedly unwilling to pay the salaries negotiated for the core team, which is reportedly the highest amount Warner Bros has ever offered for a creative team and lead actors.

However, a different insider disputed this, saying that the individual compensation is not as “historic” as the combined figure.

It’s been claimed that Gerwig and Baumbach have an idea for a sequel, but have rejected each of the six offers made to the core team of four over the past three years.

The report suggests that what’s on the table does not compare to the “considerable” financial asks from Robbie, Gosling, who is reportedly asking for $20m (£14.8m), Gerwig and Baumbach, which are said to have considerably increased from the original film.

open image in gallery The cast and creative team behind 'Barbie' ( Getty )

The Independent has contacted Warner Bros for comment.

Upon its release, Barbie became a cultural phenomenon, with fans rocking up to the cinema in pink and cinema-goers urged to turn the experience into an unexpected double feature with Christopher Nolan’s Oppenheimer, a cultural phenomenon dubbed “Barbenheimer”.

News.title: Who is supporting Gianni Infantino? Every country’s stance on Fifa president crisis
News.content:
