World.title: Egypt calls for more responsive global financial system for emerging economies
World.content:
Finance Minister Ahmed Kouchouk on Wednesday, August 12, 2026, called for a more responsive global financial system that better addresses the growth and development priorities of emerging economies.

Kouchouk also urged a greater role for multilateral development banks in providing low-cost financing to help developing countries manage risks.

Speaking at a meeting of BRICS finance ministers and central bank governors in India, Kouchouk said strengthening the resilience and innovation capacity of developing economies would advance inclusive and sustainable development.

He also called for developing countries to have a stronger voice in shaping a fairer and more inclusive international financial architecture.

Kouchouk urged the integration of digital systems and artificial intelligence into structural reforms to develop human capital, boost productivity and enhance competitiveness, while calling for stronger trade and investment ties among Global South countries to mitigate economic and geopolitical volatility.

World.title: Egypt, Venezuela discuss expanding air connectivity, tourism cooperation
World.content:
Civil Aviation Minister Sameh al-Hefny affirmed Egypt’s readiness to support Venezuelan airlines, in line with applicable regulations, to facilitate their operations and expand air services between the two countries, boosting travel, tourism and trade.

During a meeting with Venezuelan Ambassador in Cairo Wilmer Omar Barrientos, the two sides discussed cooperation in civil aviation and the latest developments on a draft air transport agreement between Egypt and Venezuela.

The agreement is expected to establish a regulatory framework to support air traffic growth and strengthen air connectivity between the two countries.

Barrientos said Venezuela plans to promote tourism and deepen ties with Middle East countries, stressing the importance of expanding air transport links with Egypt and open new avenues for cooperation.

World.title: Colombia limits foreign rescue teams as earthquake survival window narrows
World.content:
Colombia has begun receiving international aid and rescuers after initially refusing some offers in the crucial hours following Monday’s devastating earthquake.

The delay is considered the first controversy of the country’s new government, led by conservative President Abelardo de la Espriella, who took office on Friday.

News of the holdup comes as the clock nears the end of the critical 72-hour window for rescuing survivors under the rubble of collapsed buildings, after which rescuers warn that the possibility of finding anyone alive drops dramatically.

Leaders across the Americas had offered support right after the 7.4 magnitude quake struck this week – just as they had done with Venezuela when it was hit by two powerful tremors in June. The difference is that Venezuela immediately received dozens of international rescue groups without question, while Colombia either turned some of them down or limited how they would help.

Political scientist Sandra Borda argued that the difficulties in aid management are related to the tense political transition between the current and previous administrations, which lacked a formal handover. Notably, it was only on Wednesday that David Tamayo Roldán was appointed director of the National Unit for Disaster Risk Management, the agency responsible for Colombia’s disaster preparedness and response.

“Without a transition and with that kind of personnel change, it was perfectly normal for these short circuits to occur,” said Borda, a professor at Universidad de los Andes.

The outlook on Tuesday was uncertain as multiple countries and organizations, including the UN, said they had not received a request for aid from Colombian authorities.

“If that happens, the United Nations system and humanitarian actors are prepared to provide all the support we can,” said Jens Laerke, spokesperson for the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

Mexico, which had prepared tons of supplies and a contingent of 255 military personnel, also it had not received a request from Colombia and that the deployment depended on it.

Meanwhile, Chinese ambassador to Colombia Zhu Jingyang “urgently” asked Colombia to establish an official channel to coordinate international assistance, saying, “We hope the Colombian Government will immediately announce the name of the official and their contact to coordinate international assistance for the earthquake victims.”

As the hours passed, coordination finally began.

A Mexican rescue worker searches through the rubble two days after an earthquake struck Cali, Colombia, on August 12. Santiago Saldarriaga/AP

Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele announced Tuesday afternoon that he was sending humanitarian aid to Colombia but noted that de la Espriella’s government requested aid “only in the form of supplies” for those affected.

“We have been informed that their rescue teams, medical personnel, and other emergency bodies are deployed and attending to the situation, so at this time, they do not require personnel support,” he said.

However, Peru confirmed Wednesday that it will dispatch volunteers to support search and rescue efforts.

The Colombian Foreign Ministry later said it was preparing a list of “specific needs” to request international aid and that it had asked the United Nations Development Programme to provide support.

The new head of disaster management also said Wednesday that the government has requested rescue teams from only four countries – the US, El Salvador, Ecuador and Israel – because, in Colombia’s view, their rescue teams have the international and national certifications required for the job.

Foreign Minister Omar Bula insisted that the country has “not excluded absolutely any country in terms of the offers that have been made to us,” adding, “We work with countries without any ideological or political consideration.”

The US confirmed Wednesday that had mobilized search and rescue teams from Virginia and California to Colombia after receiving a request from its government.

Borda commented that the new government showed “a deep distrust of some parts of the international community,” which she considered “difficult to understand.”

She added that there was “no clarity about the procedure that was to be followed” regarding the arrival of rescuers, saying, “I think this happened to us at a very difficult time. It is truly a regrettable situation.”

She also said that the subsequent acceptance of the arrival of experts undermined the argument that they were not needed.

“There was a perception from the beginning that the rescue teams would be sufficient, although a technical assessment was never made public to confirm that they would indeed be enough to deal with all the damage and destruction caused by the earthquake,” she said.

In any case, it is also unclear where international personnel are needed. The emergency chief of the fire department in Cali, one of the most affected cities, indicated that volunteers should not approach collapsed sites “because there are already enough specialized personnel to carry out the rescue work without complications.”

The Topos Tlatelolco Rescue Brigade, a Mexican group with extensive experience responding to natural disasters, said Wednesday that Colombian authorities “will not allow the entry of external rescue groups” because the work is being handled by national rescuers.

Meanwhile, in Pereira, another severely affected city, the foreign ministry celebrated the arrival of 19.5 tons of aid from Mexico.

“Additional flights are expected in the coming days. Colombia is not alone! The international community is with us,” the ministry said on X.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum confirmed that her government had finally coordinated with its Colombian counterparts, who “requested specific items” and that the flight also included “members of the Mexican Army to assist in the efforts.”

World.title: Lebanon’s president seeks to allay concerns over negotiations with Israel
World.content:
Lebanon’s president has sought to allay concerns over the negotiations between his country and Israel, following a seventh round of heated talks in Rome.

President Joseph Aoun said in a post on X that negotiators and he will not allow Israel to remain “on a single inch of our land, nor a single soldier of its army to stay on our soil,” re-stating Beirut’s central demand in the negotiations.

The seventh round of talks, held last week in Rome, ended without any apparent progress on expanding the number of “pilot zones” in Lebanon – small pockets of territory from which Israel withdraws its troops and hands over control to the Lebanese armed forces, on the understanding that the area will be kept free of Hezbollah militants.

An Israeli source told CNN on Monday that no date had been set for the next round of talks, but Lebanon’s president, in his post on X, re-stated his commitment to a negotiated solution.

“We always hear slogans saying that what is taken by force will only be recovered by force, but the facts on the ground have proven the falsehood of this saying,” he said.

World.title: Sell Ukraine 10% of US Patriots and ‘we will destroy all the Russians’ ballistic missiles,’ Zelensky tells CNN
World.content:
Kyiv — has only a tenth of the interceptor missiles it urgently needs from the United States to stop surging Russian ballistic missile attacks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told CNN in an interview, adding his days are spent in “millions” of phone calls, in opaque deal-making with allies for more. Ukraine has only a tenth of the interceptor missiles it urgently needs from the United States to stop surging Russian ballistic missile attacks, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky told CNN in an interview, adding his days are spent in “millions” of phone calls, in opaque deal-making with allies for more.

Russian ballistic attacks have risen fast in recent weeks, hitting the capital Kyiv particularly hard, as Moscow exploits Ukraine’s near-zero stocks of Patriot interceptor missiles. Zelensky said a tenth of the US current stockpile would be enough to stop all Russian ballistic missile attacks, but 5 percent would be enough to get Ukraine through the winter.

“This year we have two and a half times less interceptors than we had in 2025,” he said. “Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before.” July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022, according to the United Nations. “Each night you have attacks, and four or five times per month we have massive attacks … terrible nights. Very heroic, very resilient people really. But they (are) tired.”

He added that if the US “sell us 5 percent, we will go through the winter and save people’s lives. If they can sell us 10 percent, we will destroy all the Russians’ ballistic missiles. I have 1 percent.”

There is a global shortage of the missiles due to the US war with Iran, where the US and Gulf states used dozens to tackle Iranian missile and low-cost drone attacks. The shortage is costing Ukraine most acutely, where cities some nights appear defenseless to Moscow’s rocket assaults.

Zelensky gave a rare window into his personal efforts daily to secure more interceptors, that involved deal-making he preferred to keep private. “This is what I live each day: from one percent to five percent. I have some months, and million phone calls … I try to exchange something to missiles … I do some things which I can’t even share. It doesn’t mean that it’s outside of the law. But I can’t speak about it.”

Zelensky said there were still doubts about how President Donald Trump’s apparent commitment to letting Ukraine build its own Patriot interceptor missiles would come to fruition.

Trump, on the sidelines of the NATO Ankara summit, said he would permit Ukraine to get a license to manufacture the complex interceptors themselves, but days later said he was unsure of the idea. The manufacturers of the Patriot missile systems have sent officials to Kyiv to discuss the idea, but results remain elusive.

President Donald Trump speaks at a press conference during the 2026 NATO Leaders Summit at the Beştepe Presidential Compound on July 8, in Ankara, Turkey. Win McNamee/Getty Images/File

“I hope that I will get it,” Zelensky said. “I don’t have now 5 percent and I don’t have such an acceptance. And this is for me is a big challenge, one of the biggest I had from the very beginning of this war.”

Zelensky said he was beseeching the White House directly, through calls, messages and indirectly through allies, to boost their Patriot assistance. But he was otherwise reluctant to provide details on his recent interactions with the Trump administration.

He confirmed he held a phone call with Vice President JD Vance recently, but declined to detail, as reported by the Financial Times, whether Vance requested Ukraine stop attacks on a Russian oil port in the Black Sea that were harming US companies and risking a surge in global energy prices.

Kyiv has also presented new proposals for the Trump-led peace process that has appeared moribund in recent months. Zelensky declined to provide details but said: “We need more involvement of the American side to the peace plan. I’m thankful to the team of President Trump that they want to continue. (Russian President Vladimir) Putin doesn’t want to stop this war now and (there’s) not enough pressure on him now.”

He also rejected the idea of Ukraine conceding the remaining territory in the Donbass that Putin seeks to conquer, saying that security guarantees remained key for Kyiv.

“Russia begins to speak about this war, and they speak about territory. The key question is why he will not come again with 1 or 2 additional million soldiers after a big pause. Why he will not come again to occupy us?”

Zelensky added he agreed with some Western assessments that Putin may seek to escalate the war against NATO, possibly attacking the smaller NATO Baltic states.

“He doesn’t know how to end this war without big occupation or big victory for his society. It’s more simple to find some smaller country … for him, it will not be important if this country is in NATO or not in NATO. He wants quick victory, 100 percent sure that he will win, occupy or destroy or control.”

World.title: Trump keeps saying the US controls the Strait of Hormuz. Does it?
World.content:
Nearly half a year into the US-Iran war, global oil stockpiles are rapidly diminishing as traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively stalled and the two powers at the center of the hostilities argue about who controls the critical waterway.

US President Donald Trump has repeatedly insisted that the strait – through which oil flows from countries like Saudi Arabia and Iraq to the rest of the world – is under US control.

“They don’t have control. We have total control. We own it, and at some point, maybe they’ll do something, and then they get blown away,” Trump told reporters on Wednesday. “Right now, we’re in a very good position.” And earlier Wednesday, he claimed the US Navy had swept the strait for mines.

But Iran says it won’t reopen the strait fully until the US meets its conditions.

The reality is far more complicated than Trump’s proclamation of control, experts say – with ships fearing for their safety amid attacks on vessels in the strait, and the ever-looming threat of US-Iran strikes resuming.

Is the strait open, or closed?

A missile fired by the Iranian navy in an unknown location, in a still image taken from a video released on May 8, 2026. Wana News Agency/Reuters

The US naval blockade of Iran is still in effect, barring ships from going to or from any Iranian port either inside or outside the strait. This has strangled Iran’s cashflow and closed the strait to Iranian maritime trade.

There is still some traffic going through the Persian Gulf, headed to non-Iranian destinations. But that traffic is still just a fraction of pre-war levels. For instance, only 14 vessels crossed the strait on Tuesday – compared with the roughly 120 ships that used to cross daily before the war.

That’s largely because “few merchant shipping companies and their ships are confident that the US can ensure their safe transit of the strait,” said Carl Schuster, former director of the US Pacific Command’s Joint Intelligence Center.

Those fears are hardly unfounded. At least four vessels belonging to the Abu Dhabi National Oil Company were attacked by drones and missiles in the strait last week alone, the company said. And these attacks drive up insurance costs – further deterring shipping companies while the war rages on.

Besides outright attacks, Iran can also harass ships by flying drones overhead and doing “targeted surveillance of merchant shipping,” said the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) in a recent advisory.

Since the war began, there have been 54 reports of damage to vessels in the strait, or the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman which sit either side of it, according to UKMTO, a Royal Navy-affiliated body that monitors maritime security and shipping in the region.

There have also been three confirmed total losses of vessels, it said, and 13 near misses.

“Until you can ensure safe use of the strait, you do not have total control,” Schuster said.

CNN military analyst and retired Air Force Col. Cedric Leighton agreed that neither side has full control right now. “What you’re really dealing with is a standoff here,” he said.

“Because of the proximity of US forces, because of the blockade, and because of Iran’s ability and willingness to at least threaten the use of mines and the use of small boats to harass vessels … neither side is really able to exercise full control over the strait.”

Who has the upper hand?

Both the US and Iran have tools in their arsenal to apply pressure on the other and to harness some control over the strait, which normally carries 20% of the world’s oil, and an even higher proportion of the natural gas that some nations are critically reliant on.

Iran, lying right on the strait, has the advantage of proximity. It also has a “psychological and political upper hand,” Schuster said, since the disrupted maritime traffic offers them a political and strategic boost.

The strait’s closure has wreaked havoc on global economies and the energy sector, piling pressure on the US to find a solution or guarantee safe passage through the waterway. This pressure could influence the upcoming US midterm elections in November – another thing that could play to Iran’s favor if the new Congress forces Trump to end the war on terms advantageous to Tehran, Schuster said.

And Iran is prepared to bide its time, it seems, with a top adviser to its Revolutionary Guards saying Tuesday that it could “prolong” the war until Trump is out of office.

“We have to attain deterrence so that the enemy never dares to attack us, so we can live with security,” Mohammad Reza Naqdi told PBS.

Qatar intercepts a missile attack on July 12, 2026, in Doha, as the US and Iran exchange strikes. Stringer/picture alliance/Getty Images

The US still has a clear military and economic advantage, with heavy sanctions on Iranian oil as well as Iranian assets frozen overseas, say experts.

But the US’ military forces in the region “are basically stretched pretty thin, and they’ve been there for quite some time,” said Leighton. That means the US needs to replenish its forces – by, for instance, rotating a new carrier battle group into the region – to increase its leverage in any negotiations with Iran over the strait.

And, he added, “the US leverage is limited by its staying power.” If the US backs off for any reason or loosens its grip on the blockade, it loses negotiating power and could have less say over the future of the strait, including which parties will govern it and what new rules are imposed for shipping.

That leaves Trump in a tough spot – at risk of losing leverage and having to make concessions if he pulls out, but under pressure to end the war and bring cost-of-living relief to his constituents ahead of crucial legislative votes, according to analysts.

World.title: Liberia: Two Months Into the Biggest Cocaine Cases, Questions of Accountability Mount
World.content:
Monrovia – Two months into Liberia’s biggest-ever drug cases, a troubling question remains unanswered: who is actually being held accountable?

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

Foreign nationals arrested in the record US$317 million Duazon warehouse cocaine bust have become the most visible faces of the investigation, while Liberian suspects named in writs of arrest—including suspects in the earlier US$19 million Roberts International Airport cocaine case—have largely disappeared from public view, with little visible movement toward trial.

At the same time, the scandal has moved deeper into Liberia’s security establishment. A deputy police commissioner was dismissed after allegedly admitting to taking a bribe, three senior security officers were reportedly sent to court over alleged links to a cocaine-trafficking syndicate, and a former LDEA commander was rearrested while attempting to leave the country.

Then came an extraordinary admission from Liberia’s Inspector General of Police, Gregory O.W. Coleman, who said the Duazon operation was “definitely sanctioned by state actors at the very, very senior level” of government.

He did not identify those officials. That admission has only sharpened the question many Liberians are now asking: If the police chief says senior state actors were involved, why does the visible face of justice remain largely two foreign nationals?

Two Cases, One Pattern: The Vanishing Suspects

Something does not add up in the way Liberia has handled its two largest drug busts of 2026. In June, authorities intercepted 237.6 kilograms of cocaine valued at about US$19 million at Roberts International Airport. Five people were eventually charged, including Oscar Browne and Michael Browne, who was charged in absentia after reportedly fleeing across the border into Sierra Leone.

A month later, the country was confronted with an even larger discovery: nearly 4,000 kilograms of cocaine, valued at roughly US$317 million, found inside a warehouse in Duazon, outside Monrovia.

Two foreign nationals—Johann David Garces Grajales and Srdan Seles—were arrested at the scene. Grajales was reportedly carrying Spanish and Colombian passports, while Seles is a Serbian national.

They quickly became the public faces of Liberia’s largest drug investigation.

But the Duazon case does not involve only two suspects.

Among those named in connection with the case are Edison Brown, Mohammed Alpha Bah, Jammel V. Jallah, Christopher Sayee, Christian L. Nyantee, Caycee Nelson, a man identified only as Sekou, Nana Tom, a man identified only as Michael, and Abednego.

The charges include importation of controlled drugs, unlicensed exportation, unlicensed sale and transportation of controlled substances, unlicensed possession, illicit trafficking, criminal conspiracy, criminal facilitation, criminal solicitation and illegal possession of a firearm under various provisions of Liberia’s Penal Law.

Yet since the charges were announced, the public has seen little evidence of those Liberian suspects being brought before the courts.

There have been writs of arrest. There have been names on charge sheets. But where are the suspects?

Where are the arrests? Where are the arraignments? Where are the trial dates? For the public, the answers remain unclear. The result is a widening perception that while the two foreign nationals are being visibly prosecuted, several Liberian suspects have effectively vanished from the case. That perception is particularly troubling because the investigation itself has increasingly pointed inward.

Coleman’s Admission Changed the Conversation

In late July, IGP Coleman told a government press briefing that the operation was “definitely sanctioned by state actors at the very, very senior level” of government.

He did not name the officials. But the significance of the statement lies in who made it. This was not an opposition politician or an activist making an allegation. It was Liberia’s top police officer speaking about an operation at the center of the country’s largest drug-trafficking investigation. The admission created another layer to the case.

If senior state actors authorized or sanctioned the operation, who were they? Were they government officials? Security officials? Political actors? Business interests? And, most importantly, are they being investigated? The public has yet to receive clear answers.

The Scandal Inside the Security Forces

Meanwhile, the investigation has produced consequences within Liberia’s own security institutions. Deputy Commissioner for Crime Services Johnny Bolar Dean was dismissed after reportedly admitting that he accepted a US$10,000 bribe in exchange for favorable treatment of suspects in custody. The episode raised questions about internal accountability within the Liberia National Police, including how Dean rose to such a senior position and whether warning signs were missed.

Separately, three senior security officers—including the Chief of Highway Patrol, the Chief of Financial Crimes and the Deputy Commander of the LDEA at Roberts International Airport—were reportedly forwarded to court over alleged connections to a cocaine-trafficking syndicate.

Then came the rearrest of Moses Jallah, a former LDEA deputy commander at Roberts International Airport who was already facing obstruction-related charges. Jallah was reportedly taken back into custody after attempting to leave the country through the same airport where the cocaine was intercepted.

These developments suggest that the drug investigations are not simply exposing foreign traffickers. They are exposing vulnerabilities—and alleged wrongdoing—within Liberia’s own security system.

Harris Is Held. Kuiah Remains a Question.

Other names have also emerged. Leroy Harris, owner of the nightclub Private Bar, was charged in connection with the separate US$19 million cocaine investigation. But it was only after mounting public pressure that the Bureau of Corrections and Rehabilitation confirmed that Harris was being held at the Monrovia Central Prison awaiting trial. That confirmation raised another question: why did it take public pressure for authorities to clarify the status of a suspect already publicly linked to such a major drug case?

Then there is Mark Egon Kuiah, the former Deputy Director of the Liberia Airport Authority. President Joseph Nyuma Boakai dismissed Kuiah over his alleged connection to the drug bust. Yet authorities have not clearly established publicly whether Kuiah has been charged.

If he has been charged, what are the charges? Where is he? Is he in custody? Has he been released on bail? If he has not been charged, why was he dismissed? These are basic questions in a case of extraordinary national importance, but clear public answers remain elusive.

U.S. Pushing Accountability

Amid the growing scrutiny, the United States Government has reaffirmed its support for Liberia’s efforts to strengthen its security and justice institutions.

In a statement issued Monday, the U.S. Embassy said Chargé d’Affaires Joe Zadrozny met with IGP Coleman and Executive Protection Service Director Sam Gaye.

The Embassy said the meeting provided an opportunity to reiterate that the United States “stands firmly” with its Liberian partners as the country works to strengthen its security and legal institutions. It said a just and accountable legal system is important not only to Liberia but also to regional stability and the longstanding relationship between Liberia and the United States. The Embassy also reaffirmed its continued partnership with the Liberian Government and people, saying it looks forward to broadening cooperation aimed at enhancing the security and prosperity of both countries.

Analysts say the timing of the engagement is significant. Liberia is facing its most serious drug-trafficking investigations in recent memory, while questions about accountability are increasingly extending beyond traffickers to officials and security personnel allegedly connected to the cases.

What This Pattern Suggests

Taken together, the cases present an uncomfortable picture.

Liberia’s drug investigations have exposed alleged wrongdoing not only among suspected traffickers but also within parts of the security establishment tasked with stopping them. Yet the most visible prosecution remains that of the two foreign nationals arrested at the Duazon warehouse.

The Liberian suspects named in arrest writs remain largely invisible.

Some have reportedly fled. Some have been dismissed from government positions. Some have been identified in court documents. Others remain the subject of unanswered questions. And the senior “state actors” referenced by the police chief remain unnamed.

Observers say this is where the credibility of Liberia’s drug investigations will ultimately be tested. The issue is not simply whether the government can seize cocaine. It is whether it can follow the evidence wherever it leads. That means identifying and prosecuting those who allegedly imported, financed, transported, stored or facilitated the drugs—regardless of nationality, political connections, wealth or position.

The government does not have to parade suspects before the public to prove that justice is being done. But it does owe the public transparency about who has been arrested, who has been charged, who is on the run, who has been released on bail and where the cases stand in court.

Because two months into Liberia’s biggest drug cases, the central question remains unanswered: If senior state actors were involved, who are they—and will Liberia’s justice system reach them? Until the government provides those answers, the vanishing suspects will remain as troubling as the drugs themselves.

World.title: Liberia: Justine Yeazeahn’s Anticipated Release Sparks Supporter-Critic Divide
World.content:
MONROVIA — On Thursday, August 13, the prison chapter of Justin Oldpa Yeazehn, better known across Liberia as “ProphetKey”, is expected to come to an end. For six months, the outspoken podcaster and political commentator has been behind the walls of the Monrovia Central Prison after the Supreme Court of Liberia found him guilty of criminal contempt and sentenced him to 180 days in prison on February 13, 2026.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

The sentence stemmed from remarks the Court deemed vulgar, degrading and contemptuous, including comments directed at Chief Justice Yamie Quiqui Gbeisay and references to his mother, alongside accusations of corruption against the judiciary that were not supported with proof.

The sentence was ordered to run from February 13 through August 13. But as the date of his expected release approaches, the more compelling story is no longer simply when ProphetKey will leave prison. It is who will emerge from the prison gates.

Will Liberia see the return of the same combative online political commentator who built a formidable following through profanity, confrontation and relentless attacks against political and public figures? Or will the six months behind bars produce a more measured ProphetKey — still outspoken, still politically engaged, but more conscious of the consequences of words spoken before thousands of followers?

That question is now at the center of the conversation surrounding his expected release. The Supreme Court has already made its position clear. ProphetKey was not only sentenced to prison. His release was tied to conditions intended to demonstrate remorse and a commitment to changed conduct, including a public apology and a behavior bond. The Court’s action has therefore transformed his release into something of a public test or whether a man who made confrontation the foundation of his public identity can now embrace restraint without surrendering his political voice.

And ProphetKey himself appears to have recognized the significance of that moment. For years, ProphetKey occupied a peculiar and increasingly influential space in the country’s political landscape. He was not a traditional politician. He was not a conventional journalist. He was an online personality who combined religion, politics, social commentary and entertainment into a style that attracted both passionate supporters and fierce critics. His greatest weapon was his voice.

He spoke loudly, directly and often without the caution associated with traditional media. He attacked political leaders, challenged government officials and routinely used profanity and personal language to make his points.

That style was not accidental. It became his brand. During the administration of former President George Weah, ProphetKey survived politically and commercially on cussing and attacking the government while operating from Morocco. His broadcasts became part of the wider opposition ecosystem, helping to keep criticism of the Weah administration alive among Liberians at home and abroad.

His supporters viewed that period differently from his critics. To his supporters, ProphetKey was fearless. He said what others were afraid to say. He confronted those in power. He used his platform to challenge government officials and mobilize public opinion.

And as Liberia moved toward the 2023 presidential election, his criticism of the Weah administration became part of the broader political environment that helped the opposition Unity Party regain power.

In that sense, ProphetKey became one of the voices that contributed to the political atmosphere that ultimately brought President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to the Executive Mansion. But political power changed hands. And ProphetKey’s microphone did not go silent.

From Opposition Firebrand to Government Critic

The most revealing aspect of ProphetKey’s political journey may be what happened after the Unity Party came to power. He did not simply become a cheerleader for the government he had helped support. Instead, he continued to criticize. That development exposed the deeper nature of his political identity. ProphetKey was never entirely about one political party. His influence was rooted in confrontation itself.

He became popular because he challenged people in power, and once power changed hands, his attention remained fixed on those occupying positions of authority.

That is precisely why his release could become politically significant.

If he returns to his microphone, Liberia’s political establishment will once again have to contend with a commentator who has demonstrated that he is willing to criticize those in government — even political forces whose return to power he previously supported. But the question is whether he will now do so differently.

Six Months Behind Bars and a Letter of Regret

Perhaps the clearest indication of ProphetKey’s current state of mind is the apology letter that surfaced as his sentence approached its conclusion.

In the letter, ProphetKey apologized to Chief Justice Gbeisay, members of the Supreme Court, judges, magistrates and the judiciary as an institution.

He also apologized to Liberian women whom he had insulted through his public commentary. His apology was not merely a private expression of regret. It was part of the conditions attached to his release.

Reports indicate that the Supreme Court required him to publish an apology in three newspapers for five consecutive days and execute a behavior bond as part of the conditions surrounding his release.

In his letter, ProphetKey acknowledged that he had accused members of the judiciary of corruption without proof and expressed remorse for his conduct. He also promised not to repeat his abusive language toward women.

The significance of that apology goes beyond the words on paper.

For a public figure whose identity was built around refusing to back down, acknowledging wrongdoing represents a dramatic departure from the image that made him famous.

The question is whether that departure is permanent.

The Supreme Court’s Warning Will Follow Him

ProphetKey may leave prison on Thursday, but the Supreme Court’s warning will not leave with him. His case has established a clear boundary between political criticism and conduct that the Court considers abusive or contemptuous.

The constitutional debate surrounding his incarceration has been intense. Liberia’s Constitution protects freedom of expression, but Article 15 also places responsibility on individuals for abuses of that freedom. Analysts and legal commentators have therefore debated whether ProphetKey’s punishment represented an excessive restriction on speech or a legitimate response to conduct that went beyond criticism.

That debate will likely continue.

But for ProphetKey personally, there is another consideration. He has already experienced the consequences. He knows that words spoken during an online broadcast can eventually lead to a courtroom. He knows that insulting a powerful institution can have consequences beyond the immediate reaction of social media.

And he knows that a second confrontation with the judiciary could carry a very different weight now that he has already been warned.

The Real Test Begins After Prison

This is why August 13 should not be viewed merely as ProphetKey’s release date. It should be viewed as the beginning of his real test. The prison sentence was imposed by the Court. The next chapter will be written by ProphetKey himself. He will have to decide whether to return immediately to the style that made him famous or reinvent his approach. There is nothing preventing him from remaining a fierce critic.

He can question President Boakai.

He can criticize the Unity Party. He can challenge senators and representatives. He can scrutinize judges and government institutions. He can expose what he believes to be corruption. He can investigate public officials. He can mobilize public opinion.

But there is a fundamental difference between doing all of those things and making unsupported personal accusations. That difference could determine whether ProphetKey remains free to operate his platform or finds himself in another confrontation with the law.

Can He Remain Relevant Without Cussing? This may be ProphetKey’s greatest challenge.

His audience became accustomed to a particular version of him — loud, aggressive, confrontational, and sometimes profane. The question is whether that audience will accept a more disciplined ProphetKey. Can he maintain thousands of viewers by replacing insults with evidence? Can he challenge corruption allegations by presenting documents rather than simply making accusations? Can he attack government policy without attacking people’s families? Can he disagree with women in public life without resorting to abusive language? Can he challenge the judiciary without personally abusing judges? If he can, ProphetKey could discover that his greatest political asset was never the profanity.

It was the audience. The audience will still be there. The microphone will still be there. The issues will still be there. What changes is the method.

A Potential Reinvention

There is an opportunity here for ProphetKey to reinvent himself. He could transform from a controversial online preacher into a more disciplined political commentator. Instead of simply alleging corruption, he could demand documents.

Instead of accusing officials of wrongdoing, he could present evidence. Instead of cussing public officials, he could interrogate their policies. Instead of personal attacks, he could use investigative questions. Such a transformation would not necessarily weaken him.It could strengthen him.

Liberia’s political environment already has enough people shouting. What is often missing is disciplined public scrutiny backed by facts. If ProphetKey can provide that, he could become even more influential.

But There Is Another Path

The alternative is equally possible. He could walk out of prison, switch on his phone, open his microphone and return to the same language and behavior that brought him before the Supreme Court.

If that happens, his apology will face its first serious test. Critics will ask whether the letter represented genuine remorse or simply compliance with a court order. Supporters may argue that his imprisonment changed nothing about the fundamental issues he has raised. And the Supreme Court will likely be watching closely. The danger for ProphetKey is that the public may interpret a return to his old behavior not as courage, but as a refusal to learn from the experience.

The Question of Accountability

There is also a larger lesson embedded in the ProphetKey case. The controversy should not be reduced to whether ProphetKey was right or wrong. It should also force Liberia to confront the quality of public debate. Political accountability requires criticism.

Democracy requires dissent.

Institutions must be questioned. Public officials must be scrutinized. But accountability also requires evidence. A democracy cannot function effectively if accusations become substitutes for proof.

At the same time, institutions cannot demand respect while avoiding legitimate questions about their own conduct.

That is why the debate surrounding ProphetKey’s case will likely survive his release. His imprisonment answered the question of whether the Supreme Court was prepared to punish what it considered contemptuous conduct. It did not necessarily settle the broader debate over how Liberia should balance free expression, public accountability and institutional dignity.

What Will His First Broadcast Look Like?

Perhaps the most anticipated moment after ProphetKey’s release will be his return to the microphone. Liberians will be watching. His supporters will want to hear him. His critics will want to know whether he has changed. Government officials will likely pay attention. And the judiciary may also be interested in whether the commitments contained in his apology become reality.

His first broadcast could therefore carry enormous symbolic weight. If he comes out thanking the Court, acknowledging his mistakes and promising to use his platform more responsibly, it could signal the beginning of a new ProphetKey. If he immediately returns to insults and accusations, the public may conclude that six months in prison changed little. That first appearance could become a defining moment.

From Prisoner to Political Watchdog?

There is another possibility. ProphetKey could emerge from prison more focused on issues and less interested in personalities. He could use his platform to examine government spending, public contracts, corruption allegations, legislative decisions, and institutional performance. He could ask difficult questions and demand answers. That would allow him to retain his identity as a government critic without repeatedly crossing the line into personal abuse.

In many ways, that could be the strongest version of ProphetKey. The man who once relied heavily on profanity could discover the power of documentation. The preacher who built an audience through confrontation could become a watchdog. The online personality who once attracted attention through controversy could command attention through evidence.

The Road Ahead

On Thursday, August 13, the prison doors are expected to open. But ProphetKey’s story will not end there. In many ways, it will begin again. The six months behind bars have given him something few public commentators receive: a forced period of reflection away from the microphone. His apology has given him an opportunity to acknowledge the damage caused by his words.

The Supreme Court’s warning has given him clear notice about the boundaries he is expected to respect. And his history has given him a platform that remains powerful.

What he does with those three things will determine the next chapter of his public life. ProphetKey has already demonstrated that he can attract an audience. He has demonstrated that he can influence political conversations.

He has demonstrated that he can survive political transitions — from his attacks on the George Weah administration while in Morocco to his continued relevance during the Unity Party’s rise and subsequent administration.

Now he has to demonstrate something different. He must show that he can wield influence without abusing it.

That may prove more difficult than cussing. It may prove more difficult than attacking politicians. It may even prove more difficult than surviving six months in prison. Because after August 13, there will be no question about whether ProphetKey has a voice.

The question will be what he chooses to say with it. And whether, after everything that has happened, Liberia will hear a different ProphetKey when he finally speaks again.

World.title: Liberia: Stalled Bridge Leaves River Cess Residents Risking Their Lives on Makeshift Log — One of Dozens of Abandoned Projects Nationwide
World.content:
Residents cross the Jo River on a makeshift log bridge after a government-funded replacement project stalled. Photo by Eric Opa Doue.

Summary:

A US$90,000 bridge project was abandoned after half of the contract value was paid, leaving farmers, traders and schoolchildren stranded and families divided.

County authorities are trying to force the Kpandu Construction Company to complete the project or repay the funds but the case is stalled at the Supreme Court.

Experts and county authorities say the case reflects broader accountability problems in county development spending causing desperate communities to lose faith in government.

By Eric Opa Doue with New Narratives

BODOWHEA, River Cess County — Every time Cecelia Garseedah thinks about visiting her parents, she must first decide whether the journey is worth risking her life.

Her parents live on the opposite side of the Jo River. She must cross a dangerous bridge of two log to get there.

The makeshift crossing was put in place by townspeople after a community-built wood bridge was dismantled in 2023 to make way for a reinforced concrete bridge. More than two years later, half the $90,000 money for the new bridge has disappeared and construction has not even begun, leaving residents to risk their lives each time they cross on the slippery and unstable log.

Garseedah says she rarely sees her parents now. “I got my parents them across the water there,” Garseedah says in Liberian English. “It hard for them to come in town.”

Garseedah’s experience is echoed across Doedein District where the unfinished bridge has isolated entire communities. Children struggle to attend school. Farmers face difficulty reaching their fields and taking goods to markets. Patients requiring treatment are referred to neighboring Nimba County because access to health facilities becomes nearly impossible during parts of the rainy season. The route is effectively cut off for months each year.

Experts say the same scene is playing out across the country when corruption, lack of capacity by companies that win contracts, and poor oversight mean projects are abandoned leaving communities to live with the consequences.

The case is an example of findings by the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia and the General Auditing Commission which have repeatedly identified weak oversight, poor procurement practices and abandoned county-funded infrastructure projects across Liberia.

The case is ”a combination of structural weaknesses we have in the system — a system that is not designed to really work for the people, but for the most part benefits a few people in high positions,” according to Anderson Miamen, executive director at the Center for Transparency and Accountability.

A project, awarded with good intentions, vanishes leaving community’s worse off

Before the government got involved, residents maintained a handmade wooden bridge that allowed people, motorbikes and goods to cross the Jo River Bridge. It was the main connection between communities in Doedein District and the shortest route to Yarpah Town and Cestos, the county capital. It linked residents to schools, health facilities, markets and farms on the opposite side of the river.

Recognizing its importance, county authorities approved a project during the 2023 County sitting to replace the aging wooden structure with a reinforced concrete bridge.

“The bridge project was intended to improve service delivery, especially health and education,” said Isaac Williams, River Cess County’s information officer.

Residents carefully guide a motorcycle across a fragile makeshift crossing over the Jo River: Photo by Eric Opa Doue

According to a turnover note from January 2024 addressed to former Internal Affairs Minister Varney A. Sirleaf, (now Ministry of Local Government) the project was among 21 development projects approved in 2023 to be funded by the River Cess County Development Funds.

According to the note, provided to FrontPage Africa/New Narratives by former River Cess County Fiscal Superintendent, C. Elijah Kayssaynee, Kpandu Construction Company, a Liberian company headed by Hamed E. Horton ll, was awarded the contract through a bidding process run by a five-man bidding committee headed by then County superintendent, J. Bismark Karbiah. Other members of the committee were: C Elijah Kassaynee, then fiscal superintendent; Mr. Amos Somah, then development superintendent; J. Fahn Dehgar, then chairman of the project management committee; and Presley E Grisby.

But what happened next violated the agreement, according to current county authorities.

Before Kpandu had done a thing, fifty five percent of the agreed costs of L$16,418,000 (about US$90,000) was paid to Kpandu by the local administration through its project management committee headed by chairperson J. Fahn Dehgar and approved by the fiscal superintendent.

The agreement actually said Kpandu was expected to pre-finance the initial phase of construction itself and complete 25 percent of the work before becoming eligible for 40 percent payment.

Residents and county authorities allege that after receiving the payment, Kpandu dismantled the existing community bridge but failed to take one step toward completing the new one. Hamed E. Horton ll and the money vanished.

County Authorities Pursue Court Action

Current River Cess officials who took over from the previous administration and have been pursuing legal action ever since taking office. Martin Tumoe, county attorney filed suit against Kpandu in February 2024. Court records show the matter later reached the Supreme Court after the contractor filed a petition for a writ of prohibition, temporarily halting proceedings in the lower court.

Dennis G. Seeboe, the current administrative officer, says the county has repeatedly raised the issue during court openings and has sought assistance from court officials in Monrovia to push the matter before the court, but they have failed to act.

“That money belongs to the people of River Cess,” says Seeboe. “Either they refund the money or continue with the contract.”

This reporter sent Hamed Horton, chief executive officer of Kpandu Construction Company, a WhatsApp message; placed direct telephone calls and sent text messages seeking comment.He replied that the firm has other projects in Grand Bassa, Montserrado and Margibi Counties though he did not provide evidence of those and FrontPage Africa/New Narratives could find no evidence of this claim. Horton initially indicated that he would respond to questions personally or through his lawyers, Nathaniel Innis, Abraham Nyonway and James B. Kaba. But no response was received before publication.

Residents of Doedein District navigate a narrow makeshift crossing over the Jo River to access farms, schools, markets, and healthcare services: Photo by Eric Opa Doue.

Communities across the country plagued by abandoned development projects

Experts say the Jo River Bridge reflects broader problems that have plagued development projects across Liberia.

“That project is one of many projects across River Cess and other counties that were abandoned, poorly administered,” said Miamen. “In some instances, the contractors were not recruited through the requisite processes or recruited transparently, and as a result we see all these abandoned, unconstructed or poorly constructed projects across the country. It raises the issue of oversight. It means that the requisite institutions or individuals that are supposed to oversee that process didn’t do well to oversee the project.”

According to Miamen, the consequences extend beyond unfinished infrastructure.

“It affects trust because what people want to get, they wouldn’t get them. It leads to frustration, reduced confidence in the system, and some people may even decide they wouldn’t vote,” Anderson Miamen, Center for Transparency and Accountability Liberia

Ove the year General Auditing Commission audits have documented a recurring pattern of abandoned and incomplete County Development Fund and Social Development Fund projects. The Commission’s latest audit of Nimba County, for example, identified nine abandoned or incomplete projects valued at more than US$735,000. These included administrative buildings, bridges and other development projects. The audit also found over US$44,100 in unsupported expenditures. Similar findings were reported in Bong County, where auditors questioned payments made for projects without evidence that work had been performed. A 2025 study by the Center for Transparency and Accountability in Liberia titled “ Open Expenditure : Examining CSDF Projects In Six Counties” identified weaknesses in project implementation, transparency, and accountability involving infrastructure projects across six counties.

Joseph Suah says his farm is located on the opposite side of the crossing, where many residents conduct farming, hunting and other economic activities: Photo by Eric Opa Doue

At Jo River, life has been upended with consequences that could extend for generations. The primary school serving many communities in the area is located in Bodowhea, requiring students to cross the river each day. For Emma Kpah, the unfinished bridge has forced an impossible choice: She says she stopped allowing her children to attend school.

“We’re scared our children them going to school, and we suppose to support them. But they spoil the bridge,” Kpah said in Liberian English. “When the river gets full, there’s no way for us to pass over it. Our children can fall down in the hole, for them to die. Ourselves here, when we make mistake, we can die here.”

The bridge’s collapse has become an economic burden for farmer Joseph Suah. His farm lies across the river, where many residents grow crops and hunt to support their families. Without a bridge, transporting produce has become exhausting.

Motorbikes that once carried cassava, rice and other crops across the bridge can no longer make the crossing.

“Because the motorbike—to cross the motorbike on the bridge—is not a small thing. Two persons can be pushing it before they can cross it on this one log,” said Suah. He missed the old bridge. “It was a good bridge. Car used to pass on it.

He says residents have grown frustrated after repeatedly appealing for help, sending a worrying message to a government that say has abandoned them.

“We have talked and we are tired now. Nobody to hear us.”

Residents allege that after work began, the existing community bridge was dismantled but the promised replacement was never done: Photo by Eric Opa Doue

Meanwhile county authorities say they are also considering temporary solutions, including securing a boat and outboard motor to help residents cross safely while the legal matter continues.

“The life of our people is our concern,” Seeboe said. “We don’t want to see our citizens losing their lives because of a common thing. That is why we are pursuing this case while also exploring temporary solutions to keep people safe.”

As dusk settles over the Jo River, residents continue making the crossing one at a time. The bridge that was supposed to improve life in Upper River Cess has instead become a symbol of how a corruption and governance failures can devastate entire communities and undermine confidence in government. And, as always say experts, it’s the poor people who are paying the price.

World.title: Liberia: Dillon Rebukes Sando Over Konneh Attack, Warns: ‘Do Not Follow Political Clapping and Cheers’
World.content:
Monrovia — Montserrado County Senator Darius Dillon has publicly rebuked Deputy Information Minister Daniel O. Sando over his attack on Senator Amara Konneh, warning his fellow Unity Party partisan to exercise restraint and avoid using religion as a weapon in political disagreements.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, gerald.koinyeneh@frontpageafricaonline .com

Dillon’s intervention came after Sando accused Konneh of helping orchestrate the defeat of then-Vice President Joseph Nyuma Boakai in the 2017 presidential election and suggested that Konneh bears moral and historical responsibility for George Weah’s subsequent presidency.

But Dillon, who described Sando as a “younger brother,” said the deputy minister’s reference to Konneh’s religion and religious beliefs was inappropriate and “out of order.”

“Your recent comments directed at Sen. Amara Konneh essentially referencing his religion and religious belief were inappropriate and out of order, from my viewpoint,” Dillon said in a public message directed at Sando.

“There are many other ways to respond to issues than the manner and path you have chosen. You need to reach out to make amends!!” he added.

Dillon’s rebuke is significant because he and Sando are members of the Liberia Party ruling Unity Party, making his intervention an unusually public call for restraint from within the governing political establishment.

‘I May Not Be the Best Moral Voice’

Dillon began his message by acknowledging his own imperfections and long experience in Liberian politics. “Let me do this in public this time around. I may not be the right or best ‘moral voice’ to advise you,” Dillon told Sando.

He said his own shortcomings as a human being and national leader did not prevent him from sharing lessons acquired through more than two decades in public service.

“I have been around for a good while now and have gained some experience in public service,” Dillon said. “I have grown from a youth to a full-grown adult in public service for over 20 years.”

Drawing on advice from his mother when he was growing up, Dillon urged Sando to slow down and exercise greater caution.

“I can still recall when I was a kid growing up, my mother used to say … ‘My son, you better take time in life; you got far way to go,’” Dillon recalled.

He said he initially misunderstood the advice, believing his mother was simply trying to prevent him from doing things his own way.

But, with the benefit of experience, Dillon said he now understands the importance of restraint.

‘I Have Seen It All’

Dillon also pointed to his own political journey, describing himself as a consequential figure both in opposition and now in collaboration with the Boakai administration.

“No doubt, I have been a relevant and consequential figure in opposition in our national politics, and now a relevant and consequential figure (with humility) in collaboration with the current, ruling administration,” he said.

“I have seen it all in my lifetime … thus far!” Dillon added.

The senator said he has experienced both praise and criticism throughout his political career.

“I have been liked at times, disliked at times, as well as booed at times and cheered on at times. I have seen it all … thus far,” he said.

His comments appeared aimed at cautioning Sando against allowing immediate political approval to influence how he conducts himself as a government official.

Sando’s Attack on Konneh

Sando’s comments came amid an increasingly heated political exchange over Konneh’s criticism of the Boakai administration, particularly its handling of Liberia’s ongoing cocaine crisis.

In a Facebook post, Sando described Konneh as a “scheming trickster” and accused him of working with unnamed co-conspirators to undermine Boakai’s presidential bid in 2017. Sando alleged that the political maneuver ultimately facilitated Weah’s election.

He further argued that Konneh bears “moral and historical responsibility” for the consequences of the Weah presidency.

Sando also questioned Konneh’s political history, arguing that the senator has never genuinely supported Boakai’s political ambitions and that his current criticism of the administration lacks credibility.

The deputy minister’s remarks became more personal when he addressed Konneh’s criticism of President Boakai’s age.

“Amara is simply beyond redemption, and I maintain he needs repentance,” Sando wrote. He defended Boakai’s record, contrasting the president’s age with what he described as the failures of the former Weah administration.

Konneh Hits Back

Konneh responded by defending his faith and his right to criticize the administration. “The lazy man blames the sun for the unfinished work!” Konneh said. He described himself as a practicing Muslim who prays five times a day, fasts, and gives charity to the poor.

“I am a proud Liberian Muslim who prays five times a day, fasts, and donates charity to the poor,” Konneh said. He rejected the suggestion that his religious beliefs should be invoked in the political debate. “I don’t need an unskilled sycophant riding on the back of an aging President to tell me to go to the mosques and pray,” Konneh said.

The senator also defended his criticism of the government’s handling of the cocaine investigation, saying he had worked to bring the Unity Party to power with a promise to fight illicit drugs.

“I speak out against this cocaine scheme because I love my country and worked hard to bring in this UP government with the promise to rid our nation of drugs,” Konneh said.

“So far, we are struggling to fulfill that promise,” he added.

Konneh maintained that his position was part of his responsibility as a national leader.

“I have earned the right to speak up, especially as a national leader and a voice for those affected by illicit drugs whose voices may not be heard,” he said.

“Silence would be complicity. I am doing my job. You do your job, too, so we can make Liberia a drug-free country and a better country than it was two and a half years ago. Everybody wins!”

Dillon’s Warning

For Dillon, however, the dispute has crossed a line that requires correction.

His central message to Sando was that political disagreement does not justify attacks touching on another official’s religion.

“You need to reach out to make amends!!” Dillon told him.

He also warned Sando about political supporters who encourage aggressive rhetoric today but may abandon those defending it tomorrow.

“Do not follow some of these political clapping and cheers … they may be temporary and can shift!!” Dillon cautioned.

The senator’s comments effectively separate political criticism from personal and religious attacks, while acknowledging Sando’s right to engage in political debate.

But Dillon made clear that, in his view, the manner in which Sando challenged Konneh was unacceptable.

A Party Dispute Becomes Public

The exchange has exposed another layer of tension within the ruling Unity Party, where officials and political actors have increasingly taken divergent positions over the government’s performance and its response to the cocaine crisis.

Konneh has emerged as a vocal critic of the administration’s handling of the drug investigation, while Sando has defended President Boakai and attacked Konneh’s political record.

Dillon’s intervention now introduces a call for moderation from within the same political camp.

While Dillon did not endorse Konneh’s broader criticisms of the administration, his message focused on the conduct of the debate and the need for Sando to reconsider the language he used.

For a government facing intense scrutiny over the cocaine investigation and other governance issues, the public disagreement among its own political allies could prove politically consequential.

Dillon’s warning suggests that, at least for some within the ruling establishment, defending the administration should not come at the expense of political restraint, respect for religious differences and responsible public discourse.

And his closing advice to Sando was direct: do not allow today’s political cheers to dictate conduct that could carry consequences long after the applause fades

World.title: Liberian Pastor Suffers Stroke in U.S. ICE Custody as Family Raises Concerns Over Medical Care
World.content:
CARY, North Carolina — The family of a 55-year-old Liberian pastor held in U.S. immigration detention is demanding answers after he suffered a stroke while in the custody of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), leaving him partially paralyzed, according to his family.

Pastor Gabriel Johnson, a Liberian immigrant who has lived legally in the United States since he was 15, was taken from his home in Cary, North Carolina, on July 15 and has since been transferred among multiple immigration detention facilities.

His family says Johnson suffered the latest stroke on July 30 while being held at an ICE detention facility in Alvarado, Texas.

The family told U.S. media outlets that Johnson has a history of high blood pressure and had previously suffered strokes. They now question whether he received adequate medical care while in immigration custody.

According to the family, Johnson is now paralyzed on the left side of his body following the stroke.

Family Raises Concerns Over Medical Care

Johnson’s relatives say they became increasingly concerned about his health and access to medication after he was detained. His daughter, Gabri, told NBC News that her father was not consistently receiving his prescribed medication while in detention. She also said he was not getting enough food and water.

The family believes the lack of consistent medical care may have contributed to the deterioration of his condition, although the circumstances surrounding his stroke and the medical treatment he received remain subject to further investigation.

Johnson spent about two weeks at the Stewart Detention Center in Lumpkin, Georgia, before being transferred to Alvarado, Texas. His multiple transfers have made it difficult for relatives to locate and visit him, the family said.

‘Difficult to Find Our Loved One’

According to the family, some relatives were eventually able to visit Johnson in Texas, but locating him became particularly difficult after he was hospitalized following the stroke. The family said they were forced to navigate a complicated detention system to determine where Johnson had been transferred and where he was receiving medical treatment.

Their concerns have now grown beyond his detention status to questions about his health and whether he is receiving adequate medical attention. Johnson’s relatives are calling for greater transparency regarding his treatment and medical condition while in ICE custody.

A Longtime U.S. Resident

Johnson’s family says he has lived in the United States legally since he was 15 years old. His detention has therefore raised additional concerns among relatives about how and why he came to be held by immigration authorities after decades in the United States.

The family is seeking answers about the circumstances that led to his arrest and detention, his transfers between facilities, and the medical care he received before and after the stroke. The case has also drawn attention to the vulnerability of detainees with serious medical conditions, particularly those who depend on regular medication.

Health Concerns in Detention

Johnson’s family says his medical history was known before his latest health emergency. In addition to previous strokes, relatives say he has a history of high blood pressure and requires consistent medical treatment. They contend that his access to medication was inconsistent while he was detained. The family also alleges that he did not receive adequate food and water.

Following the July 30 stroke, relatives say Johnson was left with paralysis on the left side of his body. The family is now pressing for answers about whether his medical needs were properly assessed and addressed during his detention.

Family Demands Answers

For Johnson’s family, the immediate priority is his health. They want authorities to explain what medical treatment he received, whether his prescribed medications were administered consistently, and why his condition deteriorated while in custody. They are also seeking clarity on his continued detention and his legal status in the United States.

The circumstances surrounding Johnson’s detention and medical treatment have not been fully resolved publicly. His case now places renewed focus on the treatment of medically vulnerable immigrants held in U.S. detention facilities — and on the responsibility of immigration authorities to ensure detainees receive appropriate medical care.

For Johnson’s family, however, the issue is personal.

They are not only asking where their loved one is being held. They want to know whether enough was done to protect his health before a medical emergency left him partially paralyzed.

World.title: Liberia: CBL Governor Warns Bad Loans Threaten Credit Access, Economic Growth
World.content:
National conference to bring banks, judiciary, businesses and policymakers together to tackle Liberia’s non-performing loan crisis.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Monrovia— Central Bank of Liberia Executive Governor Henry F. Saamoi has warned that Liberia’s growing challenge with non-performing loans could undermine access to credit, private-sector development and broader economic growth if left unaddressed.

Saamoi made the statement Wednesday, August 12, during a media orientation at the Central Bank of Liberia ahead of the National Non-Performing Loans Conference, which is expected to bring together policymakers, financial institutions, members of the judiciary, legal professionals, development partners, business leaders, legislators and other stakeholders.

The Governor described the upcoming conference as more than a financial-sector gathering, calling it a “strategic national dialogue” aimed at confronting one of the persistent constraints to Liberia’s economic development.

“When a significant portion of loans are not repaid according to agreed terms, financial institutions become more cautious in extending new credit, businesses face financing constraints, investors lose confidence, and economic expansion slows,” Saamoi said.

He stressed that the impact of non-performing loans extends beyond commercial banks.

The problem, he said, affects entrepreneurs seeking capital to expand their businesses, farmers looking for financing to increase productivity, young people pursuing economic opportunities, women-owned enterprises seeking to grow and communities in need of jobs and investment.

“Therefore, addressing the NPL challenge is not only a banking-sector priority; it is a national development imperative,” Saamoi said.

Building a Stronger Credit Culture

The conference will focus on practical and sustainable measures to improve loan recovery, collateral enforcement, credit discipline and responsible lending.

According to Saamoi, the Central Bank’s objective is to help build “a stronger credit culture that promotes greater access to financing while safeguarding financial stability.”

A major component of the discussions will be the modernization of Liberia’s credit infrastructure, including the Enhanced Collateral Registry System.

Saamoi said an effective collateral-management system is critical to expanding financial inclusion and improving access to credit, particularly for small and medium-sized enterprises.

By strengthening the legal and operational framework governing secured transactions, he said, Liberia can increase lenders’ confidence while creating more financing opportunities for businesses and households.

Loan Recovery and the Justice System

The conference is also expected to examine the legal and institutional challenges that have historically complicated loan recovery in Liberia.

Saamoi said predictable legal and regulatory mechanisms are necessary to ensure that disputes involving lenders and borrowers can be resolved efficiently.

He emphasized that financial-sector stability requires a balance between protecting financial institutions and ensuring that responsible borrowers have access to financing.

“The Central Bank believes that sustainable economic growth requires a financial system that is both stable and inclusive,” he said.

That, he added, means creating an environment in which responsible borrowers can obtain financing, financial institutions operate within effective risk-management frameworks, and disputes are resolved through predictable legal and regulatory processes.

CBL Appeals to Media

The CBL Governor also urged journalists to help translate technical discussions about non-performing loans into information that ordinary Liberians can understand.

He said issues surrounding bad loans, access to credit, collateral systems, debt obligations and financial-sector reforms directly affect households, businesses and communities.

“We therefore encourage you to help bridge the gap between technical policy discussions and public understanding,” Saamoi told journalists.

He called for accurate, balanced and insightful reporting on the conference and its outcomes, arguing that informed public debate could help strengthen financial literacy and encourage responsible borrowing and repayment.

Saamoi also encouraged journalists attending the conference to ask questions and seek clarification on complex issues surrounding Liberia’s credit market.

A National Development Issue

The Central Bank’s position is that addressing non-performing loans must form part of a broader effort to strengthen Liberia’s financial system and support economic expansion.

High levels of unpaid or distressed loans can restrict banks’ ability and willingness to lend, potentially making credit more expensive or difficult to obtain for businesses and individuals.

For a country seeking to expand private-sector activity, increase financial inclusion and create employment opportunities, Saamoi said, resolving these challenges is essential.

The Governor said the success of the National Non-Performing Loans Conference will ultimately depend not only on the quality of discussions among stakeholders but also on whether its recommendations can be translated into meaningful reforms and understood by the wider public.

He pledged the Central Bank’s commitment to working with stakeholders toward “a more resilient financial sector, a stronger credit culture, expanded access to finance, and a more prosperous Liberia.”

World.title: EXILE BY DESIGN: 36 YEARS OF Research Brings Controversial Liberia-America History to Light
World.content:
Torli H. Krua’s book challenges the traditional narrative of slavery, colonization and Liberia as the author prepares for Friday’s Liberian launch

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh

Monrovia — After 36 years of research, refugee advocacy and historical inquiry, Liberian author and human rights advocate Rev. Torli H. Krua is bringing his latest book, Exile by Design: The Hidden Story of Mumbet, American Colonization, Liberia, and Juneteenth Across the Atlantic, to Liberia.

The book will be officially launched in Liberia on Friday, August 14, 2026, at 10:30 a.m. at the Royal Kings & Queens International Academy in Disco Hill, Robertsfield Highway, Margibi County, ten days ahead of its official United States launch at Boston City Hall Plaza on August 24.

The U.S. launch is scheduled to coincide with Elizabeth “Mumbet” Freeman Day and Liberia Flag Day, linking the story of an enslaved Black woman who challenged slavery in colonial America with Liberia’s own complicated history of freedom, colonization and the relationship between Africa and the United States.

For Krua, however, the book is more than a historical account.

It is an attempt to challenge what he describes as a 245-year-old narrative of American freedom that has never been fully extended to Black Americans, while also questioning Liberia’s traditional account of its own founding.

A Book Born From 36 Years of Research

Krua says Exile by Design is the culmination of nearly four decades of research shaped by his own experiences as a refugee and immigration advocate.

At the center of the book is the story of Elizabeth “Mumbet” Freeman, an enslaved Black woman who successfully challenged her enslavement in Massachusetts and became an important figure in the history of American liberty and equality.

Krua argues that Freeman’s story deserves greater attention because it demonstrates that an enslaved Black woman, despite having no formal education, was able to invoke principles of liberty and equality to challenge an institution that denied her freedom.

The author connects Freeman’s story to the broader history of American colonization, Liberia and the transatlantic consequences of slavery.

He argues that the promise of “equality, liberty and justice for all” remains incomplete for Black Americans and that the history of Liberia cannot be separated from America’s unresolved contradictions over slavery, citizenship and race.

The book therefore seeks to connect events that are often treated separately: slavery in America, the struggle for Black freedom, the creation of Liberia, Juneteenth and the continuing debate over America’s founding ideals.

Why Krua Says He Wrote the Book

Krua says the central motivation behind the book is to bring what he describes as a “truth buried for 245 years” into public discussion.

As America prepares to mark 250 years since its founding, he believes the country must confront the contradictions between its democratic ideals and the historical treatment of Black people.

His argument extends to Liberia.

Krua challenges what he describes as a “false narrative” surrounding the founding of Liberia, particularly the portrayal of colonization and the historical relationship between formerly enslaved people, American colonizationists and African communities.

Rather than presenting Liberia’s history simply as a story of the “Love of Liberty,” Krua says the country must confront the complicated and sometimes painful realities surrounding its creation.

He believes that confronting these histories is necessary for reconciliation between Liberia and the United States.

His message is not limited to historical criticism.

Krua says the lessons of Mumbet Freeman’s life should inspire Liberians to recognize that ordinary citizens can become agents of national transformation.

From “There to Here and Back”

A major theme running through the book is what Krua calls “From There to Here and Back.”

The concept emerged from his 36 years of work with refugees and immigrants.
