World.title: Africa: Leaders' Medical Secrecy Harms Public Trust
World.content:
blog

Long, mysterious absences promote the idea that unaccountable forces are at the levers of power.

Aging leaders. Mysterious medical appointments. Elected officials' long absences from public duties, explained in the vaguest of terms or not at all. These increasingly common features of political life in the United States are familiar to many followers of African politics. Their corrosive effect on public trust and accountability in African states should serve as a warning to Americans.

In Cameroon, citizens are wondering whether their 93-year-old president, Paul Biya, will ever return to the country he purports to lead. Biya has long had a habit of making frequent trips to Europe, but his latest stay in Switzerland has now lasted over two months. Rumors of his failing health abound, and intrigue surrounds the question of possible successors, as the post of vice-president remains vacant. Legally, only Biya can make that appointment. But it's anyone's guess as to whether the decrees emanating from Switzerland are actually coming from the President, or from powerful members of his inner circle. Any appointment made under these circumstances might not be accepted. The country could be left at sea, with no clearly legitimate process to right the ship. The costs to Cameroon--already apparent among investors-- could be enormous, and instability could spread beyond the country's borders.



Why do some elected officials cling to a powerful position at all costs, despite their inability to perform their duties? Perhaps they fear that they and their closest associates would be left vulnerable to politically-motivated retribution. Perhaps they have committed serious crimes, and fear that accountability might reach them when the protections of their office are gone. Perhaps they have convinced themselves that the greater good can only be served when they are in control--however delusional their sense of control might be. They believe potential successors or powerful opponents to be so dangerous as to imperil the state itself. It's a level of self-aggrandizement totally incompatible with public service, or with any viable national project.

This behavior doesn't just set the stage for messy transitions, as in Cameroon. It has a toxic effect on public trust and government accountability. Health secrecy and long absences invite speculation about who is really making day-to-day decisions, and this idea of hidden hands pulling strings behind the scenes fuels wild conspiracy theories; in 2018 some Gabonese were convinced that their then-President Ali Bongo, who suffered a stroke and was out of the country recovering for months, had actually died and been replaced by a clone. Similar rumors dogged former Nigerian President Muhammadu Buhari after his prolonged medical leave in the UK in 2017, perhaps because Nigerians had experience with bizarre, prolonged periods of uncertainty regarding presidential health. In November 2009, then-President Yar'Adua left Nigeria for medical treatment in Saudi Arabia and was never seen in public again. A power vacuum followed, forcing the Nigerian Supreme Court to demand proof of his fitness and the Senate to invoke the doctrine of necessity to transfer executive power to then-Vice President Goodluck Jonathan. Yar'Adua's body was returned to Nigeria secretly and his death was announced in May 2010, but speculation about who was behind the transfer of power and when he actually died persists today.

Close 

Elected officials are human beings. They do not owe the public every miniscule personal health detail; some have weathered serious health crises with transparency and gone on to serve their constituents commendably. But when a measure of privacy becomes a campaign of subterfuge and authority becomes mysterious, citizens understand that unseen, unknown powers are accountable to no one.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Race to Find Ebola Vaccine As DR Congo Outbreak Kills More Than 2,000
World.content:
The latest outbreak of Ebola has killed more than 2,000 people in the Democratic Republic of Congo, according to health authorities. Meanwhile, international efforts have been stepped up to test a vaccine for the highly contagious haemorrhagic fever.

According to figures released on Tuesday by Congolese health authorities, 2,011 people have died in the latest outbreak, out of 4,381 confirmed cases of the virus.

The latest toll puts it close behind the DRC's deadliest Ebola outbreak to date in 2018 to 2020, when nearly 2,300 people died out of 3,500 recorded cases.

The DRC's 17th surge of the highly contagious disease, the current outbreak is already considered the largest in the country's history "and could well become the largest outbreak ever", Sania Nishtar, chief executive of the Gavi global vaccine alliance, has said.



Concentrated in the DRC's eastern and northeastern regions, it was declared on 15 May but is thought to have been spreading for several weeks before then.

The surge began in northeastern Ituri province and spread to several other provinces, notably North Kivu, regions subject to years of conflict where health infrastructure and a state presence are largely lacking.

Ebola cases near 4,000 as DRC struggles to contain fast-spreading outbreak

Response criticised

The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is estimated by Congolese health authorities to be 45.9 percent.

"We haven't reached the peak yet," Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba said in an interview shared on social media by his ministry on Tuesday.

"Within the next three months, we expect to have already brought the spread under control and to start seeing it decline," he added.

Insecurity due to the presence of armed groups and mistrust of the local population have hampered the response to the outbreak in the affected regions.

"We are only seeing 30 percent (of infected people), where 70 percent of people are dying at home. This is why this Ebola is different," Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the World Health Organization's regional director for Africa, told reporters in Ituri's provincial capital, Bunia, on Monday.

Congolese virologist Jean-Jacques Muyembe, who helped discover Ebola in 1976, said in an interview with Tuesday's Le Monde newspaper that the response had been "slow and ineffective".

"There is an internal problem at the level of the national coordination of the response," he said.

"Everyone wanted to show they were doing something, even though nothing had actually been organised."

Vaccine trials underway

On Friday, WHO vaccine experts recommended a full-scale human trial of the only existing approved Ebola vaccine to see if it offered cross-protection against the strain of Ebola currently spreading in the DRC, against which no specific vaccine currently exists.

The Ervebo vaccine has proved safe and efficacious against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola virus and WHO experts said that early data, notably from animal trials, showed it may also give some protection against the rare Bundibugyo strain exploding in the DRC.

The Gavi global vaccine alliance - set up in 2000 to help developing countries acquire affordable vaccines - maintains a stockpile of 500,000 Ervebo doses.

It said doses from the stockpile were to be made available for the trials, with some already in the DRC.

DRC trials experimental treatment for rare Ebola strain as outbreak worsens

Close 

Two potential Bundibugyo vaccines are in the early stages of clinical trials on humans, while a third is being worked on to bring it to that stage.

The United States announced last Wednesday that it had allocated more than $242 million (€209 million) in additional funding to combat the worsening outbreak.

The new funding brings direct US financial assistance in response to the outbreak to more than $500 million (€433 million), the State Department said, underlining that the United States remained "the largest financial contributor to the Ebola response".

Ebola is spread by contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever. It has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa in the last 50 years.

The WHO emergency committee is set to meet to discuss the epidemic next Tuesday.

(with AFP)

World.title: Harvard-China links unearthed as Congress finds 140 papers co-authored by CCP military universities
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

FIRST ON FOX: Harvard allegedly failed to adequately safeguard research collaborations with Chinese institutions, including universities tied to Beijing’s military and defense-industrial base, according to a report from the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.

Researchers affiliated with the New England Ivy League co-authored more than 140 publications with other researchers affiliated with a group of Chinese universities, according to the report reviewed by Fox News Digital ahead of its public release.

The "Seven Sons of National Defense" are a group of Chinese universities identified by the Pentagon and other U.S. officials as central to China’s defense research and military modernization efforts. The House Committee created to crackdown on China argues Harvard’s approach to research security opened the door for collaborations that could advance technological and military capabilities of the hostile nation.

Harvard also reported received more than $600 million from China under the federal Section 117 foreign-gift disclosure system — more than any other American university, according to the Education Department dashboard cited in the report. The committee argues the U.S. university's financial ties to China heighten the need for strict oversight of its research partnerships and foreign-funding disclosures.

HARVARD TOPS NATION IN FOREIGN CASH HAUL AS COTTON DEMANDS PROBE INTO CHINA FUNDING

The stakes in the latest report extend far beyond Harvard. U.S. officials have warned for years that China uses academic partnerships and access to Western research to advance CCP strategic capabilities in military, surveillance and other areas.

The House Select Committee on China argues that universities receiving U.S. taxpayer funding must do more than meet the narrowest legal requirements when collaborating with institutions embedded in China’s military research system, particularly when it comes to technology with potential defense or military uses.

The report highlights a 2023 paper on bio-inspired soft robots for deep-sea exploration co-authored by a Harvard-affiliated researcher and a researcher from Beihang University, one of the Seven Sons institutions. Beihang, also known as Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, has appeared on the Commerce Department’s Entity List since 2001.

The committee report argues the work examined in the paper has potential military applications, including underwater detection, while Harvard’s research-compliance office characterized the project as nonmilitary research.

FOREIGN ROBOT BAN TARGETS CHINA OVER SECURITY FEARS

Harvard researchers also co-authored a 2023 paper with a researcher at China’s National University of Defense Technology, another institution on a U.S. restricted list, according to the report. That study involved magnetic materials and acknowledged partial support from the U.S. Army Research Office.

The committee said it reviewed publications spanning dozens of disciplines and found that engineering accounted for the largest share of Harvard-affiliated research involving Seven Sons institutions.

"From allowing violence against anti-China protestors to collaborating with entities linked to the PLA, Harvard has made serious mistakes and must act now to prevent more. It should use this investigation as a catalyst for significant reforms that end CCP influence on campus and prioritize secure American research," committee chairman Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., said in a statement.

The report also examines Harvard’s executive education program with China’s National Healthcare Security Administration, which trained Chinese health officials on international health-insurance systems.

According to the report, attendance and registration records show officials affiliated with the Xinjiang Production and Construction Corps, or XPCC, were listed in connection with some sessions. The Treasury Department sanctioned XPCC in 2020 over human-rights abuses against Uyghurs and other ethnic minorities in Xinjiang.

The report acknowledges it is unclear whether XPCC officials ultimately attended every program in question.

It alleges, however, that Harvard had advance participant information for a 2020 online session that included XPCC-affiliated officials and did not take further action.

Harvard professor Winnie Yip, who helped organize the executive education program, told committee investigators she did not know XPCC was a sanctioned entity at the time and had not received training on sanctions compliance, according to the report.

The report further alleges Harvard’s research-security practices focused too narrowly on technical legal compliance and failed to account for broader national-security risks posed by work with Chinese military-linked institutions.

It cites testimony from Harvard research official John H. Shaw, who said the university evaluates research collaborations case by case and does not prohibit all work involving robotics or Chinese institutions. The committee criticized that approach, arguing research with entities embedded in China’s military-civil fusion system can have military applications even when the research is unclassified and intended for publication.

The report also raises questions about Harvard Global Research and Support Services, a nonprofit affiliated with the university that can accept awards when Harvard is unable to accept a sponsor’s terms directly. The committee alleges the entity could be used to circumvent federal foreign-gift reporting requirements, an allegation Harvard will likely dispute.

Harvard did not respond to Fox News’ request for comment on the House Committee report’s findings.

The report recommends that Harvard prohibit research relationships with entities on U.S. government restricted or sanctioned lists and centralize its research-security oversight. It also urges Congress to strengthen foreign-funding disclosure requirements for universities.

It is not often that I write critically of a Republican United States senator. But that happened in February 2023, when Alabama Sen. Tommy Tuberville placed a hold on military promotions to protest a Department of Defense policy that covered travel expenses for service members seeking reproductive healthcare across state lines. Tuberville's hold ultimately delayed the promotions of more than 400 senior military officers, many of whom were colonels or Navy captains awaiting promotion to general or flag rank, for roughly 10 months.

The "Tuberville Blockade" upended the lives and careers of hundreds of Army, Air Force and Marine Corps colonels and Navy captains by seriously disrupting carefully planned career paths and assignments. It also disrupted the carefully constructed career paths of the generals and admirals who were sidelined by the ill-considered embargo.

Career military officers ought never again to be held hostage for political goals. Sen. Tuberville eventually relented after months of mounting pressure from senators in both parties. He lifted his blanket "hold" after long meetings with his Senate colleagues, who emphasized to him that he was damaging the careers of people who had provided exemplary service over decades.

MORNING GLORY: MICHIGAN’S DEMOCRATIC SENATE PRIMARY HAD TWO WINNERS — BUT ONLY ONE WAS ON THE BALLOT

El-Sayed is a sworn enemy of the State of Israel, and I fear that it is very unlikely that he will be a supporter of the American military. World.title: America needs thousands of blue-collar workers to manufacture our AI future
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The future of artificial intelligence may depend less on coders than on construction workers, electricians and factory technicians.

Tech companies are pouring money into new artificial intelligence (AI) data centers at an astounding clip, with Alphabet, Microsoft, Meta and Amazon expected to spend roughly $700 billion this year alone. And that doesn't include the costs of grid modernization and semiconductor capacity. But those ambitions keep running into the same problem – there aren't enough skilled workers to build the infrastructure that will power the AI economy.

By one estimate, the United States will need 140,000 additional skilled trades workers like electricians, HVAC technicians, welders and construction workers by 2030 to support AI infrastructure. How will we meet that demand?

A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES

The answer may lie across the Atlantic – in Switzerland. That nation's apprenticeship system has helped build one of the world's most innovative economies. And it's achieved this by creating clear pathways into skilled technical careers for generations of young people.

At a moment when America's AI ambitions are colliding with labor shortages, a Swiss-style model may offer exactly the kind of workforce pipeline the United States needs.

Switzerland's Vocational Education and Training system – or apprenticeship model, as it's commonly known – allows students as young as 15 to apprentice at companies across the country. These young people gain hands-on experience in the workplace while also developing industry-specific skills in the classroom.

The system has proven wildly popular, with roughly 70% of each Swiss age cohort participating in apprenticeship programs in industries ranging from manufacturing and pharmaceuticals to construction, banking, and healthcare. Crucially, these pathways are not educational dead ends. In fact, after completing their apprenticeships, students can either remain in their field or continue on to a university degree.

For companies, these apprenticeships are often sound investments, earning an average internal rate of return of 7% to 10%. They are also self-sustaining, as many apprentices end up staying with the firms where they trained, helping businesses recruit and develop new talent.

And since these programs are largely directed by private companies, they tend to align closely with the needs of the labor market. In this way, employers are able to teach apprentices the most relevant skills, allowing training programs to adapt quickly in fast-changing industries and helping companies fill critical workforce gaps.

This kind of model could help address the United States' current labor shortages.

After all, demand for these workers is only going to grow. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang recently predicted "six-figure salaries for people who are building chip factories or computer factories or AI factories."At the same time, many young Americans are gravitating toward more vocational work and trade schools – particularly amid rising higher-education costs and an increasingly uncertain white-collar job market.

ALL HANDS ON DECK: THE UNLIKELY WORKFORCE THAT CAN REBUILD AMERICA’S FLEET

Companies can build on that momentum – not just by offering higher pay, but by investing in Swiss-style apprenticeship programs. Some states are already doing exactly that.

For companies, these apprenticeships are often sound investments, earning an average internal rate of return of 7% to 10%.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Colorado's CareerWise program, which was modeled in part on the Swiss system, allows students to split time between the classroom and paid apprenticeships in industries ranging from advanced manufacturing to information technology. Similar programs are beginning to spread to other states as employers search for new ways to build long-term talent pipelines.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The next era of digital technology won't just depend on software and computing power – but on the workers needed to wire data centers, install electrical systems and construct the physical backbone of the AI economy. Switzerland has spent decades cultivating that workforce. America can learn from that example.

World.title: Mamdani’s affordability revolution stumbled as rent costs soar to record highs
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani rode his promise to make one of America’s most expensive cities more affordable all the way to City Hall. But for New Yorkers hunting for an apartment, rents have never been higher.

The citywide median asking rent reached $4,200 in June, up 5% from a year earlier and the highest recorded by StreetEasy since it began tracking the market in 2010. In Manhattan — the most densely populated NYC borough — the median cost of monthly rent climbed 5.1% to $4,965.

At the same time, apartments are becoming harder to find. The number of rentals available across the city fell 1.4% from a year ago, while Manhattan saw a 4.4% drop. It was even more dire for larger apartments in Manhattan, where the number of available two-bedroom units fell 9.3% and three-bedroom units dropped 11%.

Simply put, there are not enough apartment units to meet demand, and costs are reflecting that squeeze.

TRUMP'S HOUSING CHIEF PAINTS A GRIM PICTURE FOR HOMEOWNERSHIP IN ONE MAJOR AMERICAN CITY

The rental unit shortage presents an early test for Mamdani’s affordability agenda in New York.

While the socialist mayor has pledged to dramatically expand the city’s housing supply, his push to freeze rents on roughly 1 million rent-stabilized apartments has drawn warnings from economists who say the policy could discourage investment and make an already tight housing market even tighter.

Adam Lehodey of the Manhattan Institute told Fox News Digital that rent increases on rent-stabilized apartments have failed to keep pace with inflation for years, even as the costs of maintaining buildings have continued to rise. As a result, he said, "slowly but surely, landlords have less to invest in their properties."

He argued that this growing gap is leaving some building owners increasingly unable to cover basic operating expenses, which can lead to deferred maintenance and reduced investment in the city’s existing housing stock.

Lehodey also pointed to a second dynamic in the rent-stabilized market: tenants paying below-market rents have a strong incentive to stay in place, which reduces turnover and makes those apartments harder for prospective renters to find.

"People who are looking for apartments can't find apartments," Lehodey said. "People aren't giving them up, even if they have too much room."

MAMDANI'S RENT FREEZE, TAX HIKES A 'ONE-TWO WEALTH DESTRUCTION PUNCH,' ECONOMISTS WARN

Other economists have sounded similar warnings, arguing that uncertainty surrounding Mamdani’s broader tax and regulatory agenda could also discourage the investment needed to expand the city’s housing supply.

"Merely the threat of a more hostile tax and regulatory environment has been enough to chill investment in New York City, and that’s already impacting prices," E.J. Antoni, chief economist at the Heritage Foundation, told Fox News Digital. "Builders and financiers aren’t going to start multi-year projects that might become unprofitable on Mamdani’s next whim."

Antoni previously told Fox News Digital that the problem goes beyond new construction, arguing that government limits on rents can reduce the number of apartments available and discourage investment in existing properties.

"Economists, whether they are on the right or on the left, essentially are in universal agreement, that when the government implements price controls in the rental market, you end up with housing shortages," Antoni said.

"And not only do you end up with fewer housing units available, but the quality of those units consistently goes down as well," he added.

Mamdani has argued that his rent freeze is only one piece of a broader effort to bring down housing costs. His administration has also laid out plans to dramatically increase the city’s housing supply, including a goal of building 200,000 new affordable homes over the next decade.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

For Mamdani, the challenge will be delivering enough new housing to ease a shortage that is already pushing rents to records, while pursuing a rent freeze that critics warn could discourage investment in the apartments New York already has.

Mamdani's office did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on surging rent costs.

World.title: New Mississippi law expands death penalty to include inmates on child sexual battery convictions
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A new Mississippi law added sexual battery of a child under 12 to the list of crimes eligible for the death penalty.

Senate Bill 2821, which took effect July 1, creates the crime of "capital sexual battery" and allows prosecutors to seek the death penalty against defendants 18 or older in qualifying cases involving victims younger than 12.

If a defendant is convicted, the jury must unanimously find at least two specific aggravating factors beyond a reasonable doubt before the defendant is eligible for the death penalty. At least 8 of the 12 jurors must then recommend death. But if the death penalty is not recommended by jurors, the mandatory sentence would be life in prison without parole.

ACCUSED CHARLIE KIRK ASSASSIN TYLER ROBINSON ASKS JUDGE TO TAKE POTENTIAL DEATH PENALTY OFF TABLE

State Sen. Jeremy England, the bill's author, said the legislation seeks to give the worst punishment for crimes against the state's most vulnerable population.

"That is a crime that, I think, shocks the conscience, certainly. Those are the worst types of crimes against the most innocent of our citizens here in Mississippi," England said, according to WLBT.

But critics question whether capital punishment serves as a deterrent to crimes against young victims or if it could lead to children becoming too afraid to come forward knowing that doing so may end someone's life.

Abraham Bonowitz, executive director of Death Penalty Action, told the outlet he once supported the death penalty but changed his position, arguing that executions are unnecessary when a life sentence keeps an inmate permanently behind bars.

"There is no need for executions when we can throw away the key," Bonowitz said.

TWO FLORIDA INMATES DIE IN RARE DOUBLE EXECUTION AFTER SCOTUS DENIES STAYS

Bonowitz also said extending the death penalty to child sexual assault cases could deter victims from alerting authorities of the abuse they endured.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Most of those kinds of crimes are by people that the child knows and you’re asking a child to then testify against a relative and try to get them executed," he said.

World.title: Police rescue 60 cats and kittens from abandoned sailboat off Washington beach after 6-day operation
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

An abandoned sailboat off a Washington beach was home to an unexpected crew: 60 cats and kittens, many of them some frightened and malnourished.

The Tacoma Police Department said the unusual rescue began Aug. 6 when its Marine Services Unit responded to reports of an abandoned 40-foot sailboat in the waters off Owen Beach.

Officers initially discovered more than 30 cats and kittens living in unsafe conditions aboard the vessel, with many appearing frightened and malnourished. Marine Services began coordinating with Animal Control and the department's Forensics Unit to safely remove the animals.

What initially appeared to be a rescue involving more than 30 cats eventually grew to 60 over the course of a rescue effort spanning six days.

FLORIDA MAN ALLEGEDLY KILLS FAMILY'S KITTENS IN FRONT OF TEENAGE DAUGHTER AS FORM OF PUNISHMENT: OFFICIALS

"That's a wrap! The final cat is off the boat. Fur real this time!" police wrote. "Final cat count: 60!"

Police said Animal Control was "as certain as they can be that all cats have officially disembarked."

"That's all for meow!" the department joked online.

Despite believing all 60 cats had been rescued, police said they would continue making trips to the boat this week as a precaution.

HERO SHEEPDOG BECOMES UNLIKELY RESCUE PARTNER AFTER UNEXPECTED MOVE AIDS FIRST RESPONDERS

"While we believe we have safely removed all of the cats from the boat, as any cat owner knows, cats are exceptionally good at hiding," police said. "Because there is always a possibility that a cat may remain onboard, our work isn't quite finished."

The department said the additional searches would be conducted under the authority of a search warrant.

Police said Marine Services has also begun the process of having the legally registered vessel moved.

Authorities asked people visiting Owen Beach or boating nearby to notify Animal Control if they spot another cat aboard the vessel, while warning members of the public not to attempt their own rescues.

FLORIDA MAIL CARRIER ACCUSED OF SNATCHING PETS ON ROUTE, TRAPPING 100-PLUS CATS AND DOGS IN ‘HOARDING’ HOUSE

"We know many animal lovers in our community want to help, and we appreciate the concern for these cats," police said. "However, this remains an active criminal case. Our teams are working hard to protect the animals while also protecting the integrity of the investigation."

"PLEASE DO NOT BOARD THE VESSEL unless you are the legal owner," police added.

The warning followed an incident in which private cat rescue trapper Camille Sutherland told KING 5 she boarded the vessel overnight and captured two cats, which she took to the Humane Society.

Sutherland told the outlet she was trying to help and believed authorities were taking too long to rescue the animals.

Police told KING 5 that the unauthorized boarding complicated their investigation into the vessel's owner.

Police have not announced any arrests or charges in connection with the case.

More than 40 of the 60 rescued cats were taken to the Humane Society for Tacoma & Pierce County, while the remaining animals were placed in foster homes in the area, according to KING 5.

World.title: Dallas-Fort Worth airport to install Islamic foot wash stations inside bathrooms
World.content:

Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport will install Islamic foot wash stations inside bathrooms at the facility, according to the Texas Department of Licensing and Regulation.

The project was officially registered with Texas regulators on July 31, according to documents detailing the project.

The installation of the Wudu ablution stations is expected to be complete by the end of the year.

"Project consists of adding Ablution stations to existing concourse level restrooms in Terminal D, one Men's ablution station in existing men's restroom and one Women's ablution station in the existing women's restroom," the project details read.

TRAVELERS CLASH AFTER TSA SHARES SURPRISING GUIDANCE ABOUT AIRPORT ETIQUETTE

It is privately funded and expected to cost around $300,000, the documents state.

The updates aim to prevent water on standard restroom floors and protect sink counters.

Similar low-level basins and interfaith spaces already exist at other major international airport hubs across the U.S., including Chicago O'Hare.

Some conservatives were outraged online over the project plan, while others urged people to take a more measured approach, noting that the new stations are not about pushing any ideology.

"People are freaking out over foot-washing stations at DFW, but let’s look at the actual facts before jumping to conclusions. This isn't about pushing an ideology—it's basic airport management," conservative activist Ryan Fournier wrote on social media.

"Safety & Plumbing: People washing their feet in standard bathroom sinks creates soaked, slippery floors and breaks the counters. Low-level wudu basins keep the restrooms dry and safe for everyone," he continued.

World.title: Single ticket bought in Illinois wins $1 billion Powerball jackpot
World.content:
To the tens of thousands and likely more dreaming about a $1 billion Powerball win, the anticipation is over: Someone who bought a ticket in Illinois won it all.

A single ticket sold in the state matched all six numbers and the Powerball to win Wednesday’s $1.04 billion jackpot, which is the eighth largest in the history of the lottery game, organizers said.

The winning numbers were 4, 26, 66, 67 and 69, with a Powerball of 9.

If it is taken all at once as a lump-sum payment, the jackpot is $450.5 million before taxes. Otherwise, it would be an annuity paid out over 29 years.

A jackpot of $1 billion was once extraordinary, but the game has made changes to increase the amount in the top prize.

The biggest one so far was the $2.04 billion jackpot won in 2022, and the second and third biggest — $1.817 billion and $1.787 billion — were both won last year.

The last time someone won the Powerball jackpot was May 2. When no one wins, the jackpot rolls over and increases. Once someone wins, it resets to a default $20 million.

The game recently expanded to allow bettors in the United Kingdom to participate. That started July 21.

In the U.S., it’s played in 45 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands.

World.title: Army gynecologist pleads not guilty to secretly recording patients
World.content:
An Army gynecologist charged with secretly video recording patients during exams pleaded not guilty Wednesday.

Dr. Blaine McGraw is charged with indecent visual recording, as well as conduct unbecoming of an officer, willful disobedience of a superior officer and making a false statement. The Army Office of Special Trial Counsel previously alleged that there were 44 victims throughout 2025. McGraw’s patients included hundreds of service members and their spouses.

McGraw appeared before Col. Jorge Rivera, a military judge, at the Lawrence Williams Judicial Center at Fort Hood, Texas, on Wednesday, according to NBC affiliate KCEN of Temple.

According to information presented in court Wednesday, McGraw now faces nine charges and 273 specifications involving 93 alleged victims, the station reported. The Army has said the alleged conduct occurred from 2021 to 2026.

The specifications include 12 of sexual assault, 79 of attempted sexual assault, 66 of indecent recording and 91 of assault consummated by a battery, KCEN reported.

He was charged in December after the Army Criminal Investigation Division opened an inquiry in October following a complaint from a patient at Fort Hood. Most of the accusations are related to medical exams of female patients at the Carl R. Darnall Army Medical Center at Fort Hood, where he worked.

Blaine McGraw. Bell County Sheriff's Office

NBC News was first to report details of the allegations against McGraw, including an interview with a former patient who sued him after having learned he had recorded “nearly the entirety of her final appointment, including both the breast and pelvic examinations, without her knowledge or consent,” her lawsuit says.

Her lawsuit alleges that there are scores of additional victims and that Army leadership allowed McGraw to continue practicing for years after it received complaints about sexual misconduct — an allegation the Army denies. She is married to an active-duty service member and sued anonymously, using the name Jane Doe, to keep her identity private.

Fort Hood officials have said they immediately suspended McGraw and opened an investigation after they received the complaint in October. The commander at Darnall Army Medical Center told NBC News in November that he had identified more than 1,400 of McGraw’s patients to inform of the investigation.

McGraw also worked at Tripler Army Medical Center in Hawaii from June 2019 to June 2023. The Army notified his former patients there about the investigation and how to report any complaints, NBC News reported.

If you or someone you know has been sexually assaulted, call the National Sexual Assault Hotline at 1-800-656-4673. The hotline, run by the Rape, Abuse, & Incest National Network (RAINN), can put you in contact with your local rape crisis center. You can also access RAINN’s online chat service at rainn.org/get-help.

World.title: ‘Creepy thing to do’: Pardoned Jan. 6 defendant convicted in hair-touching case
World.content:
A pardoned Jan. 6 defendant was found guilty Wednesday of a single count of simple assault for sitting behind a woman on a train, touching her hair and posting the incident to social media.

Bryan Betancur, of Silver Spring, Maryland, was found guilty in Washington, D.C., Superior Court of surreptitiously fondling a woman’s hair on a Metro Red Line train in February.

“It’s just a creepy thing to do,” the judge said in court.

The victim identified in the video also spoke in court, saying, “I think about this video every single day. I think about this video every time I get on the Metro, which is twice every single day.”

She said it’s changed how she feels about being in public and that she feels paranoid and exposed after the incident.

“It was very upsetting and unsettling to see someone had touched me and posted about it on the internet without my consent,” she testified.

The maximum sentence for the charge, which is a misdemeanor, is 180 days. Betancur has already served 125 days after a judge ordered him held in custody in April over an alleged bail violation.

Bryan Betancur displays his certificate of pardon from President Donald Trump at a Jan. 6 memorial march in Washington this year. Chip Somodevilla / Getty Images file

Prosecutors indicated they would argue for more jail time, rather than giving Betancur credit for time served. In addition to jail time, he could receive a $1,000 fine.

A sentencing hearing is set for Thursday afternoon.

Betancur is also facing a stalking charge in Washington, D.C., and an additional assault and battery charge in Arlington, Virginia. The Arlington charge stems from an incident similar to the one he was convicted of Wednesday: He is accused of livestreaming himself fondling the hair of a different woman on a train there.

The FBI has said Betancur is a self-professed white supremacist, who was photographed holding a Confederate flag during the Jan. 6 insurrection.

It was part of a federal case against Betancur in which the FBI said he was on parole for burglary charges and wearing an ankle monitor while taking part in the insurrection of the Capitol. He was sentenced to jail but was later pardoned by President Donald Trump.

World.title: 3 takeaways from David Crowley’s comeback: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, we break down the key lessons from last night’s Wisconsin primary upset. Plus, Andrea Mitchell digs into the fraying relationship between President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.

— Adam Wollner

3 takeaways from David Crowley’s comeback

Analysis by Adam Wollner

Five weeks ago, Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley dropped out of the Wisconsin governor’s race, saying “it has become clear that I will not be the Democratic nominee.”

Today, that’s exactly what he is. Crowley’s primary victory is one of the more astonishing political comebacks in recent memory. He relaunched his campaign 10 days after he ended it, as establishment Democrats embarked on a last-minute mission to stop the rise of state Rep. Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist.

Here are three reasons that help explain how he pulled it off.

1. An unusually volatile race. There were several twists and turns that shook up the final stretch of the primary. In addition to Crowley’s re-emergence, two other prominent contenders — Lt. Gov. Sara Rodriguez and former Lt. Gov. Mandela Barnes — also abruptly dropped out last month.

Left with two leading candidates in Hong and Crowley, neither of whom had ever run statewide, a large chunk of the electorate didn’t decide who they were backing until late. A Marquette University Law School poll conducted July 22-27 showed that a third of primary voters were undecided and 16% backed Barnes, who would end his campaign days later. The survey showed Hong at 38% — close to her final vote share, as Bridget Bowman points out — and Crowley at 7%.

That suggests undecided voters who weren’t previously tuned in to the midsummer contest swung sharply to Crowley in the closing days.

2. Democratic voters still prize electability. Another important development that happened after the well-regarded Marquette poll was in the field: Hong underwent more intense scrutiny. During a series of national interviews, Hong was pressed on — and walked back — some of her past controversial positions, fueling concerns she was too far outside the mainstream to win a general election in the swing state.

That argument was furthered by Tony Evers, the popular outgoing two-term governor, as he barnstormed the state with Crowley.

Madison voter Ali Plummer told Shaquille Brewster that she backed a lot of Hong’s policies, but ultimately cast her ballot for Crowley because she’s a “risk-averse person.”

“In the primary, you want to vote for your conscience, but I really was like, we’d have to beat Tom Tiffany, so I voted for David Crowley,” Plummer said.

3. The importance of TV ads. As far as competitive statewide contests go, Wisconsin didn’t see much in the way of ad spending. But the ads that did air were largely pro-Crowley leading up to primary day.

Crowley’s campaign and allied outside groups spent $4 million on ads after he got back into the race. By comparison, Hong’s campaign and groups supporting her spent less than a half-million dollars on ads throughout the primary — none of which ran on broadcast or cable TV.

Even though campaigns have been forced to adapt to an increasingly fractured media environment, old-fashioned TV ads have not outlived their usefulness.

🗳️ More from last night’s primaries:

Minnesota Senate: Progressive Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan defeated moderate Rep. Angie Craig in the Democratic primary. She will face former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya in November.

John Larson became the 10th House incumbent to lose a primary this year, falling to former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin , who had called for generational change.

Rep. became the 10th House incumbent to lose a primary this year, falling to former Hartford Mayor , who had called for generational change. Wisconsin’s 3rd District: Rebecca Cooke won the Democratic nomination, setting up a rematch against GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden this fall.

won the Democratic nomination, setting up a rematch against GOP Rep. this fall. South Carolina Senate: Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman advanced to a runoff in the special Republican primary.

The troubled Trump-Netanyahu alliance

Analysis by Andrea Mitchell

What had once been a close alliance, if not a friendship, between President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu seems to have gone off course.

As Netanyahu faces what could be an existential election showdown at the end of October, and Trump is mired in a military stalemate with Iran that could jeopardize Republican hopes in the midterms a week later, their political goals are diverging.

That was apparent during the prime minister’s trip to Washington last week to attend the funeral of the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. Extending his visit for two more days, Netanyahu and Trump exchanged the requisite public expressions of solidarity during an Oval Office meeting. And, perhaps for security reasons, Trump extended Netanyahu the privilege of staying literally across the street in Blair House, the official guest house, enabling easy access for top White House and Cabinet officials to come over for meetings.

Still, fractures became apparent in their once rock-solid relationship. With questions swirling about a profanity-laced phone call Trump had in June with Netanyahu about Israel’s continued strikes in Lebanon, their military strategies in the region are no longer aligned. Netanyahu was cut out of the June memorandum of understanding that U.S. negotiators and their Arab intermediaries reached with Iran for what was to be a six-week ceasefire while the adversaries pursued a longer-term nuclear agreement. The ceasefire did not hold.

More recently, it is not clear that Trump ever mentioned during last week’s Oval Office meeting that the White House would be announcing a purported disarmament agreement for Gaza two days later.

It was billed as a breakthrough — the second phase of last fall’s Gaza agreement, which paved the way for the exchange of Palestinian prisoners of war for the remaining Israeli hostages. Now, according to senior administration officials, Hamas would disarm and relinquish power in Gaza as Israel gradually withdrew from the strip. An international stabilization force — still unspecified — would monitor the ceasefire, while an unnamed verification committee would oversee Hamas’ disarmament. The White House also proclaimed a major achievement for its much-heralded Board of Peace.

The announcement was so lacking in specifics that analysts speculated it was timed to distract from the failure to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and obtain a ceasefire with Iran. On a promising note, Hamas seemed to offer its provisional agreement. But for several days, there was official silence from Israel.

Then, after it was denounced by Netanyahu’s two right-wing national security ministers, key members of his coalition government, the prime minister flatly rejected the 15-point plan as a nonstarter. He made it clear that Israel will not withdraw from Gaza before Hamas disarms. And while the original deal had called for Israel to occupy only 53% of Gaza, it has taken back more than 70% of the territory. Israel also won’t agree to Hamas turning its weapons over to a Palestinian police force, as the plan envisions.

Since Netanyahu’s verbal blast, Trump has commented on the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool controversy, the successful confirmation of Attorney General Todd Blanche and his covert departure from last month’s NATO meeting in Ankara. As of now, he has said nothing about his erstwhile partner in the war against Iran.

Back-to-school season is here, and before you know it, so will the end of summer. And like every change in the season, there’s also a change in wardrobe. You may swap your t-shirts and swimsuits for sweaters and coats and your sandals for boots. If you’re a college student, then chances are you’re on the lookout for items to store under your dorm bed.

To make the most of that area, we consulted organizing experts on what to keep in mind when buying under-bed storage, and compiled a list of recommendations with their guidance in mind.

Want more from NBC Selected? 

The best under-bed storage

To find the best under-bed storage, we asked three experts for recommendations: Rachel Winkler, owner of home organizing service Tidyspot, home organizer Pia Thompson and Nancy Meck of Meck Organizing.

Our list also includes options that have at least a 4-star average rating from 500 reviews or more on Amazon or at least 50 reviews on their brand sites.

Best wheeled under-bed storage

You can take away its structure by removing its internal board, making it easy to fold up and store. It currently comes in three colors.

Best vacuum storage bags

These vacuum sealable options are ideal long-term storage, since packing the bags and sucking the air from the bags can be more of a process. That said, they give you a lot more space than the other options on this list. This pack from Spacesaver contains six bags. Each bag comes with a double-zip seal and triple-seal turbo valve to get all the air from the bag in the suction process, reducing the volume of the bag by 80%, according to Spacesaver.

How we picked the best under-bed storage

There are a few important factors to remember when choosing the best under-bed storage option for your living space. Here’s everything our experts recommended keeping in mind to make this list:

Bed height : Whether you are a college student, recent grad or are just looking for a set of under-bed storage containers, you must consider how tall your bed and bed frame will sit above the floor, especially if you have risers. This will determine the best height for the containers that you get. If you have a bed frame with a specific height, such as ones common in dorm rooms, then it’s best to go with tall containers since you’ll have to use more vertical space. If you have a bed frame that only sits above the floor a foot or less, then you should opt for flat under bed storage options that optimize surface area instead of height.

What you’ll be storing: You should also keep in mind that different under bed storage containers are best for different types of clothing, accessories and other items. For example, a storage container that is tall rather than flat is best for items that are stackable or won’t get damaged when piled on something, such as first aid kits, toiletries, folded clothes and books. A flat and wide under bed storage container is best for items that aren’t tall or ones that are compatible with lying flat, such as a blanket, some types of shoes and sandals, office supplies and more.

For example, a storage container that is tall rather than flat is best for items that are stackable or won’t get damaged when piled on something, such as first aid kits, toiletries, folded clothes and books. A flat and wide under bed storage container is best for items that aren’t tall or ones that are compatible with lying flat, such as a blanket, some types of shoes and sandals, office supplies and more. Features: Another important part of looking for under bed storage is prioritizing ones that have features that make them easy to maneuver and remove from under the bed. Examples of this include ones with handles on the top and sides, wheels on the bottom and divers for shoes. I made sure to include options with these features and more.

How to shop for under-bed storage

Before buying under bed storage — whether it’s plastic bins, boxes or fabric containers — you should determine your ideal measurements and preferred materials.

Measurements

First and foremost, you probably want to take out a tape measure, suggests Winkler and Thompson. “Before purchasing under-bed storage, you must measure the area under your bed, taking into account the height as well as the location of any support beams,” says Winkler. “All beds are different, so you want to ensure what you buy will fit.”

If your bed is lower to the floor, bed risers could be an option for added height. “These have come a long way since the ones from our college days,” says Thompson. Instead of ones made from plastic that can clash with the rest of your bedroom’s design, retailers like Walmart and Wayfair offer them in wood, metal and more.

Materials and features

Under-bed storage itself is usually made from plastic, canvas or felt. Deciding between them depends on how much you have to pack away. Winkler recommends canvas for storing bulkier bedding and jackets since the material is more “malleable than a standard under-the-bed plastic storage box.” But that doesn’t mean you should completely cut off plastic — clear plastic can be helpful for knowing exactly what’s inside a container, she added. For special items like a wedding dress or a vintage, unique piece, Thompson advises looking for archival garment bags. These bags are designed to keep clothes preserved and protected from humidity and other potential damage.

For everyday items, search for storage that’s designed to repel dust and dirt since both are more likely to gather underneath a bed, Thompson suggests. Accordingly, seek out containers with closed lids or zippers to avoid finding dusty items once you open an under bed storage. And wheels “allow you to easily access what you need, especially if they are heavy and help you avoid using your arm strength to pull out storage,” according to Thompson.

World.title: Lindsay Clancy sobs loudly, says "I can't do it" amid gruesome trial testimony
World.content:
Lindsay Clancy's murder trial was paused multiple times Wednesday afternoon as she sobbed loudly and said "I can't do it" during testimony about the injuries her children suffered when they were killed.

Jurors were sent out twice for recess as Clancy had emotional reactions to the testimony.

Clancy, 36, is charged with first-degree murder in the deaths of her three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan, in their Duxbury home on Jan. 24, 2023. She has pleaded not guilty.

Prosecutors Jennifer Sprague and Shanan Buckingham said Clancy planned the murders and faked a suicide attempt.

Clancy's attorney Kevin Reddington said Clancy admits to killing her children but says she should not be held criminally responsible because she was overmedicated and suffering from postpartum psychosis.

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington consoles his client, Lindsay Clancy, who is sobbing, during Clancy's murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Mark Stockwell/Boston Herald via AP, Pool

Lindsay Clancy sobs during testimony

Dr. Renee Stonebridge from the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner in Boston took the stand Wednesday afternoon. She spoke about the injuries observed on the three Clancy children when the autopsies were performed.

The direct questioning from the prosecution lasted less than 10 minutes, and Reddington did not cross-examine the witness. Clancy could be seen crying during the testimony.

As Sprague began to call the next witness, Judge William Sullivan called for a recess as Clancy was loudly sobbing with her head in her hands. WBZ-TV's Penny Kmitt, who was in the courtroom, said that Clancy's father was crying as well.

After about 15 minutes, all parties came back into the courtroom, including Clancy and the 18 jurors.

Judge Sullivan issued a reminder to the jurors.

"Members of the jury, I just kind of want to revisit an instruction I've given you a few times, I think, during the course of this trial. It's important to understand, remember sometimes as evidence is presented in the trial that creates an emotional reaction, but as jurors who have taken an oath to follow the law, I'm instructing you that the law says you must separate any emotional reaction on your part from the informational value and weight that the evidence produces," Sullivan said. "Your verdict in this case is going to have to be based solely on the evidence and it cannot be based on sympathy, or anger, or passion or prejudice. So you've got to keep that in mind."

Medical Examiner Dr. Barbara Olsen then took the stand. After several minutes, Clancy began to cry again and could be heard on the courtroom microphone saying "I can't do it."

Judge Sullivan sent jurors out of the room. Several minutes later, all parties were back in the courtroom and Olsen was on the stand again.

As Olsen continued to testify, Clancy began sobbing again and laid her head on the table.

Reddington objected at one point, saying, "It's obvious what she wants." He objected several times, becoming visibly frustrated.

Olsen was able to complete her testimony and court ended for the day around 4 p.m. as scheduled.

Witness Latiesha Dukes, a mental health clinician, testifies during Lindsay Clancy's murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Mark Stockwell/Boston Herald via AP, Pool

Mental health counselor takes witness stand

Earlier, Latiesha Dukes, a mental health counselor who worked with Clancy, was on the stand for about two hours and stepped down just before 1 p.m.

Dukes, who worked at the time for South Shore Hospital, first met with Clancy in late November 2022 into early December of that year. She met with Clancy four times total during that time period.

Dukes said she worked closest on Clancy's case with Rebecca Jollotta, a psychiatric nurse practitioner who finished her testimony on Tuesday.

"Her presenting concerns were anxiety, lack of sleep, suicidal ideation, thoughts of no longer wanting to live or be here," Dukes said.

Dukes testified that her feeling about Clancy's diagnosis was postpartum anxiety because she did not have anxiety about most things. She recommended outpatient therapy, continued use of medications, and seeing her for weekly therapy.

On Dec. 5, 2022, Clancy reported that she had a difficult weekend and had intrusive thoughts about wanting to die.

Following her meeting with Clancy that day, Dukes said she recommended partial hospitalization.

On Dec. 19, 2022, Dukes said Clancy seemed more engaged during a telehealth visit, was able to smile and laugh and was enjoying time with her family.

Dukes testified that on her last visit with Clancy, she seemed to show an improvement of mood and ability to connect with others. She said that Clancy did not show signs of mania, delusions, paranoia or psychosis.

On cross-examination, Reddington asked about Clancy's reluctance to take medications.

"She was concerned about becoming addicted to medication, yes," Dukes said.

On Tuesday with Jollotta on the stand, Reddington attempted to show that Clancy tried to attend an outpatient postpartum program at Women and Infants Hospital of Rhode Island for two weeks in December 2022, but was turned away on the first day because they wanted to find out if she was overmedicated.

"Would you be surprised if I told you that they said they could not help her because she was overmedicated?" Reddington asked Dukes on Wednesday.

"It would surprise me, yes," Dukes said.

Reddington also questioned Dukes over her testimony that Clancy laughed during her final visit, saying it was not in her notes.

After Dukes stepped down, Cameron Daley, who was working for the Duxbury Police Department and stood watch outside of Clancy's room at Brigham and Women's Hospital after she killed her children, testified for less than five minutes.

Massachusetts State Police investigator testifies

Earlier, Sgt. Dan Lawlor testified. Lawlor has worked for the Massachusetts State Police for nine years.

The night of the children's deaths, Lawlor went to South Shore Hospital in Weymouth and saw Clancy, who was unable to speak and suffering from injuries after jumping out a second-floor window.

Lawlor went to Boston Children's Hospital to check on 8-month-old Callan's status, then later went to Brigham and Women's Hospital, where Clancy was transferred, to stand watch outside the room.

Reddington took over cross-examination after about 15 minutes. The defense attorney asked Lawlor about how no one was allowed to get into Clancy's hospital room. Eventually, Reddington got a court order for psychologist Paul Zeizel to enter the room to meet with Clancy.

"Isn't it fair to say that one of the contentions of the district attorneys is that Paul Zeizel, my doctor, that I got a court order to get in and see her, told her to call Pat and tell him that she heard voices?" Reddington asked.

When Reddington referred to Pat, he was speaking about Patrick Clancy. Lindsay and Patrick Clancy were married at the time of their children's deaths, but have since divorced.

Following that question, the judge asked to see attorneys at sidebar due to an objection by the prosecution. After about 20 minutes, the judge sent jurors out of the room to question Lawlor without the jury present.

With the jury out of the room, Reddington asked about Lawlor's recollection that lead investigator Josh McKelligan had told him that at some point when Clancy was hospitalized, she called Patrick to indicate she was hearing voices. Reddington suggested that the theory investigators were trying to use was that Zeizel had suggested Clancy make the phone call.

"I don't know if it's a theory or not, I just recall the conversation," Lawlor said.

The prosecutor then questioned Lawlor without the jury present.

"You never had a conversation with the prosecution about what the theory was, did you?" she asked. Lawlor said he had not, saying it was only with the fellow trooper.

"Is this conversation guiding your testimony?" Buckingham asked. Lawlor said it was not.

The judge took arguments under advisement and the jury returned a short time later.

With the jury back in the room, Reddington asked Lawlor if he and McKelligan talked about the theory that Zeizel "is the reason that she told her husband she heard voices." Lawlor said they did talk about that theory.

"There's no investigator basis for that, that's McKelligan's speculation, correct?" Reddington asked. Lawlor said that was correct.

Buckingham then questioned Lawlor.

"Is it fair to say you oftentimes will have conversations as investigations are unfolding with other investigators that you're working on the case with about the case, potential evidence, theories of the case?" Buckingham asked.

Lawlor said that was true, and added that theories can change over time.

Buckingham asked Lawlor, "You didn't hear anything that occurred in that room that day that you were there when Dr. Zeizel was there, did you?"

"I did not hear anything," Lawlor said, concluding his testimony at around 10:45 a.m.

Lindsay Clancy listens to testimony during her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Mark Stockwell/Boston Herald via AP, Pool

Lindsay Clancy trial

The jury heard from a psychiatric nurse practitioner Tuesday who specializes in postpartum patients. Rebecca Jollotta said she met with Clancy three times late in 2022, a few weeks before the murders. Jollotta was the 62nd witness in the trial.

Judge William Sullivan said the attorneys told him the proceedings are "well on schedule and somewhat ahead of schedule."

If convicted of first-degree murder, Clancy faces life in prison without parole. If the jury finds that she was not criminally responsible for the deaths of her children, she will be sent to a state psychiatric hospital in Massachusetts.

If you or someone you know is in emotional distress or a suicidal crisis, you can reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline by calling or texting 988. You can also chat with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline here.

For more information about mental health care resources and support, The National Alliance on Mental Illness HelpLine can be reached Monday through Friday, 10 a.m. to 10 p.m. ET, at 1-800-950-NAMI (6264) or email info@nami.org.

World.title: My husband was kicked out of hospice. Here's what I learned.
World.content:
"No more operations," he said.

It was mid-January 2026, and my then-73-year-old husband, Mike Salmon, had just started bouncing back from a three-month ordeal of three operations related to aortic aneurysms, sepsis, and a terrifying descent into delirium tied to a stay in the intensive care unit. Now, after another potentially fatal aortic aneurysm and ambulance ride, the doctors clustered around his hospital bed said the fix involved two more major, risky operations.

If Mike did nothing, the aneurysm or sepsis would likely kill him, they predicted. How soon? "Weeks," one doctor said. "I'm astonished I've made it this far," Mike said. So, abruptly, we were shunted onto hospice care — the dead-end spur of the American medical system.

Mike Salmon's health improved so much under hospice care that he got kicked out. Kim Clark for KFF Health News

Hospice agencies manage care for patients expected to die within six months. They don't provide curative procedures or drugs. Instead, they aim to help families make terminally ill patients comfortable, typically at home, as an illness reaches its inevitable conclusion. Families provide most of the day-to-day care, and 85% have suggested they are very satisfied with their hospice's services, which include supplies of drugs and medical equipment, and visits from nurses, therapists, and aides.

More than 1.9 million Americans were enrolled in hospice in the last fiscal year. Over 80% of those patients stayed on hospice until they died — within four weeks, on average. But each year, about 6% of patients are kicked out because a hospice doctor decides they have stabilized or improved enough that they are no longer likely to die in the next six months.

In May, Mike joined that select group. His experience in and out of the hospice system revealed surprising lessons about how families can manage care. And getting removed from hospice revealed a little-known process that can represent a welcome respite for families like ours — but can be devastating for patients with serious chronic illnesses.

Here's what we learned in our four months on and off hospice.

Check before you choose

"Choose one." A hospital nurse handed me a list of local hospice agencies. The sooner we signed up, the sooner Mike could go home. Stunned by the suddenness of Mike's health emergency, I just pointed to the name at the top of the alphabetical list, assuming they were pretty much the same.

Big mistake. Medicare sets basic standards for the hospice agencies it reimburses, but some agencies are understaffed or poorly run. Amy Tucci, president of the Hospice Foundation of America, noted that some agencies provide extra therapy, aide support, and other services.

The problems with the organization I had chosen started immediately. Staffers were often late. They entered inaccurate medical information on Mike's paperwork and didn't make corrections when alerted. Medicare allows you to quit or change agencies, so I asked neighbors for recommendations. That was a good start, but Kristina Newport, chief medical officer of the American Academy of Hospice and Palliative Medicine, said I should also have checked the quality ratings on Medicare's Care Compare site and the National Hospice Locator. Those sites would have alerted me to our first agency's low ratings. Ideally, Newport said, patients or caregivers should call their area's top-rated agencies to find those that provide the services you need, such as staff members who speak the patient's native language, provide spiritual care that aligns with the patient's beliefs, or are stationed nearby to arrive quickly in an emergency.

The local, long-established nonprofit that neighbors recommended handled the transfer seamlessly. Its staff was punctual, accurate, and kind. The chef's kiss after we switched: A nurse from the original company we chose called to say she hoped I hadn't initiated the change because of "concerns about our care of your mother."

Some people get better on hospice

Research hasn't yet fully explored why, but some people actually see their health improve under hospice care. Studies have found, for example, that hospice patients with congestive heart failure or lung cancer live about a month longer, on average, than similar patients in the standard medical system.

Terry Bertholet, who teaches courses on elder law and hospice care at the University of Connecticut, said many patients benefit from hospice's careful pain management, and from leaving hospitals, where they risk infection and overtreatment. Returning home allowed Mike to get up and walk without waiting hours for an overworked nurse to unplug a bunch of monitors, and to enjoy real food. Also, the hospice nurse gave him medicine to help him sleep through the night. He soon started regaining weight and strength.

You can flunk out of hospice for not dying quickly enough

Medicare and many other insurers pay for hospice services only for patients whom physicians certify are likely to die within six months of the most recent assessment (not the date of enrollment), so hospice staff regularly reassess patients. Medicare audits agencies to check for fraud and demands repayment of funds provided for care of patients its auditors deem have not proved to be terminal. Hospices, good and bad, worry about their bottom lines and Medicare's fraud audits. They may feel pressure to discharge patients who threaten the organization's finances, even though such discharges can remove important care. "Medicare is worried about fraud and abuse, not about people not getting enough care," Bertholet said.

Especially for diagnoses with uncertain prognoses — such as dementia — if a patient improves or even stabilizes, hospice physicians might discharge the patient because they can no longer certify a likelihood of death within six months.

For some lucky reason, Mike's aneurysm and sepsis held off. By early May, his wounds had healed, and his strength had improved enough that he returned to gardening, playing bridge, and whipping up his signature lattice-topped blueberry-cinnamon pies. While we appreciated the convenience of the nurse's visits and the drug and medical supply delivery, we realized Mike no longer needed care, so we agreed with our agency's decision to discharge him.

For patients suffering from more debilitating diseases, discharges can be a "nightmare," said Krista Harrison, a hospice researcher at the University of California-San Francisco. Discharges often happen quickly. Medicare requires giving patients a minimum of two days' notice.

When Harrison's father-in-law, suffering from a neurodegenerative disease similar to Parkinson's, was discharged because his health seemed to plateau, the family scrambled to replace and pay for hospice-provided equipment such as a hospital bed and oxygen supply, and they had to quickly find and hire aides to replace the hospice aides. "Just getting his prescriptions reestablished and filled was a big deal," she said. Her father-in-law died six weeks after discharge, she said.

Do your homework to ensure appropriate care

Arming yourself with information about your risks and rights can help you get the hospice care you need when you need it.

Know your diagnosis. Discharges are unlikely for most cancer patients. But patients with dementia, heart disease, and Parkinson's often plateau. So they are disproportionately likely to be discharged, UCSF's Harrison said.

Discharges are unlikely for most cancer patients. But patients with dementia, heart disease, and Parkinson's often plateau. So they are disproportionately likely to be discharged, UCSF's Harrison said. Choose a highly rated hospice. Research shows for-profit hospice agencies are more likely to discharge patients than nonprofits. Medicare's Care Compare site will alert you to which is which.

Research shows for-profit hospice agencies are more likely to discharge patients than nonprofits. Medicare's Care Compare site will alert you to which is which. Keep your own records. Caregivers who can document, say, a patient's growing need for eating assistance can help hospice staff approve continuing care, or build a stronger appeal, UCSF's Harrison said.

Caregivers who can document, say, a patient's growing need for eating assistance can help hospice staff approve continuing care, or build a stronger appeal, UCSF's Harrison said. Keep your family doctor more informed. Doctors "don't have the financial interest" the hospice faces and could help you dispute a discharge, Bertholet advised.

Doctors "don't have the financial interest" the hospice faces and could help you dispute a discharge, Bertholet advised. Appeal quickly. Hospice agencies must provide information on appealing a discharge. But you must file the appeal (online or by phone) by noon on the day before the termination date, which may mean you have only a few hours if you've been given the minimum two days' notice, said Wey-Wey Kwok, a senior attorney for the Center for Medicare Advocacy.

Hospice agencies must provide information on appealing a discharge. But you must file the appeal (online or by phone) by noon on the day before the termination date, which may mean you have only a few hours if you've been given the minimum two days' notice, said Wey-Wey Kwok, a senior attorney for the Center for Medicare Advocacy. Reenroll. Patients can try reenrolling in hospice at any time. Another hospice agency may take you immediately. Or you can wait until the patient's health declines and try reenrolling with your original hospice agency, the Hospice Foundation's Tucci advised.

That last option is our plan. For now, Mike and I are enjoying these unexpected bonus days. But whenever fate catches up with him, Mike said, he's comforted to know he'll get good care from the hospice's staff. "They'll try to improve the quality of what time I have left," he said.

KFF Health News is a national newsroom that produces in-depth journalism about health issues and is one of the core operating programs at KFF — the independent source for health policy research, polling, and journalism.

World.title: $1.04 billion Powerball jackpot won in Illinois
World.content:
A single ticket in Illinois won a Powerball jackpot of $1.04 billion Wednesday night, the game says. The ticket was purchased at a gas station in the city of Quincy, which is on the Mississippi River about halfway down the Illinois coast.

The winning numbers were 4, 26, 66, 67 and 69, with a Powerball of 9.

The jackpot, which reached the $1 billion mark soon after Monday's drawing didn't produce a winner, was the eighth-largest Powerball grand prize ever and 15th $1 billion pot of gold in U.S. lottery history.

The cash value for a lump-sum payment was $450.5 million. Winners can also choose to take their prize in 30 payments over 29 years that increase by 5% per year. Both the lump sum payout and the annuity payout totals are before taxes.

Wednesday's jackpot was Powerball's biggest of 2026.

The last time a billion-dollar jackpot was won was in December, when one ticket in Arkansas had all the numbers for a $1.82 billion prize — lotto's second-largest.

Wednesday's drawing was the 44th since a Powerball jackpot was won on May 2, when tickets purchased in Florida and Texas split a $20 million prize.

The drawing was the first to possibly have a winner from the U.K., which began selling tickets in late July. Powerball is played in 45 states, the U.S. Virgin Islands and Washington, D.C. Tickets are $2 each.

The odds of winning a Powerball jackpot are just 1 in 292.2 million.

World.title: Student shot during argument in Georgia high school bathroom, officials say
World.content:
A Warner Robins high school will stay closed for the rest of the week after one student was injured in a shooting Wednesday afternoon on the campus, officials said. A 14-year-old student is in custody.

The Houston County Sheriff's Office reports that the shooting happened at Warner Robins High School. The sheriff's office said that one student was injured in the gunfire and was taken to a local hospital for treatment.

The sheriff's office had initially stated that two people were injured, but Houston County Sheriff Matt Moulton later clarified that only one person was hurt.

An argument in the bathroom of a high school in Warner Robins, Georgia, ended with one student shot and another in custody, officials said. WGXA

In a news briefing Wednesday night, Moulton said the shooting happened at around 2:15 p.m. local time in one of the school's bathrooms. Investigators believe two ninth-grade students got into an argument that eventually escalated, and one of the students pulled out a gun and shot the other, the sheriff told reporters.

The 14-year-old who fired the gun fled the school on foot, Moulton said. The teen was eventually apprehended in a nearby neighborhood.

"Fortunately, what could have been a much worse incident was minimized to us only having one student injured," Moulton said.

Authorities have not said how the teen obtained the firearm, or who it may be registered to. They have also not shared what he may be facing.

Officials say that Warner Robins High School will be closed for the rest of the week for all students. Staff will not come in on Thursday. The school's crisis team will be on campus on Friday and Monday to support students and staff.

Warner Robins is located in Central Georgia, about 100 miles south of Atlanta.

Officials react to shooting at Warner Robins High School

Georgia lawmakers say the Houston County community is in their thoughts after Wednesday's shooting.

Warner Robins Mayor LaRhonda W. Patrick said her community was saddened to hear that the incident could happen so close to home.

"This type of incident impacts our students, faculty, and parents, but also our entire community. We appreciate all of our public safety officers, police and fire, for their rapid response in protection of our children," she wrote on Facebook. "We shall overcome together."

In a statement on X, Gov. Brian Kemp said he was grateful for the men and women who responded to the scene at the high school.

"Their action quickly brought the situation under control and kept students, faculty, and staff safe," Kemp wrote. "As we wait for more details to emerge, we're thankful for all those who keep our classrooms safe."

Sen. Raphael Warnock said he and his office were closely following the reports and that his prayers were with the student who was injured.

"I'm grateful to the law enforcement officers and first responders on the scene," Warnock wrote.
