World.title: ‘That wasn’t my son’: Mother of Berlin Pride attacker confronts his turn to terror
World.content:
In the wake of the devastating events of July 25, Abdul Ballout's mother tries to reconcile the son she knew with what authorities have established about his radicalization.

The woman whose son brought terror to Berlin is sitting on a worn red leather couch in a three-room apartment in Berlin’s Tiergarten district. It is Thursday afternoon, and she is pointing to the several missed calls on her phone screen.

They are all from the evening of July 25. They are all from the same person: Abdul Ballout, her son.

“He was terribly afraid for me,” she says quietly, her voice trembling. “I didn’t know why.”

She scrolls through the call log — the last traces of her child from the day of the attack, the day the unknown 21-year-old became the most wanted man in Germany.





She wants the public to get to know him — the son, the brother, the young man that she knew. “I find the way people talk about him incredibly painful, to be honest,” she says. “He was a good person.”

These are the subjective recollections of a mother who cannot and will not accept what her son did — and whose account is difficult to reconcile with what authorities established about him both before and after the attack.

She asks that her name not be published, nor any photograph or recording of her voice.

“I have two other children I have to think about,” she says.

* * *

On the evening of July 25, Ballout drove a rented van into a crowd on the fringes of Berlin’s Christopher Street Day parade.

After coming to a stop, he got out of the car and, according to authorities, began attacking people with a machete before fleeing on foot. One person was killed, and at least 29 were injured.

Around 20 hours later, special forces tracked Ballout to a garden in suburban Spandau, where he allegedly attempted to attack officers with a knife when they tried to arrest him. Police opened fire, and Ballout was shot dead. Nine days later, he was buried at Gatow Cemetery in Berlin.

A digital display on a bus stop in Berlin shows the photo of Abdul Ballout on July 26, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images

The person killed in Ballout’s attack was a 65-year-old woman from Poland who had traveled to Berlin with her daughter specifically for Christopher Street Day.

Not far away, a gay refugee from Iraq was celebrating at an electronic music event when panic spread through the streets. He had fled a country where being openly gay could put his life at risk. Germany was supposed to be different.

Granted anonymity to speak openly, he said: “For many people, freedom is something they never have to think about. For me, it means being able to love someone, to leave the house in the morning without wondering whether I could be attacked or killed for who I am.”

After the attack, he said, that feeling of safety cracked. “That old fear was suddenly back.”

Sitting across from me just weeks later, Ballout’s mother is dressed in all black, her headscarf framing a face that looks exhausted. There are deep shadows beneath her eyes. She speaks so quietly that at times I have to lean in to hear. The only other sound in the room is the monotonous hum of a fan.





On the coffee table lay empty coffee cups, an open packet of TUC crackers and a box of iron tablets. Propped between them is a framed photograph of Ballout, a faint grin on his face.

She doesn’t want to begin our conversation with the attack; she wants to start with her son. She reaches for her phone and starts showing me videos. In one, he is a little boy in swim trunks, running along a beach and laughing. In another, he is an adult, dancing exuberantly through the living room with his family. He jumps onto the couch and pulls his sisters along, making everyone laugh.

His mother talks of evenings spent together watching television or playing Monopoly, how he would sometimes cheat if he were about to lose. As she speaks, her smiles give way to tears, and her tears give way to smiles.

The contrast with the image of the terrorist could hardly be greater.

* * *

Four days before our interview, I visited the neighborhood where Ballout grew up. Children were crisscrossing a courtyard, neighbors leaning out of windows or standing outside doorways. I asked them about him.

All their answers were strikingly similar: “He always said hello;” “he was polite;” “he was helpful.”

No one disputed what Ballout did. No one tried to excuse it. And yet, no one could explain how the young man they knew was capable of such an act.

German police stand near a white van used in the attack. | Omer Messinger/Getty Images

Sitting in his mother’s living room a few days later, her phone rings, and for a brief moment, Arabic singing fills the room. “That’s his voice,” she says. Her ringtone is a recording of her son reciting an Islamic prayer.

But is it just an innocuous recording?

Court records show Ballout repeatedly posted videos containing Islamic State propaganda dating back to 2024, before starting to circulate recordings of his own. In some of the audio files obtained by WELT, which is — like POLITICO — part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters network, he recited the Quran; in others, he appeared to preach. He had hundreds of followers on TikTok and Telegram, with comments praising his voice.

But Ballout’s online messages were radical, speaking of “unbelievers,” God’s “agonizing punishment,” and his rejection of democracy and the German legal system.





Online, he went by the name Abu Muawiyah — a reference to the first caliph of the Umayyad dynasty who emerged victorious over the Prophet Muhammad’s son-in-law Ali and his followers, from which Shiite Islam later emerged. It is also a signal of his shifting faith, as Ballout converted from Shiite to Sunni Islam in 2021.

Was this also a break with his family? His mother gives no indication it was.

She speaks calmly about religion, and without hesitation. She says she was born in Beirut and grew up in Germany. She can neither read nor write Arabic and has therefore never read the Quran in its original language.

German policemen scan the ground of Tiergarten park, near the scene of the attack. | Omer Messinger/Getty Images

“I’m not particularly strict about religion,” she says. But her son was different.

For the last several years, he had increasingly been trying to push her toward stricter observance, urging her to pray regularly, to take her religious obligations more seriously and to engage more deeply with Islam.

“He told me every single day how important it was to pray and that it was my duty.”

* * *

Speaking about the days leading up to the attack, one word keeps coming up in our conversation: fear.

Her son had changed, she says. He seemed more nervous, more tense, more restless. He had started changing his phone number constantly — at least five times in 10 days.

“Why are you changing your number again?” she had asked him. But his answer was always roughly the same. Some people kept calling him; he felt followed, harassed and no longer safe.





To this day, it makes no sense to his mother. But to investigators, this is the behavior of someone who had realized he was on their radar — and was planning something big.

In late May 2026, Germany’s Federal Criminal Police Office classified Ballout as a high-risk individual capable of committing a serious act of politically motivated violence. And the reasons for this are documented across dozens of pages of case files.

In 2021, Ballout took part in street dawah events organized by a Salafist group in Berlin, where Islamists seek new followers and often distribute copies of the Quran. This is where Berlin’s State Criminal Police Office first took an interest in him.

From 2023 onward, he increasingly frequented mosques influenced by Salafist ideology — which espouses an ultraconservative, fundamentalist view of Sunni Islam — while investigators noted he began openly expressing his rejection of Germany’s free democratic order.

Flowers and candles lie at a makeshift memorial in Tiergarten park on July 27, 2026, two days after the attack. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images

In the summer of 2024, he repeatedly posted propaganda from the Islamic State organization, and in May 2025, attempted to join the terrorist group in Africa but was refused entry into Mauritania. Shortly after, he tried to travel to Syria via Lebanon to receive weapons training, communicating with IS members through Telegram.

Lebanese authorities arrested Ballout in July 2025, and a military court sentenced him to three months in prison for incitement to religious conflict. In court, he spoke of two cousins on his father’s side who had died fighting in Syria.

Returning to Germany in November 2025, Ballout was then arrested at Berlin airport and taken into custody on suspicion of preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state. According to the case files, he presented himself as a preacher in prison. His religious fervor intensified, and his appearance changed. Ballout’s father later told Der Spiegel that he had argued with his son over his long hair and beard, which he regarded as a sign of religious extremism.





Finally, in May of this year, Ballout was sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison but was initially released under the supervision of a probation officer while the court deferred its verdict on whether to suspend the sentence. This judicial decision is now at the center of a heated debate in Germany over how the country handles high-risk Islamist offenders.

From then on, police kept him under surveillance.

Did his mother know any of this? She shakes her head.

* * *

There is only one incident Ballout’s mother is willing to discuss: July 2 this year, his birthday. That day, she says, showed just how closely her son was being monitored.

Ballout had been playing outside with his sister, spraying her with a water gun, she says. Shortly afterward, officers from the State Criminal Police Office appeared. They had assessed the situation as a possible threat.

But investigators describe the scene differently.

It was already dark, and Ballout had stepped outside for just a few seconds, holding what appeared to be a handgun but was difficult to identify, they said. He tucked it into his waistband and went back inside. When officers eventually searched the apartment, they found only a toy gun.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz speaks at the Marienkirche church in Berlin on July 26, 2026. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images

Investigators believe the 21-year-old was testing whether he was under surveillance — and how much time he had before police would intervene.

And while his mother insists she noticed nothing that would suggest Ballout was preparing an attack, she does not rule out the possibility that others knew of her son’s plans. However, she gives no names.

He spent most of his time with family, she says. He had few friends, at least no one she knew particularly well.

* * *

The day of the attack began, in her memory, just like any other. Both mother and son slept in late, then ran errands. Ballout was unemployed and had no particular obligations, she says. In the late afternoon, he left the apartment before a family gathering that evening.

Then, suddenly, the calls started piling up.

At 5:10 p.m., Ballout called his mother. An hour later, he called again. Then again. Each time, she says, the conversation revolved around the same question: “Are you okay?” He had never done that before.





Then, after one of the calls, she received a short message: “Take care of yourself.”

The words still haunt her today.

At 7:05 p.m., Ballout called again. He asked that his mother inform her partner of over two years that he had a new phone number again. Ballout’s parents have been divorced for three years, but Ballout continued to see and speak with his father regularly, she says. And as the family prepared for the evening, the phone kept ringing.

They were supposed to have dinner at his sister’s place. Schnitzel, his favorite meal, was on the menu. Ballout loved these family gatherings, his mother says. “They always made him happy.” That is precisely why so much of what happened next is incomprehensible to her.

Police investigation marks on the ground near the scene of the attack. | Filip Singer/EPA

“He wanted to live,” she says, her voice rough.

He had spoken of the future, about having a family of his own, about all the things that still lay ahead of him. Nothing had suggested this might be a farewell.

Shortly before 10 p.m., her partner received one more call. They were the last words Ballout deliberately addressed to his family: “Get my mother to safety.”

Minutes later, the van drove into the crowd.

* * *

By the time Ballout’s mother was driven home by her partner that night, the first reports of the attack had started to circulate. At that point, she still didn’t know exactly what had taken place. But when she entered the apartment, she says, something immediately caught her attention.

A key was still in the door.

And right beside it, on the hallway shoe cabinet, were documents that seemed to be deliberately placed where they could not be overlooked. It was the rental agreement for a small van. It listed Ballout as the renter.





“That was when I knew immediately that it couldn’t mean anything good,” she says.

That same night, she took the documents to the police. And as she was questioned, a picture slowly started to emerge — one she initially refused to accept.

At the same time, she kept trying to reach her son, sending message after message. But there was no reply. She only learned the truth the next day, when her daughters called and told her about the reports on the news.

Her son was dead.

Since then, she has spent hour after hour in her Berlin apartment searching for explanations, her thoughts circling endlessly around her son’s last words, his fear and whether there may have been something in those calls that she failed to recognize. She cannot let go of the distorted image she has of her son, of the good boy who wanted to start a family.





Asked what she would say to the victims of the terrorist attack, she thinks for a long time. She is sorry, she eventually says.

“I would also tell them that wasn’t my son.”

Additional reporting by Lennart Pfahler.

Julia Zabert is a trainee journalist with the Global Reporters Network at the Axel Springer Academy. The Academy trains the next generation of leading journalists through hands-on, innovative work with a clear focus on the future of journalism. More information at axelspringeracademy.com.

World.title: The one French politician who’s not on vacation this summer
World.content:
Gabriel Attal, center, shakes hands with a police officer during a campaign visit to Vannes, France on July 25, 2026. | Sebastien Salom-Gomis/AFP via Getty Images

Presidential candidate Gabriel Attal is forgoing the traditional August holiday in a desperate attempt to catch up with his rivals.

PARIS — Former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal is trying to jump-start his presidential prospects by taking advantage of his rivals enjoying France’s cherished August break.

Attal, a former prime minister who now leads President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist political party Renaissance, is betting that by keeping a busy schedule during the holiday and meeting with people across the country — including those at vineyards, markets and ports as well as vacationers in picturesque seaside towns — he can show voters what sets him apart from the field.

“It’s a rather bourgeois assumption to think that all French people take time off or go on vacation,” said a representative for Attal’s team who, like others in this story, was granted anonymity to speak candidly about campaign dynamics. “There’s no way he’s going to suspend his campaign over the summer.”



But political reality is also forcing Attal to campaign in August for the vote in April of next year. If he wants a real shot at catching up in the polls, there’s little time to waste.

Surveys have consistently shown the 37-year-old trailing Edouard Philippe, his main ideological rival for centrist and center-right votes. Given the contest goes to a two-candidate runoff if nobody wins a majority in the first round, the two men have tentatively agreed that only one of them should be on the ballot so they don’t split their shared voter base — which could cost both of them a spot in the second round.

Philippe, far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen, far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon and conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau are all among the presidential hopefuls taking long summer breaks, only interrupting their time off for the occasional op-ed or statement on major events like the wildfires that ravaged southwest France.

Edouard Philippe speaks at a rally in northern Paris on July 5, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images

Their reasoning for slowing down during the peak holiday season is straightforward: Voters want to rest and recharge, so candidates shouldn’t harass them with politics and should instead enjoy one last bit of respite before the race enters its decisive stretch.

“We shouldn’t bother the French people while they’re on vacation,” said a Retailleau adviser.

Attal is betting otherwise that a summer spent campaigning can help close the gap in the polls.

“A campaign is about winning over the French one by one … [Attal] wants to show that he’s more determined than the others,” added his adviser.

The right track

It’s unclear for now to what extent Attal’s summer work will reap dividends with voters, as most pollsters who would investigate that question have themselves set out-of-office messages.

But the absence of other candidates on the campaign trail has given Attal an opportunity to dominate headlines, and he’s used it to make a play for right-wing voters.



At the start of the month, Attal, a member of parliament who represents a Paris suburb, gave an interview to the right-wing weekly Le Journal du Dimanche in which he called for lower immigration, a sweeping streamlining of France’s administrative procedures and more effective enforcement of criminal sentences.

He then traveled to western France, where, in front of cameras, he confronted a group of French gens du voyage — a legal classification for traditionally itinerant communities, including Roma and Manouche, and long a target of the French right — who had occupied land without authorization.

The encounter can be seen below in a report from CNEWS, in French.

French municipalities are required to provide designated stopping sites for traveling communities, but those obligations are not always met — or the sites provided are insufficient — sometimes resulting in unauthorized occupations of public or private land.

For both Attal and Philippe, making inroads on the right will be crucial. Macron’s 2022 reelection was buoyed by older, more affluent voters who had traditionally backed conservatives.

But Philippe begins that contest with a built-in advantage.



He is a former member of the conservative party Les Républicains and has always identified as a man of the right. Attal, who started his political career in the youth wing of the center-left Socialists, has resisted the label.

One conservative minister in the current French government, who has not endorsed a candidate for 2027, readily described Philippe as belonging to his political camp. Attal, the minister said, has a “very flexible” ideological spine.

Sarah Paillou and Anthony Lattier contributed to this report.

World.title: Nigel Farage paints himself as local hero in fight to win Clacton
World.content:
One Meta ad suggests he is the only candidate to have visited forgotten areas of the constituency. A further clip shows a local resident giving Farage a positive review of his work — and is presented as proof that opposition complaints he has neglected the patch since his 2024 general election victory in the seat are “cobblers.”

With over 7 million followers across the leading social media platforms — making him by far the most-followed U.K. party leader — Farage has also been churning out election content across TikTok, Instagram and X.

Even with that reach, the Reform UK leader appears to be the only candidate running in Clacton who has used paid Meta features to bolster his online campaign.

Almost £1,000 has been spent on videos of Farage urging local supporters to request the party deliver and install an “I’m with Nigel” garden sign. Meanwhile, around £500 went to ads asking voters to return their postal votes and “send a message to the establishment.”

The largest single sum — between £4,000-£4,500 — was spent on an almost five-minute campaign video in which Farage waxes lyrical about the connection he’s made with local constituents, while claiming his party’s surging success has resulted in the powers-that-be using “foul means” to hamper him.

“Rather than being judged by the political class and the mainstream media, I am going to let you, the voters in the Clacton constituency, make a decision,” he said. “I want you to be my judge, not the political elite.”

World.title: How Russian attacks, European protectionism and drought are trapping Ukraine’s vital grain
World.content:
With missile strikes keeping cargo ships away from its ports, Kyiv is scrambling, yet again, for a way out via Europe. But its fallback routes run overland through EU countries, including Poland, Hungary and Slovakia, where previous waves of Ukrainian grain left governments facing a fierce domestic backlash.

The last surge of Ukrainian agricultural exports through Eastern Europe unleashed mass protests from farmers, particularly in Poland, who complained that cheap Ukrainian produce that was meant to merely pass through the region was instead ending up on their domestic markets. Poland imposed a ban on Ukrainian grain in 2023, alongside similar measures in Hungary and Slovakia, defying EU trade rules and souring relations with Ukraine.

Kyiv's fresh pleas — and insistence that the grain would only transit through its EU neighbors — have prompted Warsaw to reassure its own farmers that none of it will end up in Poland.

“We are doing everything to keep the embargo,” Polish Agriculture Minister Stefan Krajewski told Radio ZET on Monday, referring to Poland’s ban on Ukrainian grain imports.

Blocked bounty

One of the world’s largest grain producers, Ukraine typically sends more than 90 percent of its agricultural exports by sea. The disruption of that trade after Russia’s 2022 invasion helped drive global food prices to record highs. This summer, Russia and Ukraine have intensified attacks on each other’s ports and shipping across the Black Sea.

Ukraine exported just 463,000 metric tons of grain in the first nine days of August — about one-third of the usual pace, said Vysotskyi. By November, when the new harvest comes in, the country risks running out of storage for grain it cannot export.

World.title: Eurovision bars countries at war or in ‘sensitive geopolitical situations’ from hosting
World.content:
Despite this, Israel has come close to winning the 2025 and 2026 editions of the competition, garnering a strong public vote. Israel’s pubic broadcaster KAN has denied claims that results were unfairly influenced by mass voting campaigns.

Eurovision is organized by the European Broadcasting Union, an alliance of 113 public service media organizations across 56 countries. Typically, the national broadcaster that wins the competition hosts the following edition in their home country.

There have been some exceptions. When Ukraine won the 2022 contest, the organizers said the country could not host the following year’s contest due to Russia’s ongoing invasion raising safety concerns.

The new rules would make a winning broadcaster automatically ineligible to host “if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region.”

The organizers could still commission an independent security assessment to determine whether a winner can safely host the contest. If a winner is deemed unable to host, the broadcasting union has the power to choose an alternative.

Organizers said the rule change follows “feedback from participating broadcasters” after the 2026 contest in Vienna. They will apply from next year, when the contest takes place in Bulgaria.

“These changes are about giving everyone involved greater clarity, protecting artists and ensuring the Contest continues to provide a safe and welcoming environment, while preserving the spirit and integrity that make the Eurovision Song Contest so special,” said Eurovision director Martin Green.

World.title: TikTok's finfluencers: How reliable is the financial advice reaching young investors?
World.content:
"Defence stocks make millionaires 95% of the time," a man tells his followers in a TikTok video before pointing viewers towards a handful of companies in the defence sector.

 

It's one of several videos offering investment tips: some feature creators while others use AI-generated personas to offer stock picks and financial advice to users scrolling through social media in Europe.

But how much of this advice should you actually trust?

A new analysis of 150 popular finance-related TikTok videos by broker comparison website BrokerListings.com suggests that viewers should be cautious.

The videos it studied amassed at least 100,000 views each, covering topics ranging from stocks and cryptocurrency to debt and personal finance.

The platform found more than 70% of the videos' creators did not display a clear relevant background in financial services or suitable qualifications sufficient to provide reliable advice to the public.

In addition, more than 60% of the videos did not adequately explain the potential risks or downsides to the financial products or situations they discussed.

Their findings come as regulators are increasingly grappling with the influence of social media on young investors.

Ulf Linke, a consumer protection expert at Germany's financial regulator BaFin, told The Cube, Euronews’ fact-checking team, that the authority sees a "clear trend" towards investment tips on social media, particularly among younger people.

A 2024 BaFin survey found that more than half of Millennial and Gen Z investors considered social media a reliable source of financial information, while 60% saw it as a good alternative to professional financial advice.

In April, the European Parliament backed calls for minimum standards for so-called "finfluencers" — influencers who provide financial advice on social media — specifically citing risks such as hidden advertising, misleading claims, scams, and AI-generated financial content.

According to MEPs, social media has become a "primary" source of financial information for many younger people.

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) also issued guidance for finfluencers earlier this year, warning that rules on investment recommendations can apply to financial content posted on social media.

Under these rules, someone recommending an investment may need to make clear who they are, separate facts from opinions and disclose if they could financially benefit from what they are promoting.

Even publicly expressing an opinion on whether a share or cryptocurrency will rise or fall can, in some circumstances, constitute an investment recommendation.

"Disclaimers such as 'This is not investment advice' will not protect you in these cases," ESMA states.

Why can financial advice on TikTok be risky?

The format of social media clips is one of the main reasons why they are a precarious source of financial or budgeting information, researchers say, as their short length can mean that a lot of important context is left out.

According to James Barra, head of content and research at BrokerListings, the nature of short-form videos on platforms such as TikTok and Instagram does not necessarily lend itself to the kind of longer, balanced explanations that financial products can require.

A short video promoting a side hustle or get-rich-quick scheme may be more engaging, he said, than a longer explanation weighing up both the potential benefits and risks.

The advice can also reach people with vastly different levels of financial knowledge and experience.

A particular investment, for example, could represent a relatively small proportion of an experienced investor's portfolio, but be much riskier for a young investor putting a large share of their savings into it.

"And that sort of nuance… you don't necessarily have room for that in these short-form videos on TikTok," Barra told The Cube.

BrokerListings also found that the most concerning content did not necessarily come from TikTok's biggest financial influencers.

Barra said larger influencers and commercial partnerships have attracted greater scrutiny from regulators and social media platforms, while smaller, organic creators can also produce content that reaches substantial audiences, but receive less scrutiny.

TikTok told us that its Community Guidelines on regulated goods, services and commercial activities set out rules that apply to this type of content. The platform said it takes enforcement action, including removing content, when it is found to violate those guidelines.

TikTok also prohibits financial scams and said that 99% of videos it removed for violating its fraud and scams policies in the first quarter of 2026 were taken down proactively before being reported by users.

Is it all unreliable?

Despite concerns, not all financial content on social media is unreliable. BrokerListings says its researchers also found creators sharing useful information on topics such as budgeting, managing debt, building emergency savings and long-term investing.

It can also offer an alternative means for young people learning about personal finance.

"You don't learn about this at school, you don't learn about it at university," Barra said. "A lot of people don't learn about it from their parents.

There are also established financial education channels which take a different approach to the quick stock picks and promises of high returns found elsewhere on social media.

For example, Germany's Finanzfluss ("Financial flow", in English), presented by former investment banking analyst Thomas Kehl, has built a large online audience around financial education, producing content on topics including ETFs (exchange-traded funds), investing basics, saving and retirement planning.

In one recent TikTok, the channel discusses the growth of actively managed ETFs in the US and Europe, explaining the product and market developments rather than directing viewers towards a particular stock and promising them they will make a return.

How can you spot unreliable financial advice online?

Nevertheless, experts warn that users should look closely at who is behind the financial content they are watching.

According to Linke, reputable creators should identify themselves, provide verifiable contact information, disclose potential conflicts of interest and explain the professional background that qualifies them to discuss investments.

If this information is missing, investors should not trust the investment tips, he added.

Linke also warned users to be suspicious of tips promising high returns without explaining the risks, and to not give in to pressure or the fear of missing out on potential returns.

Another warning sign, according to Barra, is content built around displays of wealth, such as expensive cars, luxury hotels or other suggestions that following a particular investment strategy could lead to a similar lifestyle.

Urgency should also raise questions. Barra pointed to videos telling viewers that a stock is about to soar or crash, or those suggesting they have only a short window in which to buy a particular cryptocurrency.

Uptick in young people getting investment advice from social media videos. Cleared

Social media users should also consider if a creator is benefiting financially from what they are promoting, with some creators receiving commission when a viewer signs up to a trading platform through their link.

Such sponsorships or affiliate relationships do not mean the information is unreliable, but European rules require such conflicts of interest to be disclosed.

ESMA recommends that consumers check information from social media against other sources before making financial decisions.

That could mean looking at information published by financial regulators such as ESMA or national authorities such as Germany's BaFin; checking official company reports if a video makes claims about a particular business; and looking for coverage from established financial news organisations.

Investors can also use national regulators' registers to check whether a company or individual offering financial services is authorised to do so.

Ultimately, the speed with which users can move from watching a TikTok to putting their own money at risk makes that scrutiny increasingly important.

Barra described how someone could watch a video recommending several stocks, ask an AI chatbot whether they were good investments and then open a trading app and buy them, all within a matter of minutes.

"The whole journey can be a lot quicker than it used to be," he said.

World.title: Historic Valbonne estate loved by Duran Duran is now up for sale
World.content:
A historic estate address tucked a short walk away from the French Riviera medieval village of Valbonne, known for its charming pastel coloured buildings, cobble streets and central square filled with an array of café tables, is now up for sale and it has some famous former residents.

 

English pop rock band Duran Duran reportedly used Domaine de La Sylviane as a base during the 1980s while recording their third studio album, Seven and the Ragged Tiger.

Surrounded by 10 hectares of land which has over 500 olive trees that produce nearly 1,000 litres of oil each year, the property comprises a total of 23 rooms, including 16 bedrooms, a gym room, pool house, tennis court bordered by fruit trees and a garage that can comfortably house six cars.

Named La Sylviane after the daughter of a general in Napoleon’s army, it was also previously the residence of members of Prince Rainier III of Monaco’s family before being sold to its current owners.

Steeped in Provençal history, the main residence with six bedrooms was first built in 1697. The adjoining three-storey cottage features an independent two-bedroom apartment, while another two villas occupy the courtyard – both comprising two bedrooms.

Domaine de La Sylviane also has its very own resident caretaker to maintain the estate’s upkeep, with the caretaker’s apartment also at the entrance to the property.

Beyond its vast size, celebrity and royal connections, Domaine de La Sylviane offers a glimpse of the French Riviera beyond the usual hotspots.

Centuries of history on the Côte d'Azur in one estate

According to Carlton International, who specialise in luxury real estate and are tasked with selling the estate, the property was settled in the 13th century and initially was an agricultural hub worked on by monks.

Philip Weiser, founder and CEO of Carlton International, said the significance of the property and its location lie in the history.

“Long before Cannes welcomed the world's cinema stars, before Cap d'Antibes became synonymous with grand estates and elegant hotels, the Riviera was a land of fishermen, monks, olive growers and hilltop villages whose rhythms followed the seasons rather than the summer holiday calendar,” Weiser told Euronews Travel.

He added that estates like La Sylviane still define the character of Provence today, with the inland Riviera remaining one of the region’s best kept secrets.

In place of the sounds of the sea, inland destinations like Valbonne are instead marked by church bells ringing, stone farmhouses rather than waterfront villas and country lanes that lead through ancient olive groves that remain virtually unchanged over hundreds of years.

While the French Riviera has become synonymous to luxurious images of glamorous yachts docked at bays overlooking the Mediterranean, golden beaches and star-studded film festivals, in a destination such as Valbonne, “luxury is measured not by visibility but by authenticity: the freedom to walk to the village bakery each morning,” he said.

The Riviera beyond the coast

Valbonne may sit inland from the Mediterranean and offer a quieter stay, but for Weiser, that position is part of its appeal.

The countryside estate is 20 minutes away from Nice International Airport and around 15 minutes from Cannes.

“The hidden Côte d'Azur does not compete with Cannes, Nice or Saint-Tropez,” he said. “It complements them, offering an altogether different experience – one that reveals the enduring soul of Provence behind the glamour of the coast.”

Its restored village centre spotlights historical monuments, including Place des Arcades square where a Friday morning market is held – Weiser said the village square especially comes alive on market days.

He added that Valbonne is also a stone’s throw away from the hilltop village of Mougins – crowned as celebrated as the gastronomic capital of the French Riviera for its refined restaurants, including those that have earned Michelin stars.

The annual Étoiles de Mougins festival, launched in 2006 by Paul Bocuse, Gaston Lenôtre, Alain Ducasse, Michel Guérard and Pierre Troisgros, gathers esteemed chefs and culinary enthusiasts for demonstrations and workshops, competitions and conferences celebrating food.

Other surrounding villages the Weiser recommended include Biot, which is renowned for its expert glassmakers, as well as Grasses, which he described as the “world capital for perfume” as it continues to cultivate the same flowers that have shaped famed perfume houses for centuries.

“Within twenty minutes, residents and visitors can enjoy the beaches of Cannes, Antibes or Juan-les-Pins, dine in Michelin-starred restaurants, play some of Europe's finest golf courses, or fly directly from Nice Côte d'Azur International Airport to destinations around the world,” Weiser said.

Despite all that the rest of the French Riviera has to offer visitors, he added: “Yet at the end of the day, they return to the tranquillity of olive groves, forests and centuries-old stone houses.”

World.title: 'I really doubt I'll carry on': Messi sees end of football career in farewell to his father
World.content:
Lionel Messi rarely shares details of his private life. Over two decades of his career, the Argentine striker has kept the media at long arm's length and reserved his emotions for his closest circle. That is why it is striking that, after his father's death, he's chosen to publish an open letter on social media in which his grief is all too apparent.

 

In the message, addressed directly to Jorge, Messi writes that he does not know how to continue without him. "I don't know what I'm going to do without you, I don't know how to carry on. I just played football and nowI have serious doubts that I'll keep doing it for much longer," the letter reads. Coming from someone who has always avoided talking about his retirement, the words carry particular weight.

The Albiceleste captain also laments, through his sadness, that his father was unable to hold on a little longer. "You were by my side from the very start, there was so little left to go. Why didn't you hang on that bit longer so we could finish together?" the statement reads.

Jorge Horacio Messi was not only Lionel's father. He was also his agent from the earliest years and the person who, as the footballer himself has acknowledged on several occasions, shouldered much of the weight of his career off the pitch.

In the letter, Messi recalls that constant closeness and regrets that his father's health, already fragile during the last World Cup, prevented him from accompanying him through to the end of the tournament.

"Dad, I still can't believe you're gone. We still had so much left to enjoy together. You kept insisting that I should play the last World Cup, and just days before it began was when you got worse," he writes. Messi says his mother assured him his father would improve enough to travel and watch him play the final, and that he himself clung to that hope. "I told you we were going to reach the final so you could travel. We made it to the final and you couldn't be there," he adds, referring to the match Argentina played and lost against Spain on 19 July in New Jersey.

"I wanted to win it to bring it to you and show you a new one. I couldn't; my legs just weren't there any more. This time I tried to push my body beyond its limits, but I couldn't. I never managed to feel right," he concludes in that part of the message, in which he acknowledges the physical wear and tear with which he arrived at the World Cup.

Contract in place and no decision yet announced

For now, Messi remains under contract with Inter Miami and has made no formal announcement about his future, either with the US club or with the Argentine national team.

The letter, however, suggests thathis father's death has triggered a bout of soul-searching he had not previously made public. The player himself admits that his relationship with football was always bound up with his father's figure, which helps explain why uncertainty over his future has emerged precisely at this moment.

Jorge Messi's funeral was held in private at the El Prado cemetery in Rosario, the hometown of both father and son, and was attended by Antonela Roccuzzo and the footballer's children. Clubs and bodies in Argentine football, among them Newell's Old Boys, the team Jorge openly supported, sent messages of farewell in the days that followed.

Six of the best - the most important moments in Messi's career

1. Barcelona first-team debut (2004). Aged just 17, Messi made his league debut for Barcelona's first team, the first step in a spell at the club that would last for more than two decades.

2. First Champions League as a leading star (Rome, 2009). Messi scored the second goal, a header, in the final against Manchester United, in a season in which Barcelona won all six trophies on offer. He has described that goal as the most important of his career.

Messi at FC Barcelona, 2009 Copyright 2009 AP. All rights reserved.

3. Qatar 2022 World Cup. The one title he was missing. Messi lifted the trophy with Argentina after beating France in a penalty shoot-out, finally becoming world champion after previously losing four finals with the senior national team.

4. Leaving Barcelona (2021). After more than two decades at the club and 35 trophies, Messi tearfully announced his departure, forced by the club's financial and institutional crisis, before signing for Paris Saint-Germain.

5. Latest Ballon d'Or (2023). The year 2023 brought his latest Ballon d'Or, the ninth of his career. The award recognises him as the best player of the year and saw him share the stage with Spain's Aitana Bonmatí, who received the prize on the women's side of the game.

5. All-time World Cup top scorer (2026). During the World Cup staged in the United States, Canada and Mexico, Messi broke Miroslav Klose's record to become the top scorer in the tournament's history, at the same World Cup in which Argentina reached the final and lost to Spain.

World.title: Inflation in Spain rises in July to 3.6%, worst rate since May 2024
World.content:
The second biggest concern for Spaniards, after housing, the performance of the economy, continues to deteriorate in light of the latest data published by the National Statistics Institute (INE). The agency's figures downgrade its July forecast by a tenth of a point and confirm that inflation rose this month to 3.6%. This is the worst figure recorded since May 2024.

 

There have now been five consecutive months with a year-on-year rate above 3 points, and the rebound has a clear culprit: the fuel crisis and soaring electricity prices. This is also happening in a month marked by strong consumer demand because of the intense heat and successive heatwaves during the dog days of summer, which are pushing electricity bills even higher.

Electricity prices in July are hovering at around €105 per megawatt hour: the biggest year-on-year increase since the same month in 2022, when the invasion of Ukraine put pressure on European supplies. Six years on, it is the partial blockages in the Red Sea and, above all, the Strait of Hormuz that are fuelling instability in energy prices.

The Economy Ministry, headed by Carlos Cuerpo, has announced that since the year-on-year increase in diesel exceeded 15% last month by seven-tenths of a point, an automatic cut in the hydrocarbons tax has been triggered; 20 cents, instead of 5, will be deducted for every litre consumed.

This measure, set out in the government's response plan to the crisis caused by the Israeli and US bombings in Iran, has been heavily criticised by parties to the left of the PSOE, who argue that distribution companies are not passing the full discount on to consumers.

The good news? The cost of the average shopping basket fell by three-tenths of a point in July. "The inflationary pressure has not been passed on to food, where the year-on-year rate was 1.6%, three-tenths of a point below the June rate and a low not seen since 2021," the Economy Ministry pointed out. Prices are still rising, but at a slightly slower pace. Fruit, vegetables and pulses have become particularly cheaper, as have textiles thanks to the summer sales.

World.title: Soaring stingray numbers off California beaches drive record injuries
World.content:
At Seal Beach, 45 km southeast of downtown Los Angeles, researcher Chris Lowe and his team caught dozens measuring and tagging them before release. Lowe estimates that more than 16,000 stingrays can gather in an area the size of a football field in a single day. The species has concentrated at the site for at least 60 years, helped by warm water discharged from a nearby power plant and fine sediments that provide suitable habitat.

 

The increase is also being felt by swimmers. Two state beaches near Huntington Beach have recorded more than 3,100 sting incidents so far in 2026, about twice the total for all of 2025. According to Chris Lowe, Southern California has the highest number of stingray injuries, largely because round stingrays bury themselves in the sand and may strike when people step on them. He expects incidents to increase as El Niño warms coastal waters and brings more subtropical rays north from Baja California.

National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration says a marine heatwave has already persisted off parts of the US West Coast for an unusually long period.

World.title: 'Ceuta and Melilla's Spanish status is beyond doubt', foreign ministry sources tell 'Euronews'
World.content:
"Spain's sovereignty over Ceuta and Melilla is beyond any doubt", Spanish diplomatic sources have told 'Euronews'.

 

"Ceuta and Melilla are part of Spain's territorial integrity, which is internationally recognised. Spain's territorial integrity has never been and will never be discussed with anyone," the same sources pointed out.

Their remarks and comments reinforce the firm message from Defence Minister Margarita Robles, who has in recent days repeatedly stressed in the Autonomous City of Ceuta that "Ceuta and Melilla are not to be touched".

Robles has sought to convey a sense of calm to the people of Ceuta and to guarantee that the Armed Forces will remain deployed to support the population.

In a brief appearance, Robles insisted that what happened on the 30th cannot be allowed to happen again: "Ceuta and Melilla are utterly Spanish", she said, before highlighting the work of the troops deployed for the past 11 days.

"People in Ceuta should know that their Armed Forces will be by their side. We are not going to abandon them," she assured.

Analysts believe the message was not only intended to reassure and dispel fears in the face of rumours of a new attempt at a mass entry of migrants this weekend; but more importantly, it was a message to Morocco.

Ouahbi publicly presents Ceuta and Melilla as a territorial claim of Morocco

The assurances from Spain comes amid territorial claims of the enclave by Morocco's Justice Minister, Abdellatif Ouahbi.

Speaking in an interview with Saudi channel 'Asharq News' on Tuesday, the Moroccan justice minister said that the debate over control of the two autonomous cities is a "pending issue".

Ouahbi stated that the question of Ceuta and Melilla "remains on the table" in meetings between representatives of Spain and Morocco.

While Morocco reopens this thorny topic, it has still not updated the number of dead or missing on its territory following the migration crisis.

Migrants who crossed from Morocco into Spain line up for food distribution on a beach in the Spanish enclave of Ceuta, Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. (AP Photo/Bernat Armangue) AP Photo/Bernat Armangue

Ouahbi criticised Madrid for "accepting" and "regularising" migrants who arrive irregularly on its territory while, he said, Rabat is trying to prevent them from leaving Morocco.

Earlier he had told the Spanish press that "Morocco is considering suspending the extradition agreement with Spain".

Situation of minors among pending issues between Madrid and Rabat

The interview in Saudi Arabia comes almost two weeks after the Ceuta migration crisis, with the situation of Moroccan minors still in the city among the pending issues between Madrid and Rabat.

The minister has called for their return to Morocco and insisted that they must be reunited with their families. "We do not abandon our children. We want and demand that our children return to Morocco," he insisted.

Related Morocco accuses Spain of assaulting migrants crossing into Ceuta and claims sovereignty over enclave

In this context, Ouahbi responded to one of the key questions raised during the crisis: whether Morocco was using mass migration as an instrument of pressure on Spain.

"We continue to assert our territorial claims" and we want to resolve the problem through dialogue," Ouahbi said, but "we have never used this issue as a tool of pressure."

Ouahbi rejected the idea that Moroccan children could stay in Spain to help meet the country's demographic needs and argued that Morocco does not have to play that role. "We are not a state whose purpose is to solve any other country's demographic problem", he concluded.

World.title: Germany news: Far-right leader backs left-wing populist
World.content:
08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 Heat-related deaths on the rise — Robert Koch Insitute

High temperatures have sometimes devastating effects on people's health Image: Rene Traut/IMAGO

Several spates of hot weather across Germany this year have caused an estimated 12,500 premature deaths so far, public health authorities have said.

The Robert Koch Institute (RKI) said its figure, released on Thursday, is a conservative estimate.

The worst-affected states were the western states of Saarland and Rhineland-Palatinate, which had more than double the national average of heat-related deaths.

The most deaths were recorded in the age group 85 years or older, at around 6,300. More than 3,100 of those who died were aged between 75 and 84, and nearly 1,900 between 65 and 74.

The severe heat wave at the end of June was especially deadly, with the RKI expecting that around 9,600 people died as a result of heat in the week from June 22 to 28 alone.

Climate scientists say that heat waves will increase in severity and frequency as the Earth continues to warm, largely owing to the human use of fossil fuels.

World.title: India news: Parliament ends turbulent monsoon session
World.content:
08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 Protests mark monsoon session of parliament

On the very first day of the monsoon session on July 20, parliament was rocked by a massive youth-led march trying to get to its gates as part of the Cockroach Janta Party movement demanding the resignation of the now former education minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam irregularities.

The protesters were met with baton-charges and tear gas firing, and since then the opposition has railed against the violent crackdown, demanding an answer in the parliament from Union Home Minister Amit Shah over alleged police brutality.

On Wednesday, Shah said that the Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government was ready for a discussion on the student protests which were triggered by a slew of medical entrance exam paper leaks. The leader of the opposition in the Lok Sabha, Congress's Rahul Gandhi, turned down the debate offer saying that the youth wanted answers on who ordered the use of force on protesters and "not a lecture" from Shah.

Addressing a press conference on Thursday, Union Minister of Parliamentarty Affairs Kiren Rijiju accused the opposition of "running away from discussions" and alleged that opposition disruptions affected parliament's productivity.

During the 19-day monsoon session several demonstrations were held by the Congress-led alliance of opposition parties called the INDIA bloc on the parliament premises against the police action and a donation embezzlement controversy linked to the Ram Temple, a shrine central to Modi's Hindu-first politics.

Lawmakers from Modi's ruling coalition also began staging their own demonstrations, including on the last day over another student protest in Jharkhand — where the Congress party is an ally of the ruling coalition. Tear gas, batons and water cannons were also used to disperse the protesters marching towards the state assembly in Ranchi.

World.title: Colombia earthquake: Rescue operation enters 'final phase'
World.content:
Rescuers are racing against a critical 72-hour window to find survivors after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake that has killed 265 people, left hundreds missing, and displaced tens of thousands across western Colombia.

Rescuers worked through a third straight night with time ticking towards the 72-hour mark since a powerful earthquake hit Colombia. That's the period aid agencies consider most critical for finding survivors alive, though it can stretch longer if trapped people have access to food and water.

"We're entering the final phase," Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said, adding that survivors could still be found afterward but that the odds grow steadily worse. He said crews were still detecting signs of life beneath the rubble and urged speed: "Every minute is vital."

Rescue workers ask for silence as they search for survivors at the site of collapsed buildings Image: Raul Arboleda/AFP

The latest on the Colombia earthquake

The death toll from the quake has climbed to 265, President Abelardo de la Espriella said Wednesday.

De la Espriella said roughly 3,500 people have been injured and nearly 500 remain unaccounted for, though a crowdsourced tracking site used by families put the number of missing far higher, at more than 4,100. More than 25,800 families have been affected in total, he said.

The magnitude 7.4 quake — the strongest to hit Colombia in decades — struck on Monday morning near San Jose del Palmar in the northwestern Choco region. It tore through cities across western Colombia, with Cali and Pereira among the hardest hit, along with Manizales and Quibdo.

In Cali, volunteer rescuer Johana Sanchez described teams pausing every 30 minutes to listen for survivors. "So far, three people have been pulled out alive and three dead," she told AFP.

Officials say 140 buildings collapsed entirely and thousands of homes were damaged or destroyed.

Families grapple with human toll

In Palmira, Santiago Lloreda told Reuters the quake killed his mother and his 13-month-old daughter, Salma, who was too young to have fingerprints on file and would need to be identified through DNA testing. He described his mother as the family's caretaker, saying she "gave everything up to look after the baby."

A man who only gave the news agency his first name, Ricardo, traveled from Miami to recover his sister's body and said his niece was awaiting surgery for a fractured skull, jaw and leg, and a collapsed lung: "She's alive. We know she's going to get better."

Colombia races against time after worst quake in a decade To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Thousands have been left homeless, with many sleeping outdoors in parks or emergency shelters set up in schools and sports arenas, either because their homes were destroyed or out of fear of aftershocks.

Colombia's geological service has recorded 130 aftershocks since Monday's quake.

International aid set to pour in

Response efforts have been especially difficult in Choco, the quake's epicenter, a remote and impoverished region already strained by decades of conflict and displacement. Additionally, lost cell service has made it hard to assess damage in communities reachable only by river.

"This earthquake compounds an already severe humanitarian situation, and there is a need for increased support for the humanitarian response," said Giovanni Rizzo, Colombia director for the Norwegian Refugee Council.

And UN resident coordinator María Jose Torres said in a statement Tuesday that aid groups already working in the region on an earlier peace effort were able to pivot quickly to disaster relief.

The United States has pledged more than $15 million and sent response teams. Mexico has sent military aircraft carrying nearly 20 tons of food along with security personnel, with more aid and rescue specialists on standby. El Salvador's president offered two planes carrying 100 tons of supplies, and a search-and-rescue team from Mexico said it arrived directly from Venezuela, which faced its own major earthquakes in June.

Quake response provides test for new Colombian president

De la Espriella, inaugurated just three days before the earthquake struck, declared an economic emergency and three days of national mourning, and pledged to establish a fund to rebuild hospitals, schools, homes and infrastructure.

"This is undoubtedly a tragedy of immense proportions," he said. "Our efforts are focused on those who remain missing." He has not yet detailed what the economic emergency measures will involve.

Notably, de la Espriella won office on a platform of reduced public spending and a tougher security approach. Analyst Tiziano Breda, of the conflict-monitoring group ACLED, told Reuters that de la Espriella had campaigned in part on cutting funding to the country's disaster-response agency — the same unit now leading the emergency effort.

Experts have cautioned that more seismic activity is possible, if not imminent. "Let's remember that Colombia is full of active fault lines," Rodrigo Leon Loya, a seismologist at the University of the Andes, told AP. "The question isn't whether it can happen again. The question is rather when an earthquake of similar magnitude will occur at another of Colombia’s seismic sources," he warned.

Edited by: Rob Turner

World.title: US: Karoline Leavitt to step down as Trump's spokesperson
World.content:
White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt is to leave her job at the end of the month, President Donald Trump says. Leavitt, 28, is the youngest-ever person to have held the position.

Karoline Leavitt, will leave her role as White House press secretary at the end of the month, US President Donald Trump said Tuesday.

Leavitt is one of the best-known faces and most ardent defenders of the MAGA movement.

Trump said in a post on his Truth Social platform that Leavitt was stepping down to "spend more time with her beautiful young children and family," adding that it was "a decision I totally understand and respect!"

Leavitt clung close to Trump as his press secretary Image: Brian Snyder/REUTERS

Who is Karoline Leavitt?

Leavitt, now 28, who took on the job in January 2025 aged 27 at the start of Trump's second term in office, has been the youngest-ever White House press secretary.

She recently returned from parental leave after giving birth to her second child, a daughter, in May. She also has a 2-year-old son.

After initially wanting to be a journalist, Leavitt soon entered politics. She joined the White House press office during Trump's first term, working under then-spokeswoman Kayleigh McEnany.

After Trump lost the 2020 presidential election to Joe Biden, Leavitt worked for the office of Congresswoman Elise Stefanik, a highly loyal Republican supporter of Trump.

Leavitt later unsuccessfully ran for a seat in the House of Representatives in 2022.

She also worked as a spokesperson for MAGA Inc., a super PAC supporting Trump, before joining his successful 2024 campaign.

'The honor and adventure of a lifetime' — Leavitt

In a post on X, Leavitt waxed lyrical about her period in the job.

"Serving as the White House Press Secretary over the past year and a half has been the honor and adventure of a lifetime," Leavitt wrote.

"I am incredibly grateful to President Trump for granting me so many extraordinary opportunities, such as working in the West Wing and spending countless hours in the Oval Office, flying around the world and meeting foreign leaders, and traveling across our beautiful country and meeting Americans from all walks of life."

She said her "bittersweet decision to depart the White House" was due to the difficulties of combining motherhood with the demands of the White House position.

Leavitt: A devoted defender of Trump

Leavitt, who Trump says will remain "one of my top outside advisors, and an influential voice within the Republican Party," has been a key figure in promoting the president's ideology and views, sometimes stretching the truth to do so.

Her very first press conference, on January 28, 2025, was notable for her false claim that $50 million (€43.4 million) in US taxpayers' money had been earmarked to buy condoms in the Gaza Strip.

Since then, she has staunchly defended Trump's hard-line policies while deflecting questions such as those concerning the president's ties with the sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

She was also known for denigrating mainstream media outlets in line with Trump's hostile attitude to reporters who gainsay him.

Her devotion has brought her consistent praise from the president, who has now called her "one ‌of the best White House Press Secretaries in the History of the Office."

World.title: Does the clean energy transition need forever chemicals?
World.content:
As nations globally move to ban forever chemicals, should renewable energy technologies be exempt for the sake of saving the climate?

From solar panels to wind turbines, batteries and hydrogen cells, many renewable energy technologies driving the energy transition share a common ingredient: a class of man-made substances known as "forever chemicals."

The group contains 10,000 synthetic chemicals also known as per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), which persist in the environment and can take thousands of years to degrade.

Widely detected in drinking water, exposure to certain levels of PFAS is linked to increased risk of cancer, suppressed immune function, decreased fertility and developmental delays in children.

These health impacts have inspired bans on well-publicized sources of toxic PFAS such as clothing waterproofing sprays, Teflon non-stick cookware, firefighting foam, packaging and cosmetic products.

While recent bans in France, New Zealand and Denmark target specific PFAS used in consumer products, the European Union wants a broader ban.

PFAS are becoming ever-present in drinking water globally Image: ZDF

The thousands of forever chemicals the EU proposes outlawing includes fluoropolymers, which are valued for their resistance to extreme temperatures, corrosion and UV degradation, and are present in numerous green technologies from lithium-ion batteries to solar panels.

In EV batteries, for example, binders created with PTFE fluoropolymers — also found in Teflon products — are used to coat dry electrodes for greater energy efficiency.

The chemicals industry has pushed back against Europe's mooted ban. An alliance of the world's leading chemical companies, the Performance Fluoropolymer Partnership (PFP) says health concerns about "some types of PFAS" are leading to "unwarranted restrictions" on fluoropolymer production and use.

In a statement on its website describing fluoropolymers as "critical in the fight against climate change," the PFP stated that any bans would "hamstring our climate and energy goals by possibly making the transition more expensive or simply impossible."

Are PFAS necessary to fight climate change?

PFP members include the chemicals arm of US multinational conglomerate, 3M — which is being sued more than $2 billion by the Australian government for its firefighting foam that has leached forever chemicals into the environment — and the Chemours Company, which manufacturers Teflon and was established by chemicals powerhouse, DuPont.

The European Environment Agency says these polymers are considered "relatively less problematic" than the building blocks for PFAS known as monomers. This is due to a larger molecular size that "limits their uptake into living cells" and potential toxicity.

PFAS in water: New solutions and recycling in focus To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet fluoropolymers still degrade over time, raising "additional environmental and human health concerns," according to the agency. Experts say these polymers will inevitably emit PFAS during their life cycle and enter the environment — and living organisms — through weathering and physical stress over long periods.

"I don't think we're going to solve the climate crisis by getting cancer," said Gretchen Salter of US-based Safer States, which lobbies to safeguard the environment from toxic chemicals. "You can't demonstrate that these chemicals aren't going to do harm."

"Since chemical makers cannot escape the fact that these types of PFAS are harming our health, they are trying to claim that they are necessary for the clean energy transition," Salter said, adding that research shows how PFAS themselves fuel climate harm and toxic pollution.

The petrochemical industry accounts for 30% of global industrial energy demand — which is higher than the iron, steel and cement sectors — and generates 18% of the industrial sector's greenhouse gas emissions. Overall, chemicals used to produce everything from pharmaceuticals to fertilizers, plastics, paints, electronics and cleaning products are responsible for around 6% of global emissions.

Salter said PFAS categorized as fluorogases (F-gases) are also being marketed as "climate-friendly" since they are used for clean tech like heat pumps, and in electric car batteries. But PFAS gases, though largely non-flammable, are "now the largest source of PFAS pollution globally," she said.

PFAS: Mothers fight against forever chemicals To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

This is partly due to their global warming impact, which is potentially thousands of times higher than carbon dioxide. F-gas leaks can happen throughout a heat pump life cycle via worn seals and improper maintenance and end-of-life disposal. F-gases are also present in fridges and air-conditioning units as a synthetic coolant, where they can leak too.

Are there PFAS-free green tech alternatives?

According to UK-based Chem Trust, which advocates for safer alternatives to toxic chemicals, a suite of PFAS-free clean energy technology is already on the market, including for heat pumps that are being rolled out across Europe as part of a transition from gas heating.

Instead of relying on F-gases, propane is just one alternative energy efficient refrigerant for domestic heat pumps, and with the right design has a negligible fire risk, notes a 2025 Chem Trust report.

The group also says several companies are now producing solar cells without fluoropolymers. Equally, polymer paint that protects wind turbine blades and makes them more efficient is available PFAS-free.

"We are seeing more companies in the EU and across the world embrace the challenge of developing PFAS-free green technologies," said Shubhi Sharma, scientific researcher at Chem Trust, in a statement.

Fluoropolymer boosters claim rechargeable lithium-ion batteries underpinning the energy transition work better with PFAS Image: DR/SP/Andia.fr/IMAGO

But plastics and chemical lobby group Plastics Europe released an assessment report of PFAS-free substitutes in May that argued that "in many critical uses" such as transport, electronics and semiconductors, these alternatives are "either not available or simply do not match the necessary criteria to be considered a viable alternative to fluoropolymers."

Salter of Safer States said efforts to exempt so-called critical and low concern PFAS from class-wide bans means "destroying any sort of incentive to switch to safer alternatives."

"As long as the chemicals industry insists that there are no alternatives, there will be no market to develop any," said the campaigner.

Chemours insists its fluoropolymers and F-gases are "made and used with minimal environmental impact," and says it will achieve a 99% PFAS emissions reduction in the manufacture of fluorinated organic compounds by the end of the decade compared to 2018.

Liz Hitchcock, director of the federal policy program at US environment nonprofit, Toxic-Free Future, told DW that the extreme persistence of PFAS in the environment will inevitably lead to human exposure.

"We've heard claims that there are better PFAS, there are safer PFAS, but we haven't seen the proof."

Edited by: Jennifer Collins

World.title: Russia's Putin angers Japan with 1st visit to Kuril Islands
World.content:
Japan says it "strongly protests" Russian President Vladimir Putin's trip to the disputed Kuril Islands. Tensions over the Russian-controlled archipelago, claimed partly by Japan, have long dogged bilateral ties.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has visited the far-eastern Kuril Islands for the first time, state media reported on Thursday, drawing anger from Japan.

Japan has long claimed ownership of four of the Kuril Islands, including the one reportedly visited by Putin, which the Soviet Union seized toward the end of World War II.

Iturup/Etorofu has a harsh climate, but mineral deposits and good fishing grounds Image: Sergei Krasnoukhov/TASS/picture alliance

What is the dispute over the Kuril Islands?

During his trip, Putin visited a fish-processing plant on the island, known as Iturup in Russian and Etorofu in Japanese, where he was given caviar, Russian media reported.

The island belongs to four that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories and that are now Russian-occupied following the Soviet Union's takeover in 1945.

At that time, Moscow deported their Japanese population of about 17,000 people, with the islands now inhabited by some 20,000 Russian citizens.

The unresolved dispute was one of the key reasons why Moscow and Tokyo never signed a formal World War II peace treaty.

Russian-Japanese relations have since suffered another major blow following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched in 2022.

The volcanic Kuril archipelago runs in an arc from Russia's Kamchatka peninsula down to Japan's main northern island of Hokkaido.

What has Japan said about Putin's visit?

In a statement on Thursday, Japan's foreign minister, Toshimitsu Motegi, expressed Tokyo's great displeasure at Putin's visit.

"The Northern Territories ... are an inherent part of Japan's territory both historically and under international law, and the government of Japan strongly protests this visit," the statement said.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi later told reporters that the visit "offends the sentiments of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable."

Strategically-located Kuril Islands

The islands have seldom been visited by Russian leaders, with then-President Dmitry Medvedev in 2010 becoming the first to travel to the disputed territory.

Medvedev also went there in 2015 as prime minister.

Putin's visit to the Kurils came after he visited the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin, where Russia's navy was conducting drills.

Putin observed a military drill by Russia's Pacific fleet in the Sakhalin Region, Image: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/REUTERS

The islands had considerable strategic importance for the Soviet Union, which kept a large military presence there during the Cold War amid tensions with the US and Japan.

Talks on the territorial issue that have been held since the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991 have so far borne no fruit.

Edited by: Rob Turner
