We cannot do what we do without your support. Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Ukrainians remain by far the largest immigrant group, followed by Belarusians. The figures also show that the overall number of registered foreign workers has risen more than 8% over the last year, a faster rate of growth than in recent years. However, the government official responsible for migration strategy says this is because stricter government measures have pushed some employers to register previously uninsured workers. The ZUS data, reported by Dziennik Gazeta Prawna (DGP), a leading daily, show that there were 1.34 million foreign workers registered in ZUS at the end of June, up from 1.24 million at the same point last year. That 8.2% increase is larger than the growth rate of around 6% seen in each of the previous two years, notes the newspaper. Maciej Duszczyk, the deputy interior minister responsible for migration, commented that the rise actually reflects the government’s tougher migration strategy, which he said “forces employers to report for insurance those who arrived earlier” but were working unregistered The official pointed to recent data showing that, in fact, in the first half of this year, Poland issued 50% fewer work permits to foreigners than in the same period of 2025. Dane ZUS pokazują dokładnie to co zakładaliśmy w Strategi Migracyjnej. Radykalny spadek liczby wydawanych, nowych zezwoleń na pracę (ponad 50% rok do roku) wymusza na pracodawcach zgłaszanie do ubezpieczenia, tych którzy przyjechali wcześniej. Tylko w pełni legalne zatrudnienie! — Maciek Duszczyk (@MaciekDuszczyk) August 11, 2026 Ukrainians remain by far the largest group of registered foreign workers, with 901,000 now in the system, a 10.1% rise from a year earlier. Belarusians (144,000, up 4.9%) remain in second. But two non-European migrant groups whose numbers have been growing rapidly in recent years now occupy third and fourth place: Indians (25,500, up 4.9%) and Colombians (23,000, up 31%, which was the fastest growth of any national group). Georgians, who had previously been the third-largest group, saw their number fall by 17% to 22,000, meaning they are now in fifth, ahead of Filipinos (15,400, down 2%), Moldovans (14,200, down 1%), Nepalis (13,400, up 8.3%), Vietnamese (12,200, up 6.1%), and Russians (11,800, down 2.5%). Latin American migration to Poland is booming, with 45,000 work permits issued last year, five times more than in 2022@Gosia_Tomczak looks at what is driving this trend and what challenges and opportunities it has created for both the migrants and Poland https://t.co/tl1wUTCaC0 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 15, 2025 ZUS’s data also show that foreign workers are increasingly establishing their own businesses in Poland, which Dziennik Gazeta Prawna notes is a sign that they are establishing longer-term ties with the country but also a result of an easier online system for registering businesses. In 2021, only 22,700 foreigners had a registered business in Poland, a figure that now is now almost five times higher, at 102,000. The rise has been driven in particular by Ukrainians, many of whom are legally entitled to establish companies in Poland under the same terms as Polish citizens. As a result, 7.6% of foreign workers now run their own business, up from 6.7% a year ago and from 2.7% before Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, which led to a wave of Ukrainian refugees settling in Poland. Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.7% last year while not raising unemployment or lowering wages, finds a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte "Whoever thinks refugees are a burden on the economy should think again," says @UNHCRPoland https://t.co/rOvtOvBNwG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 12, 2025 Over the last decade, even before the war in Ukraine, Poland has experienced a wave of migration unprecedented in its history and among the largest anywhere in Europe. For six years running, between 2017 and 2022, it issued more first residence permits to immigrants from outside the European Union than did any other member state. Much of the surge in immigration came during the rule of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government from 2015 to 2023, despite its strong anti-migrant rhetoric. The current government, a more liberal coalition led by Prime Minister Donald Tusk, came to power pledging to reduce immigration, which it said had got out of control under PiS. Under Tusk’s government, in 2024, Poland issued the lowest number of residence permits to non-EU immigrants in a decade. In 2025, the government introduced tougher entry requirements for foreign workers and students. It has also stepped up deportations of foreigners who have broken the law. However, Duszczyk notes that the current government still sees “selective and responsible migration” as a way to “maintain the competitiveness of the economy without limiting wage growth”. ​ Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Mother bear and cubs spotted on busy hiking trail in Poland
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. A female brown bear and her three cubs have been spotted in Poland’s Tatra mountains crossing a popular trail filled with hikers, with the animals coming unusually close to people. According to an official from Tatra National Park, where the incident took place, the behaviour could be a survival strategy by the mother to protect her young from male bears, which can kill cubs but tend to avoid humans. In a video posted on Sunday, the mother and three cubs were seen crossing the Chochołowska Valley trail in broad daylight, as crowds of people looked on Videos of the bear family have appeared increasingly often on social media, prompting questions about whether the animals are becoming less wary of people. But park officials say the female’s behaviour may have a biological explanation. “As we know, male brown bears are infanticidal. They kill not only other bears’ cubs, but their own as well. So the females, to avoid contact with the males, tend to stay closer to people,” Tomasz Zwijacz-Kozica, a park official, told local newspaper Gazeta Krakowska. “Females sense this instinctively and generally use the presence of people as a sort of shield to defend themselves against these males,” he added. The park staff hope to gather more detailed data on the female bear’s movements and behaviour in the future by possibly fitting her with a telemetry collar. They note that similar behaviour has been seen before. Around 20 years ago, a female bear drew attention when hundreds of tourists photographed her. They advise visitors to remain calm if they encounter a bear and to follow several basic rules, including staying calm and not running or making sudden movements, which may trigger a pursuit; not approaching the animals; and not attempting to take close-up photographs or use a flash. If a bear is encountered, visitors should slowly retreat in the direction from which they came while maintaining eye contact with the animal. Particular caution is required when cubs are present. Visitors should also avoid feeding bears or leaving rubbish behind. The smell of food can attract animals to trails and encourage behaviour that brings them into dangerous contact with people. A woman has died after being attacked by a bear in a forest in southeastern Poland. Such incidents are extremely rare, with the last fatal bear attack in the country reported in 2014 https://t.co/sAC2MPAvfh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) April 23, 2026 Estimates of Poland’s brown bear population vary between 120 and 400, with most found in the southeastern Bieszczady mountains as well as the Tatras and Beskids further west. The population is thought to be growing, with a rise in reports of encounters with humans. In April this year, a woman was killed in a bear attack, Poland’s first such fatality since 2014. Another bear attack earlier in the year in the same region left a man with head and limb injuries. In March, the government launched a new 16 million zloty (€3.7 million) scheme aimed at both protecting bears and ensuring the safety of their human neighbours. It includes the creation of a special force to monitor and respond to bear sightings, including fitting the animals with tracking collars. In 2022, the town of Zakopane, located at the foot of the Tatra mountains, installed bear-proof rubbish bins to prevent animals from foraging in them – and thereby coming closer to areas of human population Poland has launched a new programme to protect brown bears and ensure the safety of their human neighbours, amid growing reports of encounters. World.title: From a Student’s Dream to a Japanese Bakery in Prague: The Story Behind Yaki-Pan
World.content:
For Hoan, opening a bakery in Prague was not a sudden business idea. It was a dream that had been taking shape for more than a decade.

After arriving in Prague as a student, Hoan watched members of the Vietnamese community build businesses across the city, most commonly in restaurants, grocery shops and nail salons.

She worked in grocery stores and restaurants herself, gradually gaining experience in the food industry while studying.

But after finishing school, she still was not sure what kind of business she wanted to open.



One thing was clear: she loved baking.

“Its my dream. It’s been my plan for a long time, more than 10 years,” she says.

Rather than opening another coffee shop, she decided to focus on what she knew best. She had visited bakeries around Prague and noticed what she saw as a gap in the city’s food scene: there were few places specialising in Japanese-style baking.

Around six years ago, she decided that she wanted to fill that gap herself.

The result was Yaki-Pan, a small bakery built around Japanese pastries and flavours. Before opening, Hoan spent roughly a year and a half — and much of that time at home — testing recipes and trying to recreate the textures and flavours she associated with Japanese baking.

Getting there was not straightforward.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Yaki-Pan (@yakipan_brunch)

Learning to work with Czech ingredients

For Hoan, authenticity was essential. She wanted the pastries at Yaki-Pan to resemble Japanese baked goods as closely as possible, but she quickly discovered that one of the most important ingredients presented a major challenge: flour.

Japanese flour differs significantly from the flour commonly available in the Czech Republic. The differences affect the texture, consistency and ultimately the finished pastry.

“The flour here is not the same as when I learnt,” she says.

Instead of simply following recipes she had learned elsewhere, Hoan had to adapt them to local ingredients. She experimented with different combinations of flour and spent months trying to achieve the texture she was looking for.

Three years ago, she travelled to China to study Japanese baking under professionals. There, she was able to work with Japanese ingredients and gain further experience. Returning to Europe meant starting another process of adjustment.

She considered importing Japanese flour to the Czech Republic, but eventually found it difficult to maintain as a long-term solution. Instead, she continued experimenting with locally available ingredients.

“I needed to test for about two years at my home,” she says.

The process has not necessarily ended with the bakery’s opening. Hoan continues to work on her recipes and ingredients, looking for ways to improve the pastries while staying as close as possible to the style she wants to create.

A warm welcome from Prague

If Hoan was worried that Japanese flavours might be unfamiliar to Prague customers, the first day quickly put those concerns to rest.

When Yaki-Pan opened, she had not prepared significantly more food than usual. Within 30 minutes, the bakery had sold out.

The first two months were particularly busy, especially at weekends. Today, the customer base includes tourists, Japanese residents and visitors who have become regulars.

Japanese customers have also played an important role in validating Hoan’s approach, frequently complimenting her on how closely the pastries resemble those they know from Japan.

Among the most popular items is shio-pan, a Japanese-style bread known for its soft texture and salty flavour. At Yaki-Pan, the vegan version has become one of the bakery’s bestsellers and regularly sells out.

Hoan’s own favourite pastry, meanwhile, changes from day to day.

The bakery’s success has also brought an unexpected question. Some customers have asked why a Vietnamese woman decided to open a Japanese bakery.

For Hoan, the answer is simple. “It’s my dream,” she says. “I put all my energy into my recipes.”

Her background, she suggests, is less important than the work she has put into learning the craft and developing the food.

Building Yaki-Pan’s future

For now, Hoan is focused on the bakery she has already built. Yaki-Pan is run by Hoan and her husband, and her previous experience working in restaurants has helped her manage the busy days herself.

The couple are already thinking about the next stage. They hope to add outdoor seating next year and, eventually, open another location.

But there is no immediate rush to expand.

“Now I want to put all my energy into this one,” Hoan says.

There are also plans to introduce another type of matcha, giving customers more choice alongside the bakery’s existing drinks.

For a business that began as an idea Hoan carried with her for more than 10 years, Yaki-Pan remains very much a work in progress. The recipes continue to evolve, customers continue to discover Japanese-style baking, and Hoan is still searching for the ingredients and techniques that bring her original vision closest to reality.

World.title: Prague Taxi Driver Arrested After Taking CZK 3.5 Million Left in His Car
World.content:
A 21-year-old taxi driver in Prague has been arrested after allegedly taking a suitcase containing CZK 3.5 million in cash that passengers accidentally left in his car.

The money was recovered by police after the driver eventually admitted what he had done and told investigators where he had hidden it. He now faces up to five years in prison.

The incident happened in late July, although police only released details of the case several days later.



The passengers were a married couple who had taken a taxi to Václav Havel Airport in the early morning. They were heading on vacation and only realized after reaching the airport that one of their suitcases was still in the vehicle.

The couple immediately contacted the driver and asked him to bring the suitcase back. According to police, he initially agreed, but the luggage never appeared despite further calls and reminders.

The couple eventually reported the matter to police. Given the amount of money involved, forensic specialists from the Prague 1 police precinct joined the investigation.

Investigators quickly located the taxi and detained the driver. A search of the vehicle, however, produced no suitcase.

The 21-year-old initially denied that the passengers had left anything behind, telling police that he had not found any luggage in the car.

His account later changed.

After being placed in a cell, the man confessed and revealed where he had hidden the cash. Police officers and forensic specialists then located the money in a forest near Kladno.

The investigation also uncovered an attempt to destroy evidence. Near the cash, investigators found the burned remains of the suitcase. Police say the driver had taken the items to the forest, piled them together and set them on fire.

The driver remains under investigation and could face a prison sentence of up to five years if convicted.

World.title: Six Prague Rooftops and Terraces to Visit Before Summer Ends
World.content:
Summer is already moving on, and Prague’s rooftop season won’t last much longer.

August is the time to make the most of the city’s terraces, sunset views and outdoor events before they disappear for another year.

Here are six rooftops and terraces worth visiting before autumn arrives.



1. REASON at Masaryčka

Eleven floors above Masaryk Station, REASON offers one of Prague’s newest rooftop dining spots, with views over the city and the Zaha Hadid-designed Masaryčka development.

This summer, its terrace is also home to the seasonal Frerejean Frères Champagne Bar, serving champagne by the glass, cocktails, oysters and light bites. The menu includes THE REASON KIR, made with herbs grown on the rooftop.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and cocktails above Masaryčka.

2. W Prague – ABOVE Rooftop

ABOVE Rooftop at W Prague brings a Mediterranean feel to the top of Wenceslas Square.

The daily Mediterranean Hour runs from 5 to 6 PM, with two spritzes and a Taste of the Mediterranean platter for CZK 990. Oysters are also served from Thursday to Saturday, alongside a programme of summer events and pop-ups.

This summer: Mediterranean Hour, sunset drinks and oysters in the centre.

3. MINUTY Rooftop Terrace

The rooftop at Fairmont Golden Prague offers views across Pařížská, Letná and the city centre from nine floors up.

MINUTY Rooftop Terrace by Golden Eye focuses on champagne, oysters, caviar and cocktails. The terrace is seasonal and is expected to remain open until September, weather permitting.

This summer: Champagne, oysters and caviar with a view.

4. Sky Lounge 360°

For the view alone, Sky Lounge 360° is hard to beat. The rooftop looks across Prague’s historic centre and becomes livelier during the summer months, with DJs, sunset events and Prague Rooftop Festival activities.

It is more about drinks and atmosphere than a long dinner — a good option for an evening that starts at sunset and continues after dark.

This summer: Sunset events, DJs and panoramic views.

5. Casablanca Sky Bar

On the sixth floor of The President Hotel, Casablanca Sky Bar looks out over the Vltava and Prague skyline.

With DJs, cocktails and regular sunset events, it has more of a party atmosphere than a traditional hotel rooftop. It is also one of the venues taking part in the Prague Rooftop Festival.

This summer: DJs, cocktails and sunset parties above the Vltava.

6. Monkey Bar

Monkey Bar at Falkensteiner Hotel Prague is a quieter alternative, with a green, jungle-style terrace close to the main railway station.

Every Thursday until the end of August, the terrace hosts BBQ & Beats, combining barbecue, live music and summer drinks. Frozen margaritas are also on the menu.

For daytime plans, there is Jungle Brunch, including a bottomless mimosa option.

This summer: BBQ & Beats every Thursday through August.

World.title: Brazilian Summer Vibes Coming to Střelecký ostrov This Weekend
World.content:
Prague’s Střelecký ostrov will turn into a Brazilian-inspired summer spot this Friday and Saturday, with live music, DJs, food, drinks and a riverside atmosphere.

The two-day event will take place from 12 p.m. to 10 p.m. on both days, bringing Brazilian music and summer energy to one of the city’s most picturesque islands.

Visitors can expect live Brazilian music and DJ sets, alongside a selection of food and drinks. The menu will include wine, cheese, Czech dishes, cocktails, frozen margaritas and frozen daiquiris.

The event offers a relaxed way to spend the weekend in central Prague, with music, drinks and food overlooking the Vltava.

World.title: Czech Rivers Reach Record Lows as Drought Deepens
World.content:
Rivers and streams across the Czech Republic are experiencing exceptionally low flows as a prolonged drought continues to worsen, with several waterways approaching or reaching their lowest levels since records began.

According to the latest data from the Czech Hydrometeorological Institute, the vast majority of monitored rivers and streams are flowing well below their long-term averages.

Some of the country’s smallest watercourses have dried up completely, while critical conditions are emerging on several major rivers.



The Elbe is among the most affected. Its flow has fallen to one of the lowest levels ever recorded and is approaching the historic minimum for the entire period of regular observations.

The Vltava is in a somewhat better position in some sections because the reservoir system is being regulated to help stabilize water levels. But even the Vltava has reached an unprecedented low in České Budějovice, where the river is recording its lowest measured flow.

The effects of the drought are particularly visible at the Orlík Reservoir. As water levels have fallen sharply, the remains of a former hydroelectric power plant at Dubrava have emerged from beneath the reservoir.

The plant was built in 1929 but was demolished and flooded in the 1960s when the Orlík Reservoir was created. Its remains have now resurfaced as the reservoir continues to shrink.

The worsening conditions are not limited to rivers and reservoirs. Groundwater levels are also declining, affecting wells and raising concerns about the availability of water supplies in some areas.

Hydrologists are not expecting a significant improvement in the coming days. According to the medium-range weather forecast, there are currently no clear conditions that would bring a substantial recovery in river flows or groundwater levels.

World.title: How to Find a GP in Prague When Practices Aren’t Accepting New Patients
World.content:
Finding a general practitioner in Prague can look simple until the first calls begin.

One practice does not answer. Another says it is full. A third can offer an appointment, but not in English. Your insurer’s list may not show who is accepting new patients today or what kind of visit is available.

If registration is blocked, first clarify whether you need long-term GP care, a one-time consultation, a specialist, an urgent route, or a private self-paid visit.



Decide whether this is really a GP problem

A GP is often the right first contact for common health concerns, preventive care, prescription questions, basic tests, and referrals. In Czech, this doctor is called a praktický lékař.

Not every situation should wait for GP registration. For a sudden and serious health problem or a possible threat to life, call 155 for the medical emergency service or 112 for the European emergency number.

If the issue clearly belongs to a dentist, gynaecologist, or specialist, ask that provider whether direct booking is possible or a referral is required. Patients in Czechia can generally approach a specialist without a GP referral, but an individual provider, insurer, or procedure may have its own requirements.

Tell the provider if you already have results, imaging, a hospital discharge report, or a specialist recommendation, because those documents may affect the next step.

Ask your insurer for help finding a provider

If you have Czech public health insurance and cannot find a GP, contact your insurer directly. Czech health insurers are responsible for helping their members access contracted care under the applicable rules on geographical and time availability.

Ask for practical information:

• Which contracted GPs in my area should be available to new patients?

• Which providers can communicate in English?

• Does the provider have a contract for my care?

• Do I need a referral, approval, or particular documents?

Availability can change, so confirm the details with the practice before travelling there.

If you have commercial insurance, check the provider network and approval process in your policy or contact the insurer. Do not assume that a clinic visit is covered simply because the clinic appears in a search result.

Understand why a practice may say no

A practice may lawfully refuse to accept a patient into care for reasons such as capacity, operational limits, distance that prevents home visits, or the absence of a contract with the patient’s public insurer.

If a provider refuses to accept you as a patient, ask for written confirmation with the reason. This gives you something concrete to show your insurer when requesting another available provider.

Clarify whether the refusal covers long-term registration, all appointments, only publicly insured care, the requested language, or a service the practice does not provide. A limited “no” does not necessarily close every route.

Separate registration from a one-time appointment

Registration and a medical appointment are related, but they are not identical.

Registration creates a long-term relationship with a primary-care doctor. It matters for continuity and for services whose public-insurance reimbursement is linked to the registered GP.

A provider may also offer care without registering you, particularly through a one-time, self-pay appointment. The scope and payment conditions vary, so never assume that a single consultation also means registration or that public insurance will cover it.

Before booking, ask whether the offer is long-term registration, a one-time consultation, a preventive check-up, an urgent appointment, specialist care, or a self-paid visit. Do not leave a clinic assuming that one consultation means you are registered there.

Prepare the information the provider needs

Share only enough information for the provider to understand the request, and use its approved secure channel for medical documents.

Prepare:

• the main reason for the appointment;

• how long the issue has been present;

• whether the request is routine, worsening, urgent, or preventive;

• your insurer or intention to self-pay;

• your preferred language;

• current medicines and allergies;

• relevant reports, results, imaging, or referrals.

A concise request helps the provider determine whether it can help and which appointment type is appropriate.

Make sure the visit has a clear ending

Getting an appointment is only the first part of the process.

A doctor may order tests, issue a referral, prescribe medication, or recommend another consultation. It should be clear who will explain the results and arrange the next step.

Before leaving, ask:

• What happens next?

• When should I expect the results?

• Who will explain them?

• Do I need another appointment?

• Should I send anything to another doctor?

A useful appointment should leave you knowing what comes afterwards.

When coordination support can help

OpenMedical helps patients find suitable English-speaking GPs and other medical specialists in Prague, confirm current availability and appointment conditions, and coordinate the booking process. The service also helps prepare documents, communicate with selected providers, and keep follow-up steps clear.

Quick checklist when GP registration is blocked

• Decide whether the situation is an emergency or can wait for a planned appointment.

• Ask your public insurer to help identify an available contracted provider.

• Ask the practice whether its refusal applies to registration or to all appointments.

• Request written confirmation if a provider refuses to take you into care.

• Confirm language, payment route, referral requirements, and whether a one-time appointment is available.

• Keep copies of medical reports and results.

• Before leaving an appointment, confirm who will explain the results and arrange the next step.

Finding a GP in Prague can take patience. A blocked registration does not mean there is no possible way forward. It means the next route needs to be identified more precisely.

Questions to ask before confirming a GP appointment

• Are you accepting new registered patients?

• Is this a registration visit or a one-time consultation?

• Can the appointment be handled in English?

• Do you have a contract with my public health insurer?

• What is the price if the appointment is self-paid?

• Do I need a referral or prior approval?

• Which documents should I provide, and how should I send them securely?

• How will results and further steps be handled?

World.title: Prague Plans 1.9 Billion Crown Reconstruction of Kasárna Karlín
World.content:
Prague plans to invest around CZK 1.93 billion, including VAT, to transform Kasárna Karlín into a mixed-use complex with shops, offices, student housing and space for cultural and artistic activities.

The city acquired the former military complex in 2023 and has since been working on plans for its long-term redevelopment.

Prague City Council has now approved the next step, allowing the city-owned Trade Centre Prague (TCP), which manages the site, to launch a tender for the preparation of the reconstruction project.



Construction is scheduled to follow between 2027 and 2032, with the investment financed from Prague’s municipal budget.

The first stage will focus on the complex’s main building. A separate building in the courtyard, currently used by the Karlín Barracks Cultural Center, will be addressed in later phases.

Deputy Mayor for Territorial and Strategic Development Petr Hlaváček said the reconstruction should open the site to the surrounding neighborhood while preserving its historic character and protected architectural elements.

One of the main changes will be to improve access to the courtyard, which currently has just one entrance and is largely hidden from the surrounding streets.

Adam Zábranský, Prague’s councilor for property, transparency and legislation, said new passages from the street would lead into the complex, with shops and services occupying the ground floor. The arcade running alongside these commercial spaces would form part of the new circulation system through the site.

The upper levels could eventually accommodate student housing, studios and offices. Zábranský also mentioned the possibility of using some of the space for businesses such as a technology park.

The exact future use of many of the rooms has not yet been decided. According to Zábranský, the project should therefore prioritize flexible layouts that can be adapted for different purposes over time.

The initial investment will focus in particular on replacing and upgrading essential infrastructure, including water, electricity and waste systems, as well as preparing the commercial areas on the ground floor. Work on the upper floors is expected to come later.

World.title: Czechia Sees Lyme Disease Surge With 90 New Cases a Day
World.content:
Lyme disease cases are rising sharply across the Czech Republic, with more than 8,000 infections recorded since the beginning of the year.

Health officials warn that the summer peak may not have arrived yet.

A total of 8,108 cases were reported through the end of July, according to data from the Czech State Institute of Health (SZÚ). July alone accounted for 2,792 infections, meaning that roughly one in three cases recorded so far this year occurred during the month.



Doctors registered an average of about 90 new cases each day in July.

The figures are significantly higher than those seen in previous years. Between January and July, the Czech Republic typically recorded between 1,500 and 2,000 Lyme disease cases.

Part of the increase may be linked to a change in the way infectious diseases are reported.

The number of tick-borne infections depends on several factors, including tick populations and seasonal weather conditions. Climate change is also playing an increasingly important role.

The highest numbers of Lyme disease infections have so far been reported in the Central Bohemian and South Moravian regions.

The risk is not limited to forests and countryside. Prague’s parks and wooded areas can also provide suitable conditions for ticks.

“Prague’s parks and forest parks create a specific microclimate where ticks thrive, so the risk of infection is real for residents even during an ordinary walk,” said Martina Marešová, head of the anti-epidemic department at the Prague Hygiene Station.

Early treatment can prevent complications

One of the most recognizable signs of Lyme disease is an expanding red rash that develops around the site of a tick bite and may have a paler area in the center.

Anyone who develops such a rash should seek medical attention rather than waiting for it to disappear.

The most common form initially affects the skin. If left untreated, the infection can progress and cause further skin problems. More serious complications can involve the nervous system, heart or eyes.

World.title: VIDEO: Hungarian pair on Europe’s Most Wanted list arrested in Spain
World.content:
Two Hungarian fugitives arrested in Tenerife had been wanted over an extensive drug-trafficking investigation in which police seized several thousand marijuana plants and more than 180 kilograms of dried narcotics. The couple had also appeared on Europe’s Most Wanted list before being tracked down in Spain.

A 32-year-old Hungarian couple suspected of holding senior positions in a drug-trafficking criminal organisation have been arrested on the Spanish island of Tenerife in a joint operation involving Hungarian and Spanish authorities, Hungarian police announced on Thursday.

The two suspects were arrested on 7 August with the involvement of a specialised Tenerife police unit after investigators established that they were hiding on the Canary Island. They are currently being held pending surrender proceedings, with Spanish authorities to decide on their transfer to Hungary.

Why the Hungarian fugitives arrested in Tenerife were wanted

Although the latest Hungarian police statement refers to the suspects only by their initials, B. B. and V. V., their public Europe’s Most Wanted profiles identify them as Bendegúz Zoltán Balló and Valentina Varga, both Hungarian citizens born in Székesfehérvár.

Their arrest is linked to a much larger investigation conducted by the criminal investigation department of the Komárom-Esztergom County Police Headquarters. According to police, the organisation operated as a tightly controlled, closed network engaged in drug trafficking. During searches carried out as part of the investigation, officers seized several thousand marijuana plants as well as more than 180 kilograms of already dried narcotics.

Police say Balló and Varga held leadership roles within the organisation but disappeared before they could be brought before the authorities. Because of the scale of the alleged offence and the particularly large quantity of drugs involved, they were placed on the Hungarian police’s TOP 50 most-wanted list.

The public European wanted notices provide further detail on the allegations. Balló was sought in Hungary for the possession and trafficking of a particularly large quantity of narcotics, specifically marijuana, while Varga was wanted for possession and trafficking of a particularly large quantity of narcotics. Their cases remained under investigation rather than being listed as convictions.

The Tatabánya District Court issued a European arrest warrant for Varga on 5 June 2025 in connection with drug trafficking and drug possession. Balló was also subject to a European arrest warrant issued by the same court over drug trafficking allegations, and his Europe’s Most Wanted profile was published in September 2025.

If you missed it: Budapest in deep trouble: more threatening individuals on streets, cheap drugs becoming increasingly widespread

Hunt leads investigators to the Canary Islands

After investigators concluded that the couple had probably left Hungary, the Komárom-Esztergom police turned to the National Bureau of Investigation’s fugitive-tracking unit for assistance. Hungarian investigators subsequently obtained information indicating that the fugitives were likely to be hiding in Spain.

The Hungarian authorities contacted their Spanish counterparts through ENFAST, the European Network of Fugitive Active Search Teams, which links specialist units responsible for tracking serious fugitives across Europe. Cooperation between the two countries eventually narrowed the pair’s location down to Tenerife.

Spanish police arrested them on 7 August. Hungarian authorities announced the operation six days later, on 13 August.

What happens next?

The two Hungarian citizens remain in surrender detention in Spain. Their return to Hungary depends on a decision by the Spanish authorities, while the international coordination of their transfer will be handled on the Hungarian side by the National Centre for International Criminal Cooperation.

The case highlights both the scale of the underlying drug investigation and the increasingly cross-border nature of fugitive searches within Europe. While much of the suspected organisation had already been dismantled in Hungary, the capture of the two alleged leaders in Tenerife closes an important part of a manhunt that had extended well beyond Hungary’s borders.

World.title: Construction down, car industry up in June: What’s happening in Hungary’s economy?
World.content:
Hungary’s construction sector weakened again in June, marking a second consecutive monthly decline after a sharp reversal in May. The latest figures show that the Hungarian construction industry remains highly volatile: a relatively strong spring was followed by two months of falling output, while the volume of new contracts also dropped steeply.

According to Telex, citing fresh data from the Hungarian Central Statistical Office (KSH), construction output in June 2026 was 1.2% lower than a year earlier based on unadjusted figures. After adjustment for working days, the annual decline reached 5%.

Compared with May, seasonally and working-day adjusted output fell by another 3.9%.

Hungarian construction industry records second monthly decline

The June figures revealed a considerable difference between the main parts of the sector.

Output in the construction of buildings decreased by 5.5% compared with June 2025, while civil engineering output – which includes projects such as roads, railways and utilities – increased by 5.6%.

Looking at construction divisions, the picture was even more uneven. Building construction fell by 22.1%, while civil engineering expanded by 28.3%. Specialised construction activities, the largest division in the industry, recorded marginal annual growth of 0.6%.

Road and railway construction was a major contributor to the stronger civil engineering result, increasing by 49.6% year-on-year, according to the KSH’s June release.

New business, however, gave a much weaker signal. The volume of new construction contracts signed in June was 41.9% below the level recorded a year earlier. New contracts for buildings fell by 16.8%, while those for civil engineering projects plunged by 58.6%.

The KSH noted that total construction output in the first six months of 2026 was 0.7% lower than in the same period of 2025.

If you missed it: new Budapest bridge to be built as project reaches important milestone – photos, video

What happened in the previous three months?

The June decline is easier to understand when viewed alongside the previous three monthly reports.

In March, the sector appeared to be recovering. The KSH reported that construction output was 3.9% higher year-on-year according to unadjusted data and 0.5% above February on a seasonally and working-day adjusted basis. Nevertheless, output in the first quarter as a whole was still 4.2% below the corresponding period of 2025.

The improvement continued in April. According to the KSH’s April release, output rose by 2.6% from a year earlier and jumped 6.9% compared with March on a seasonally and working-day adjusted basis. Civil engineering was particularly strong, rising by 13.9% year-on-year, while the construction of buildings declined by 6.2%.

Then came a dramatic reversal in May. The KSH initially reported a 10.7% annual decline in unadjusted construction output and a 6.5% monthly fall after seasonal and working-day adjustment. Civil engineering output was reported to have fallen by 21.9% from a year earlier.

The statistical office has subsequently revised parts of the earlier monthly series in its latest dataset. However, the overall sequence remains clear: output strengthened during March and April before falling in May and declining again in June.

Hungarian automotive industry output surges 21pc in June

Output of the automotive industry, Hungary’s biggest manufacturing sector, climbed 21pc year-on-year in June, a detailed reading of data released by the Central Statistics Office (KSH) on Thursday shows.

The automotive segment accounted for 27pc of manufacturing output during the month, MTI said.

Output of the computer, electronics and optical equipment segment, which accounted for 15pc of manufacturing, jumped 50pc, boosted by production of peripherals.

Output of the food, drinks and tobacco products segment, making up 12pc of manufacturing, slipped 1.5pc.

Output of the electrical equipment segment, accounting for 8.3pc of manufacturing, edged up 1.8pc.

KSH confirmed that headline industrial output rose 10.1pc year-on-year in June.

Output rose 4.1pc when adjusted for the number of workdays, of which there were two more than in the base period.

In a month-on-month comparison, output edged down a seasonally- and workday-adjusted 1.4pc.

In January-June, industrial output rose 2.4pc.

Why the figures matter for foreign readers

For international readers, it is important to distinguish between the two broad categories used in Hungarian construction statistics. Building construction covers residential and non-residential buildings, while civil engineering encompasses infrastructure such as roads, railway lines and utility networks.

The latest figures therefore do not show a uniform collapse across the Hungarian construction industry. Infrastructure construction remained relatively strong in June, while building-related activity was much weaker. At the same time, the industrial data point to a very different trend in another key part of the economy: output in Hungary’s automotive industry, the country’s largest manufacturing segment, surged 21pc year-on-year and accounted for 27pc of total manufacturing output in June. Its strong performance was a major positive signal in a month when headline industrial production rose 10.1pc year-on-year, even though output slipped 1.4pc compared with May on a seasonally and workday-adjusted basis.

Taken together, the figures underline how uneven Hungary’s economic performance remains. Construction is still facing weak demand and a sharp fall in new contracts, while manufacturing – particularly the automotive and electronics industries – showed much stronger annual growth in June. The next releases from KSH will therefore be important in showing whether the weakness in construction becomes more persistent and whether the strong automotive performance can be sustained beyond a single month.

World.title: The danger is not over: Budapest water supply under pressure again
World.content:
Hungary’s main water utility for the capital has once again urged consumers to reduce unnecessary water use as persistently low levels on the Danube put growing pressure on the Budapest water supply. The situation is particularly serious in Dunabogdány, north of the capital, where the remaining capacity of the local system has fallen to a critical level.

According to 24.hu, Budapest Waterworks (Fővárosi Vízművek) warned that although the Danube could temporarily rise by a few centimetres, a lack of rainfall across its catchment area means water levels may soon begin falling again.

The company said the latest forecast required both close attention and responsible water use. While the utility is working to maintain a secure drinking-water supply, prolonged low water levels on the Danube are creating increasingly difficult conditions for water production.

Budapest water supply: residents asked to avoid unnecessary use

Budapest Waterworks has asked all consumers to moderate their use of mains drinking water and prioritise essential everyday needs.

Large-scale uses that can be postponed should be avoided, the company said. Such activities typically include filling swimming pools, washing cars and extensive garden watering.

The issue is particularly important for foreign residents and visitors to understand because much of Budapest’s drinking water is closely linked to the Danube. The capital relies heavily on bank-filtered water: wells located along the river draw naturally filtered groundwater from gravel layers connected to the Danube.

Low river levels therefore do not automatically mean that Budapest is running out of drinking water, but prolonged drought can make extraction more difficult and increase the technical and energy demands on the system.

This is not the first water-saving warning of 2026

The latest appeal is not an isolated event this year.

During the extreme heat at the end of June, water consumption across the area served by Budapest Waterworks rose sharply. On 29 June, around 640 million litres of drinking water were consumed in a single day, according to an earlier report by the Budapest municipal news portal Énbudapestem. In some parts of the capital and surrounding settlements, consumption was several times higher than the 2025 daily average.

At the time, Budapest Waterworks was already asking consumers to use water carefully and, where possible, to avoid carrying out water-intensive activities during peak evening hours.

The warnings became even more urgent in Dunabogdány in July. On 30 July, Sokszínű Vidék reported that the utility had already appealed to local residents several times to reduce consumption, asking them to avoid watering gardens, filling pools and washing cars. Despite those requests, demand continued to rise.

As we wrote yesterday, PM Magyar announces moves to raise the Danube near Paks nuclear power plant

Dunabogdány faces the most critical situation

Conditions are currently most severe in Dunabogdány, a popular settlement on the Danube Bend roughly north of Budapest.

Local wells are producing around 1,000–1,050 cubic metres of water per day, while daily consumption stands at approximately 1,100–1,150 cubic metres, according to 24.hu. Production capacity could fall further if the Danube continues to recede.

Budapest Waterworks warned that reserves in the local system have been reduced to a minimum, meaning that any further increase in consumption or an unexpected technical problem could threaten the continuity of drinking-water supplies.

Dunabogdány Mayor András Liebhardt has pushed back against criticism of local residents. In an earlier statement reported by Sokszínű Vidék, he argued that higher summer consumption also reflects the seasonal increase in the village’s population due to tourism and people temporarily living there.

Low Danube levels causing wider problems in Hungary

The exceptionally low Danube has implications well beyond the Budapest water supply.

During the extreme heat around the end of July and beginning of August, the river fell to exceptionally low levels. The conditions also affected operations at Hungary’s Paks Nuclear Power Plant, illustrating how prolonged heat, drought and low river flows can place simultaneous pressure on the country’s water and energy infrastructure.

For Budapest Waterworks, the immediate message remains precautionary rather than a declaration of a capital-wide water shortage. Consumers are nevertheless being asked to avoid unnecessary high-volume water use as long as the Danube remains unusually low and rainfall across its catchment area remains limited.

World.title: Horror crash on Hungarian motorway: Child thrown from British-registered car
World.content:
Four people, including two children, were injured in a serious crash on Hungary’s M7 motorway near Zalakomár on Wednesday afternoon, after a British-registered car collided with a road maintenance truck.

One of the children was thrown from the car in the impact and was airlifted to hospital. According to the National Ambulance Service, the child suffered serious injuries but was in a stable condition. Two adults and the other child sustained minor injuries.

British-registered car crashed into maintenance truck

According to 24.hu, the accident happened on the Budapest-bound carriageway of the M7 motorway, between kilometres 189 and 190 near Zalakomár in Zala County. As per the police, the British-registered passenger car crashed into a road maintenance vehicle for reasons that are not yet known. All four occupants of the car were injured.

The force of the collision caused one of the children to be thrown out of the vehicle. Several ambulance units, including an air ambulance, were dispatched to the scene. The seriously injured child was transported to hospital by helicopter, while the two adults and the other child were taken to hospital with less serious injuries.

M7 motorway temporarily closed

The Budapest-bound side of the M7 was completely closed while police investigated the crash and emergency crews carried out the necessary rescue and recovery work. Drivers were diverted towards Route 7 at the Zalakomár junction, causing disruption to traffic in the area.

The closure was later lifted on Wednesday afternoon, and the M7 motorway at Zalakomár was reopened to traffic. The circumstances of the crash are under investigation.

World.title: Was there really any difference between András Baka’s removal in 2011 and Tamás Sulyok’s in 2026?
World.content:
Many see András Baka becoming Hungary’s next president as a form of historical justice after his controversial removal. But does that make the removal of Sulyok any more democratic?

The similarities between the removal of András Baka in 2011 and that of Tamás Sulyok in 2026 are difficult to ignore. In both cases, a constitutional change was used to bring the mandate of an incumbent constitutional office-holder to an early end.

That makes Baka’s election as Hungary’s next president all the more intriguing. Many see it as historical justice after his controversial removal under the Orbán government. But it also raises a difficult question for Tisza: if Baka’s removal was an abuse of constitutional power, what makes Sulyok’s removal any different?

What happened to András Baka?

András Baka became President of Hungary’s Supreme Court in 2009. He publicly criticised several government reforms affecting the judiciary and warned that they threatened judicial independence.

His mandate was then terminated years before it was due to expire, as the constitutional framework of Hungary’s judiciary was fundamentally reorganised.

The case eventually reached the European Court of Human Rights. In 2016, the Court ruled that Hungary had violated Baka’s rights, finding that the premature termination of his mandate was linked to his public criticism of constitutional and legislative reforms concerning the judiciary.

The story therefore seems almost tailor-made for historical justice. The former chief justice who became one of the symbols of the Orbán era’s rule-of-law problems has now been elected president in the middle of a political transition whose central promise is to restore the rule of law. But this is exactly where the comparison becomes uncomfortable.

The resemblance is striking

Let us put the two cases next to each other and look at the constitutional mechanism itself. Baka’s mandate was brought to an early end by a constitutional provision stating:

The mandates of the President of the Supreme Court and the President and members of

the National Council of Justice shall be terminated when the Fundamental Law comes into force.

Sulyok’s mandate, meanwhile, is being terminated by another constitutional provision:

On the day following the entry into force of the Seventeenth Amendment to the

Fundamental Law, the mandate of the President of the Republic in office shall terminate.

The circumstances are certainly not identical. András Baka was the President of the Supreme Court, and his removal took place amid a fundamental restructuring of the judiciary. The European Court of Human Rights subsequently found a violation of his Convention rights.

Sulyok, by contrast, is being removed by a newly elected parliamentary majority that has the constitutional majority required to amend the Fundamental Law.

But the central question remains. Should a parliamentary majority be able to change the constitution specifically so that the mandate of an incumbent constitutional office-holder ends? If the answer was no when Orbán’s government did it, why should the answer automatically become yes when Tisza does it?

Was electing Baka a mistake?

Politically, probably not. Baka is an exceptionally powerful symbol for Tisza. His career allows the new government to present the presidency as part of a restoration of judicial independence and democratic institutions.

Fidesz, meanwhile, can hardly attack András Baka without reopening the uncomfortable question of why he was removed in the first place. In the short term, therefore, his election is a clever political move. In the longer term, however, Baka could become one of Tisza’s biggest constitutional headaches.

From now on, whenever the legality or legitimacy of Sulyok’s removal is debated, Baka’s name will inevitably be brought into the discussion. Critics can draw the parallel in a single sentence: In 2011, one government used constitutional change to remove an inconvenient constitutional figure. In 2026, another government did something remarkably similar.

Of course, Tisza can argue that it is dismantling a political and constitutional system built by Orbán and that it has received a democratic mandate to do so. But that is precisely where the rule-of-law test begins. Constitutional safeguards are not supposed to protect only the politicians we support. They are supposed to protect institutions even when the people in power are the ones we strongly disagree with.

And that is why Baka’s election is such a powerful — and potentially awkward — symbol. The former chief justice removed through constitutional engineering has returned as president. The question is whether Hungary has truly learned the lesson of his case. Or whether it has simply changed who gets to use the same constitutional tools.

But why did Tisza ultimately choose András Baka over Judit Polgár for the presidency? We explored the reasons in more detail in this article.

World.title: Hungary could get a new public holiday: Christmas Eve could become a day off this year!
World.content:
Christmas Eve could become a genuine public holiday in Hungary as early as this year, meaning employees may no longer have to make up the day by working a Saturday. A new proposal says the change could be introduced with a simple parliamentary majority.

24 December could become a statutory day off

Hungary could make 24 December a public holiday as early as 2026, with no referendum or two-thirds parliamentary majority required under the current legal framework.

According to Világgazdaság, the National Federation of Workers’ Councils (Munkástanácsok Országos Szövetsége) and trade union organisation Egyenlő.hu submitted a concrete proposal to the Ministry of Social and Family Affairs in July. If the proposal reaches Parliament in the autumn and is approved, Christmas Eve could become a public holiday without requiring employees to make up the day by working a Saturday.

The proposed solution is legally simpler than the issue might suggest. Rather than creating a new national holiday, 24 December would simply be added to the list of statutory public holidays in Hungary’s Labour Code.

At present, the list includes 1 January, 15 March, Good Friday, Easter Monday, 1 May, Whit Monday, 20 August, 23 October, 1 November, and 25 and 26 December.

Under the current system, 24 December is not a public holiday. Instead, the government can designate it as a rest day in the annual working-time schedule, with employees then required to work on a nearby Saturday.

This is exactly what is planned for 2026: Christmas Eve falls on a Thursday, making 24 December a designated rest day, but employees are currently scheduled to work on Saturday, 12 December in exchange. The proposed amendment would change this arrangement permanently.

No more Saturday make-up day

If 24 December were added to the Labour Code’s list of public holidays, it would no longer need to be designated as a day off through a separate ministerial decree every year. Most importantly, the Saturday make-up working day would disappear as well.

According to the organisations behind the proposal, amending the Labour Code would only require a simple parliamentary majority. There would be no need to amend the Fundamental Law’s provisions concerning public holidays, meaning a two-thirds majority would not be necessary.

It would be more than just another day off

There is an important legal distinction between a holiday and a statutory public holiday. Simply declaring a date a holiday does not automatically mean employees cannot be required to work. A statutory public holiday, however, comes with specific employment-law protections.

Csaba Bubenkó, deputy president of Munkástanácsok, said the proposed amendment would guarantee exemption from work and introduce stricter conditions for those who could still legally be scheduled to work. The rules on holiday pay supplements and compensation for absence would also apply.

The change would have a direct impact on retailers, too. Under the proposal, no separate shop-opening regulations would be necessary: designating 24 December as a public holiday would itself mean that shops could not open, while essential food supplies and public services would continue to be taken into account.

A referendum may no longer be necessary

Other trade unions have also been working towards making Christmas Eve a public holiday. The Trade Union of Commercial Employees (Kereskedelmi Alkalmazottak Szakszervezete) has been working to collect the 200,000 signatures required for a referendum initiative certified by Hungary’s National Election Office.

The new legal proposal could make that process unnecessary. If Parliament simply adds 24 December to the Labour Code’s list of public holidays, there would be no need for the longer and more costly referendum process.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar previously promised that Christmas Eve would become a public holiday that would not have to be made up by working another day. In July, he also said he hoped the change could take effect as early as this year. However, the exact timing will depend on the legislative process and Parliament’s decision, so it is not yet certain that the new rules will apply this Christmas.

If Parliament approves the amendment in the autumn, 2026 could nevertheless become the first year in which 24 December is a fully fledged statutory public holiday rather than a transferred day off. And that would mean one thing many Hungarian workers will certainly welcome: no Saturday at work just to get Christmas Eve off.

World.title: Hungarian Wizz Air opens new base in another European city!
World.content:
Wizz Air is expanding its presence in Romania once again, announcing a new operational base at Brașov-Ghimbav International Airport from December 2026. The move will bring four new routes to the Transylvanian city and expand Wizz Air’s Brașov network to 15 destinations across seven countries.

The airline’s expansion comes despite a challenging financial period, with Wizz Air recently reporting a significant loss for the first quarter of its current financial year.

Wizz Air to base an aircraft in Brașov

From December, Brașov-Ghimbav International Airport will become home to one Airbus A321neo operated by Wizz Air, making Brașov (Brassó) the airline’s 10th operational base in Romania, Maszol.ro writes based on the report of economica.net. The new base will support four new routes connecting Brașov with:

Chișinău, Moldova

Barcelona, Spain

Madrid, Spain

Karlsruhe/Baden-Baden, Germany

Once the expansion is complete, passengers flying from Brașov will be able to reach 15 cities in seven countries with Wizz Air. The new routes are expected to significantly strengthen the airport’s international connectivity, particularly for travellers in southern Transylvania.

800,000 passengers have already flown with Wizz Air from Brașov

Wizz Air has operated from Brașov since August 2023. According to data from the local county council, its services have carried around 800,000 passengers from the airport so far. The airline says its continued presence demonstrates its long-term commitment to the region.

“Over the past three years, through our uninterrupted operations at Brașov Airport, we have demonstrated our long-term commitment to the region,” said András Radó, Wizz Air’s communications director.

He also described Romania as a key market for the airline. The new Brașov base comes just nine months after Wizz Air opened another base in Transylvania, at Târgu Mureș.

Romania a key market for Wizz Air

Wizz Air has been operating in Romania since 2006 and has established itself as the country’s leading low-cost airline. The carrier currently employs around 1,900 people in Romania and connects 14 Romanian cities with 83 destinations across 26 countries, operating a total of around 230 routes.

The expansion in Brașov therefore represents another significant step in the airline’s Romanian network, particularly as demand for international travel from regional airports continues to grow.

Photo: Wizz Air

If you missed it: Wizz Air Budapest-Tallinn flight returns to Budapest shortly after take-off

Wizz Air reports nearly EUR 200 million quarterly loss

The expansion comes at an interesting time for the airline financially. Wizz Air recently reported a EUR 198 million loss for the three months ending in June. This compares with a EUR 38.4 million profit recorded during the same period a year earlier.

Despite the substantial loss, the airline’s revenue increased by 5.5% year-on-year to EUR 1.51 billion, although this was slightly below analysts’ expectations of EUR 1.54 billion. The Brașov expansion nevertheless signals that Wizz Air continues to see considerable growth potential in Romania.

With a new aircraft based locally and four additional international destinations on the way, Brașov is set to become an increasingly important part of Wizz Air’s Romanian network from the end of this year.

World.title: Budapest’s long-awaited metro extension is finally moving: dozens of homes stand in its way
World.content:
Budapest’s long-discussed plan to extend Metro Line 3 could finally be moving towards construction, with the city now reviewing existing plans for a new section reaching Rákospalota-Újpest. But before work can begin, around 24 properties – most of them residential – must be acquired, while the project faces a tight timetable and an unusual challenge: the extension would initially have to be served by the line’s existing Russian-built trains.

M3 extension plans are back on the table

The Budapest Transport Centre (BKK) has begun reviewing the existing plans for extending Metro Line 3 from Újpest-Központ towards Rákospalota-Újpest. The review will assess how the roughly 1.9-kilometre extension could be built, how the project could be divided into phases, how long construction might take and what risks could stand in its way.

Metro Line 3 reached Újpest-Központ from the city centre in 1990. Despite earlier plans to continue the line towards Káposztásmegyer, the extension never materialised.

The project has now returned to the agenda as part of the government’s Baross Gábor Railway Development Plan. The first phase would extend the line as far as Rákospalota-Újpest railway station.

If you missed it: Hungary set to launch EUR 5.5 billion railway upgrade as development plan gets green light

Two new stations could transform northern Budapest connections

According to the existing plans, the new section would begin near Árpád út 119, at the end of the existing underground structure, and run for approximately 1.9 kilometres. Two new stations would be built: one near Rózsa Street and another at Rákospalota-Újpest railway station.

The latter could be particularly significant for commuters, as it would create connections with the Budapest–Vác–Szob and Budapest–Veresegyház–Vác railway lines. Passengers arriving from the northern suburbs could therefore transfer to the M3 at Újpest rather than travelling all the way to Nyugati railway station.

The extension is planned using a cut-and-cover construction method rather than conventional deep tunnelling. BKK has also extended all the relevant railway authority permits, which will remain valid until December 2028. The organisation is now preparing to order the tender documentation needed for the construction procurement process.

24 properties need to be acquired first

There is, however, a major obstacle before construction can get properly underway.

Around 24 properties along the planned route would have to be acquired. Most are residential buildings located on land that was designated for the future metro project decades ago.

The Budapest municipal asset management company will therefore have to begin purchasing the properties or launching compulsory acquisition procedures as soon as possible. A 2021 estimate put the cost of acquiring the properties at around HUF 2.8 billion, although the current figure could be considerably higher following changes in property prices.

The project will also require close cooperation between the capital, its companies and the municipalities of Budapest’s Districts IV and XV.

Never miss a headline: join Daily News Hungary’s official WhatsApp channel!

The clock is already ticking

BKK has warned that the project could only be delivered under an extremely tight schedule. The amount of time available is limited compared with the scale and complexity of the investment, making cooperation between national and local authorities particularly important.

The permits expiring at the end of 2028 add another deadline to the equation. If sufficient progress is not made by then, further extensions or additional permitting work could be required. The construction itself could also be a substantial investment. An earlier analysis by MBH Bank estimated that, at current prices, the two-station extension could cost HUF 120–160 billion.

The project would not necessarily pay for itself through ticket revenue. Its wider benefits, however, could include shorter journeys, lower commuting costs, better access to employment, fewer road accidents and reduced environmental damage.

The analysis estimated that the extension would need to generate around HUF 8 billion in annual indirect social benefits to be considered economically worthwhile over a 30-year assessment period.

The new metro connection could also push up property values around the future stations. According to the analysis, homes within roughly 500–800 metres of Rákospalota-Újpest station could eventually be worth up to 10% more than they would be without the investment.

The Russian-built trains are here to stay

One of the project’s more unusual challenges concerns the trains themselves. BKK says the M3’s existing Metrowagonmash rolling stock will have to be treated as a given for at least the next 20 years. That means the planned extension to Rákospalota-Újpest would initially have to be operated using the existing fleet.

This would put greater pressure on BKV’s fleet management, although BKK believes the current trains could still be sufficient to operate the two-stop extension.

The situation is partly a consequence of the fact that an option for seven additional trains under BKV’s contract with the Russian manufacturer has expired. Metrowagonmash is also subject to sanctions because of Russia’s war against Ukraine, making the straightforward purchase of additional trains impossible at present. New rolling stock would become more important if the full extension to Káposztásmegyer eventually goes ahead.

Could Budapest finally get the extension it has been waiting for?

The M3 extension is not necessarily the most urgent rail transport investment Budapest could undertake. However, it has one major advantage over many other proposed projects: much of the groundwork has already been done.

The current review will determine whether the existing plans, permits, property arrangements and available trains provide a realistic basis for finally moving the project from paper to construction. After more than three decades of waiting since the M3 reached Újpest-Központ, the long-promised northern extension may finally be getting another chance.

World.title: Romanian president again challenges law allowing hydropower projects in protected areas
World.content:
Romanian president Nicușor Dan has asked Parliament to reconsider legislation allowing the construction and completion of hydropower projects in protected areas, reopening a dispute over the balance between energy security and environmental protection.

Dan submitted the request to Parliament on August 12, according to Economedia, after the Constitutional Court rejected his objections to the legislation in June.

"Beyond the limits of constitutional control, we consider that the current assessment of the necessity, opportunity and efficiency of the adopted legislative solutions is required, including from the perspective of developments that have occurred since the initiation of the legislative proposal," Dan said in the note accompanying his request.

The president had previously argued that the legislation could allow protected-area boundaries to be reduced and environmental assessments to be waived for entire categories of energy projects, including projects declared by the Supreme Council for National Defence to be of national security interest.

The legislation, initiated by Social Democratic Party (PSD) senator Daniel Zamfir, is designed to facilitate the completion of unfinished hydropower projects.

State-controlled Hidroelectrica plans to resume and complete several projects originally started during the communist period. The Energy Ministry has proposed completing around 10 unfinished hydropower plants with a combined capacity of about 700 MW, arguing that substantial investments have already been made in the projects.

The projects have remained unfinished for years, with some facing environmental and legal obstacles. Their completion has gained renewed attention amid pressure to increase domestic electricity generation and strengthen Romania’s energy security.

Environmental organisations, including Declic and other civic groups, oppose the resumption of some of the projects because of their potential impact on river ecosystems. They argue that upgrading existing hydropower capacity could deliver energy gains with lower environmental costs than completing older projects in protected areas.

The dispute comes as Romania faces pressure on its electricity system following the shutdown of both reactors at the Cernavoda nuclear power plant because of exceptionally low Danube water levels. The government has also sought to maintain additional coal-fired generation capacity beyond existing decarbonisation deadlines.

Parliament will now have to reconsider the legislation following the president’s request, despite the Constitutional Court having already ruled on its constitutionality.

World.title: Northern Romania: resort of Sângeorz-Băi aims to build modern spa center
World.content:
Sângeorz-Băi, once a well-known balneoclimateric resort town in northern Romania, aims to resurrect its large hotels, which have been either closed or operating at minimum capacity, through the development of a modern spa center, according to G4Media.

The mayor of the town, Cătălin Bota, said that the only asset remaining in the ownership of the town is Mineral Water Spring 6. Based on this, the town hall submitted a project for a treatment facility and a spa complex in the resort park, but political changes and changes at the ministerial level have delayed the financing.

Some of the largest hotels in the town have already closed. The famous Someșul Hotel, owned by the trade unions, has been closed and abandoned for four years, having been emptied of furniture. Hotel Hebe, privatized, operates only during the summer, with minimal investments and a degraded treatment facility, moved to the ground floor.

Nevertheless, the local administration has modernized the utility networks and streets and is carrying out a project financed from European funds for the rehabilitation of the resort park. It will include an open-air museum created in collaboration with the Museum of Comparative Art, where 25 statues have already been restored.

“In the absence of funds from the government, the town hall intends to access European funds under the 2028-2034 financial framework, even if the co-financing rate is 50%,” said Cătălin Bota.

Representatives of the town hall claimed that public investment is the only chance to attract tourists again and to prompt private owners to invest, given that spa tourism has been neglected at the national level in recent years.

World.title: Transylvania Tapes: Found footage horror movie filmed in Romania has local premiere at Biertan festival
World.content:
Transylvania Tapes, a mix of the found footage and Eurohorror genres directed by filmmaker Brad Sykes, will have its Romanian premiere at the Lună Plină/ Full Moon Horror and Fantasy Film Festival in Biertan on August 16.

The film, shot entirely in Bucharest and Sighisoara, follows Mara Enescu, a young woman in her 30s who travels from Los Angeles to her home country of Romania to discover the truth about her mother’s disappearance in Transylvania years ago. Together with a cameraman friend, she journeys from Bucharest “to the birthplace of Dracula himself.”

The movie, produced by Josephina Sykes, stars newcomer Valeria Badiuc (in opening photo) as well as Gabriel Spahiu, who recently had roles in Radu Jude’s Kontinental '25 and Dracula, and Ion Haiduc, recently seen in Trancers: The Whole Dethly Affair.

Transylvania Tapes had its world premiere this June at the Horror-on-Sea Film Festival in the UK. It also screened at GrossFest Film Festival in Pittsburgh.

“Transylvania Tapes is a unique mix of found footage and Eurohorror genres that my wife and producer, Josephina, and I have been wanting to make for twenty years. After writing several different scripts, creating multiple budgets and taking far too many meetings, we finally decided last year that if we wanted to make our dream project, we needed to make it completely independently with the resources we had available. This meant calling in favors from friends going back to the late 1990s, when Josephina and I first met on a Romanian movie set, as well as working with some brand-new talent. Making Transylvania Tapes was an exciting journey for all of us and one of the most intimate, personal movies I have ever directed,” director Brad Sykes explains.

Filmmaker and author Brad Sykes graduated cum laude from Boston University’s film program. After moving to Los Angeles and working in production and development for companies including Paramount Pictures, Scott Free, and Full Moon Entertainment, Sykes made his professional writing/directing debut with the horror comedy Scream Queen, starring genre icon Linnea Quigley. Since then, he has written and directed over twenty-five feature films, including the digital 3D horror movie Camp Blood.

Sykes’ film Death Factory was its distributor's all-time top-grossing title. His other writing-directing credits include Goth, Mad Jack, Demon's Kiss, Plaguers (winner of Best Screenplay at the 2008 Estepona Film Festival and Best Actor Steve Railsback at 2008 Shockerfest), Hi-8: Horror Independent Eight and its sequels Hi-Death and Hi-Fear. He lives in Los Angeles with his wife, producer Josephina Sykes, where they operate Nightfall Pictures, a full-service development and production company.

Josephina Sykes, who was born in Bucharest, graduated in 1999 from the National University of Theatre and Film UNATC with a major in screenwriting. She also spent a semester at La FEMIS film school in Paris in 1998, on a scholarship from the French Foreign Ministry. After graduation, she worked for film studios Castel Film and Media Pro Pictures. Since relocating to Los Angeles in 2001, she has continued to work in film, both as a screenwriter and in production on various indie features. In 2004, she founded Nightfall Pictures, a full-service development and production company, with her husband.

She has produced several feature films, including the thriller Within the Woods, the drama Dead Letters, starring C. Thomas Howell, actioner Mutation, the debut of Katie Featherston, and the award-winning sci-fi/horror film Plaguers, starring Steve Railsback. She is one of the co-creators and executive producers of the horror anthology Hi-8: Horror Independent Eight, which was selected in the official competition of over twenty film festivals.

(Photos: Nightfall Pictures)
