World.title: Irakli Kobakhidze: “‘Deep state’ is trying to artificially fuel Russophobia in Georgia”
World.content:
“Radical anti-Russian sentiment in the country is being artificially fuelled and is part of a new campaign against Georgia,” Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze said at a briefing. He said attempts to intensify Russophobia in Georgia were part of a plan carried out by agents of the “deep state”.

Kobakhidze recalled that the Georgian government had repeatedly said that, after Russia launched its full-scale war against Ukraine in 2022, the so-called “global war party” had tried to draw Georgia into the conflict and open a “second front” in the country.

The prime minister said this “window of opportunity” created an “existential threat” to Georgia and its population. He said calls for Georgia to join international sanctions against Russia soon followed. According to the government, complying with those demands would have had serious consequences for the country’s economy.

“Because the Georgian government refused to comply with these demands, pursued a sovereign policy and acted in the interests of the state, our country became a target for the European bureaucracy and Western leaders working in tandem with informal oligarchic forces,” Kobakhidze said.

He also addressed the sanctions imposed by Western countries on the Georgian government. According to Kobakhidze, pressure mechanisms, including sanctions, were already being used when the previous US administration under Joe Biden was in power.

Kobakhidze said the sanctions had targeted senior Georgian government officials, ruling party honorary chairman Bidzina Ivanishvili, judges, senior police officers and others.

He said the West had also used Georgia’s EU membership prospects as a tool to pressure the government.

“They failed to break the ruling party, which enjoys the support of the Georgian people, so now they are trying to use their agents to drag Georgia into a new provocation,” he added.

Kobakhidze said a “new stage of the attack” on Georgia, its people and its sovereignty had begun:

“This is a qualitatively new stage of the attack on Georgia, the Georgian people and the country’s sovereignty, unfolding simultaneously on several fronts.”

Background

Several days before the anniversary of the August 2008 war, Irakli Kobakhidze published a lengthy letter addressing the issue of “Russophobia”.

In the letter, Kobakhidze discussed the links between Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Georgia’s domestic political situation and the opposition’s position. He said the “global war party” benefited from the ongoing conflict in Ukraine because it wanted to “fuel Russophobia at the highest level among its agents around the world, including in Georgia”.

Kobakhidze accused the opposition and civil society of changing their attitude towards Russia. He described their current tough stance towards Moscow as “Russophobia”.

The letter reignited political disputes over the events of the 2008 war. This time, however, the debate focused not only on the circumstances that led to the war and Russia’s responsibility. The prime minister shifted the focus from Russia’s actions to the position of his Georgian opponents.

Georgian PM on “Russophobia”

World.title: Ilham Aliyev’s AzTV interview during Nakhchivan visit: industrial park, energy projects and Zangezur Corridor
World.content:
Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Nakhchivan

On 11 August, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and First Vice-President Mehriban Aliyeva visited the Nakhchivan Autonomous Republic. It was Aliyev’s 17th visit to Nakhchivan since he became president.

During the visit, officials held foundation-laying ceremonies and opened several facilities. Aliyev also visited historical sites and presented battle flags to military units.

The visit ended with an interview with Azerbaijan Television (AzTV), in which Aliyev outlined his plans for Nakhchivan’s development.

The interview focused on the autonomous republic’s economic and social development, energy security and transport infrastructure. Aliyev also discussed Nakhchivan’s place in Azerbaijan’s broader strategy, particularly its future development in conjunction with Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur, territories that came under Baku’s control after the Second Karabakh War.

Key events during the visit

During the visit to Nakhchivan, President Ilham Aliyev and First Lady Mehriban Aliyeva inspected work at the Shams-1 and Garbi Ufug solar power plants, which have a combined capacity of 50 MW.

One of the key events was the laying of the foundation stone for the Nakhchivan Industrial Park. It will be Azerbaijan’s second-largest industrial park by area, after the Sumgayit Industrial Park. A 300 MW thermal power plant is also planned for the site.

Nakhchivan’s total generating capacity currently stands at around 200 MW. Once the new plant comes online, this will increase by roughly half.

The visit programme also included:

the opening of the Nakhchivan Regional DOST Centre;

the presentation of new electric buses and an inspection of railway infrastructure reconstruction works;

the laying of the foundation stone for the Nakhchivan hotel complex, which is expected to be completed by around 2028;

the laying of the foundation stone for a social housing complex;

an inspection of restoration work at the Momine Khatun Mausoleum and the unveiling of a monument to architect Ajami Nakhchivani;

the presentation of Nakhchivan’s General Development Plan through 2044, which envisages expanding the city and increasing its population;

the presentation of battle flags to new commando units of the Separate Combined Arms Army.

Key points from the AzTV interview

Aliyev described his visit to Nakhchivan as a “sign of the autonomous republic’s comprehensive development”. He said every visit should produce concrete results. He highlighted strengthening defence capabilities, energy security, job creation, preserving historical and cultural heritage, and developing transport links as key priorities.

Defence and governance

Aliyev said Nakhchivan’s geographical position – particularly its lack of a direct land connection with mainland Azerbaijan – requires special attention to the region’s defence. He highlighted the creation of the Separate Combined Arms Army and new commando units as key steps.

According to the president, “Azerbaijan’s Armed Forces carry weight in the region”. He also said Nakhchivan had introduced a system of special presidential representatives, similar to the model used in Karabakh and Eastern Zangezur. Aliyev said the benefits of this system of governance were already becoming apparent.

Energy

Nakhchivan has been fully supplied with gas for around 15 years, Aliyev said, thanks to a gas swap agreement with Iran.

The president also placed particular emphasis on the region’s solar energy potential. He said Nakhchivan was Azerbaijan’s most favourable region for solar power generation. More than 600 hectares of land have already been allocated for the development of this sector. The potential is estimated at at least 500 MW and could reach 1 GW in the future.

Aliyev also highlighted the growing role of the private sector. Projects to build solar power plants with a combined capacity of 50 MW are already under way.

The president described electricity exports as a strategic priority. Iran and Turkey are currently the main destinations, but Azerbaijan ultimately hopes to export electricity from Nakhchivan to the European market as well.

Zangezur Corridor – TRIPP

Aliyev said that “the creation of the Zangezur Corridor was our initiative”, recalling that connecting mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan, an integral part of the country, had remained one of Baku’s strategic goals for many years.

He said he had insisted that a provision on the corridor be included in the trilateral statement signed by Azerbaijan, Russia and Armenia on 10 November 2020. Aliyev claims the Armenian side did not want to agree to this, but had no other alternative because continuing the war was not in its interests.

Noting that there had been no practical progress on the issue for five years, Aliyev said a solution emerged after the Washington summit on 8 August 2025, when the TRIPP project (Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity) was launched.

Speaking about the current state of the work, the president said the Horadiz-Aghband highway was almost complete, with only minor technical issues remaining. He said construction of the railway was also progressing rapidly.

Aliyev added that a project for power transmission lines linking mainland Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenia had already been prepared, and locations for the pylons had been identified.

Aliyev predicted that these projects would eventually turn Nakhchivan into one of the region’s key transport and energy hubs.

A unified development concept

The president stressed that Nakhchivan, Eastern Zangezur and Karabakh should develop under a unified concept. He said the geographical proximity of the three regions requires a common approach to their development.

Aliyev noted that master plans for cities in the territories that came under Azerbaijan’s control after the Second Karabakh War had already been approved. He also said he had ordered the preparation of a similar document for Nakhchivan. The “Nakhchivan City Development Master Plan through 2044” was presented to the president during the current visit.

Speaking about the region’s tourism potential, Aliyev said Nakhchivan had significant opportunities thanks to its rich historical heritage, scenic landscapes and clean air. At the same time, he acknowledged that the hotel infrastructure remained underdeveloped and that the existing hotels were generally of a low standard, hindering the growth of tourism.

He said that to address the problem, construction had begun on a new five-star hotel complex in the city centre. The project is expected to be completed around 2028.

Ilham Aliyev’s visit to Nakhchivan

World.title: Child seats, rear-seat seat belts and alcohol interlocks: changes to Georgia’s traffic rules
World.content:
New road safety rules in Georgia

Georgia plans to tighten road safety rules under the National Road Safety Strategy for 2026–2030, approved by the government on 5 August 2026. The strategy includes changes in several areas.

At this stage, the measures remain proposals, and some will require further legislative amendments before they can take effect.

What is changing:

Child seats will become mandatory for pre-school children. This means that when transporting a child of the relevant age, it will no longer be enough simply to seat them in the car or secure them with a standard seat belt.

This means that when transporting a child of the relevant age, it will no longer be enough simply to seat them in the car or secure them with a standard seat belt. Rear-seat seat belts could become mandatory. The government strategy provides for mandatory seat-belt use by passengers sitting in the back. However, authorities must first establish the necessary legal framework and an enforcement mechanism.

Drunk drivers could be prevented from driving. The strategy provides for the introduction of so-called “alcohol interlocks”. Georgia plans to establish a standard for alcohol-based ignition interlock systems. Under the strategy, authorities intend to take alcohol interlock technology into account when setting requirements for vehicles entering the Georgian market. Authorities also plan to run awareness campaigns for pedestrians on the importance of following traffic rules. Infrastructure will be adapted for vulnerable groups. Future infrastructure projects are expected to give greater consideration to the safety of people with disabilities.

The government strategy says seat-belt use is one of the key ways to reduce deaths and serious injuries in road accidents. It pays particular attention to rear-seat seat belts because unrestrained passengers in the back can endanger not only themselves but also people sitting in the front of the vehicle.

The strategy is not limited to introducing new requirements. The government also plans to raise awareness of road safety, run public campaigns and educational programmes, and improve technical tools for detecting violations.

It is important to note that the government strategy sets out some of these measures only in broad terms. Where necessary, authorities will have to introduce additional legislative and regulatory amendments to implement specific commitments.

World.title: Lasha Bugadze becomes first modern Georgian writer whose book was barred from being sent to prison
World.content:
Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

The administration of Rustavi Prison refused to allow Lasha Bugadze’s new novel, The Observer, to be delivered to the prison. The book was intended for Nana Sander, who was convicted over her participation in a protest on 4 October 2025.

Notably, the penitentiary code contains no provision explicitly banning fiction from being brought into prisons.

The book’s synopsis describes a fictional political reality involving the long rule of a “despot”, the “division of the country into zones” and a “cult of the leader”. It also mentions the scheduling of elections and a decision by the country’s population on whether they should take place.

According to Bugadze, a prison official refused to allow the book in, saying the novel contained “political content”.

The writer says it is unclear to him who determined that the book contained political content and what criteria they used. He suspects the decision may have been prompted by words and phrases in the novel, such as “despot” and “cult of the leader”.

“The employee told me directly that the book could not be delivered because it was political in nature. I don’t think he sat down and read the book. I doubt he even read the synopsis,” Bugadze said.

In his view, someone appears to have judged the work to be political without giving any clear reason.

“Who put this label on the text? [Who decided] whether it was political or not? What does that even mean? And, excuse me, even if the content is political, why should a citizen – whether a prisoner or anyone else – not have the right to read such a book?” the writer said.

Bugadze sees the incident as a potential precedent for censoring literary works:

“It can be described as the first significant example of literary censorship in modern Georgian history. This is an extremely dangerous precedent, and under no circumstances should it be considered normal. The situation requires a response. No one has the right to stop someone from reading.”

The head of the human rights organisation Sapari, Baia Pataraia, announced that legal proceedings would begin over the incident:

“We are taking legal steps. <…> First, we will demand a written and reasoned refusal.”

The organisation PEN Georgia also responded to the case. It described the incident as an alarming precedent for censorship of a literary work, linked not only to the novel’s content but also to the author’s political and civic stance. The organisation stressed that censoring fiction and restricting freedom of expression are unacceptable in a democratic society.

Lasha Bugadze’s The Observer

Precedent for literary censorship in Georgia

World.title: Armenia seeks alternatives amid concerns over possible Russian gas price hike
World.content:
Russian gas pressure on Armenia

If the issue of raising gas tariffs arises, the Armenian authorities will discuss it with their Russian counterparts in a friendly atmosphere, Sargis Khandanyan, an MP from the ruling Civil Contract faction, told journalists.

Khandanyan added that he had no information about any negotiations with Russia over gas tariffs. However, he expressed confidence that, if necessary, Armenia would be able to find alternatives to Russian gas. These could include supplies from Iran, although this is not the only option.

Yerevan and Tehran have already discussed the issue. Following talks held with Iranian partners by Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure, Davit Khudatyan, it emerged that the volume of Iranian gas supplies could potentially be doubled.

“This decision has nothing to do with any other country, Russia in particular. It is a profitable economic activity that both countries are interested in expanding,” the Armenian minister said.

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan notes that there has recently been increasingly frequent talk of a possible revision of Russian gas prices. He views the issue in the context of the levers of pressure being used against Armenia. In his view, Moscow has already exhausted much of its arsenal and is now resorting to economic leverage, including in the energy sector.

“Political, cultural and terrorist levers, as well as the influence of the criminal subculture, are no longer working for various reasons. And Russia, in order to prevent Armenia from strengthening its independence, has decided to make full use of its last remaining lever,” Ghevondyan said.

‘This scenario cannot be ruled out’: On gas imports from Azerbaijan

Journalists asked MP Sargis Khandanyan how likely it was that the tariff on gas imports from Russia could change by the end of the year.

“I am not aware of when this issue was last discussed with Russia. Nor am I aware of any information that would give grounds to believe that the gas tariff could change,” he replied.

At the same time, the MP noted that the government attaches great importance to diversifying supplies. He recalled the agreements reached during the visit of Armenia’s Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure to Iran. According to him, the “Trump Route” could also be considered as one such opportunity:

“As part of the transit route that will connect Azerbaijan with Nakhchivan through Armenian territory, a gas pipeline will be built. This could provide another opportunity. We could consider this pipeline as an additional source. Of course, this is a very theoretical idea, but it would not be difficult to implement.”

Asked about the possibility of importing gas from Azerbaijan, Khandanyan said that Yerevan and Baku were discussing a broad range of issues:

“I do not know how far we have progressed on the issue of gas supplies, but this scenario cannot be ruled out.”

In late October 2025, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev announced that all restrictions on transit to Armenia would be lifted. Since then, Armenia has been receiving petroleum products from the neighbouring country by rail. According to official figures, Azerbaijan has already supplied Armenia with 20,000 tonnes of petroleum products.

Yerevan and Tehran agree to increase gas supplies. Can Moscow stand in the way?

Minister of Territorial Administration and Infrastructure Davit Khudatyan paid a three-day visit to Iran. Upon returning from Tehran, he said that the volume of Iranian gas supplied under the “Gas for Electricity” programme could be at least doubled. He explained that the pipeline’s capacity exceeds the volume of gas currently being supplied.

Under the programme, Armenia has been receiving gas from Iran since 2009, converting it into electricity which is then supplied back to Iran.

To increase gas imports and export a corresponding volume of electricity to Iran, construction of the Iran-Armenia high-voltage power transmission line needs to be completed. The Armenian government hopes that the long-delayed project will be completed by the end of the year.

Meanwhile, since 2015, the Armenian section of the pipeline carrying gas from Iran has been controlled by Russian company Gazprom.

As a result, some experts doubt whether Iranian gas supplies can be increased without Moscow’s consent. The Armenian government, however, has assured that there will be no obstacles to expanding supplies under the “Gas for Electricity” programme.

Expert commentaty

Political commentator Artem Yerkanyan says:

“Russian Security Council Deputy Secretary Alexei Shevtsov threatened that unless Armenia revises its foreign policy course, it will have to pay $800 for Russian gas instead of the current $177. Compensating for that difference would cost at least $1bn. That is more than the €50m the European Union has promised Armenia as compensation for the impact of strained relations with Russia.

It is worth explaining what the figures of $177 and $800 actually mean. Russia’s Gazprom sells gas for $177 to Gazprom Armenia, which is owned by Gazprom itself. In other words, it also earns revenue from the distribution of the gas, and that revenue also goes to Gazprom. Therefore, I think it would be incorrect to say that Armenia buys gas for $177.

It is also unclear where the figure of $800 comes from, considering the following:

China buys Russian gas for $258;

Turkey for $280;

Hungary, Serbia and Slovakia for $400;

Spain, France and Belgium for $450.

Moreover, according to a forecast by Russia’s Ministry of Economic Development, by the end of this year the average price at which Russia will sell gas to countries outside the EAEU [an economic bloc led by Russia] will be $290.

If the average price is $290, why are they planning to sell it to Armenia for $800? That is unclear.”

Political analyst Robert Ghevondyan argues:

“Following the elections, the Armenian authorities have continued to pursue a multi-vector foreign policy. Dependence on Russia is steadily declining, with the economic dimension playing an increasingly important role in this process.

While Russia is trying to exert economic pressure, Armenia is opening up new markets that Armenian businesses previously ‘failed to notice’ because of their excessive focus on the Russian market. Although problems remain with some goods, economic diversification is advancing rapidly.

In the energy sector, Armenia has alternatives when it comes to building a new nuclear reactor, which in itself is a headache for Russia.

It is no coincidence that, alongside economic blackmail, Rosatom executives periodically make Armenia ‘attractive’ offers to build a new Russian nuclear reactor. However, the Armenian authorities are likely to opt for a different proposal.

A rise in gas prices could initially cause problems. But Armenia has alternatives here as well: Iranian, Turkmen and now Azerbaijani gas.

Consequently, in the near future, Russian gas may find itself merely competing on the market. This would limit the Kremlin’s ability to use gas prices to blackmail Armenia.

In conclusion, it should be noted that increased pressure from Russia is having the opposite effect. Armenia is steadily ‘freeing itself’ from excessive Russian influence and diversifying its economy. The Kremlin does not appear to recognise this yet, but that is its problem.”

World.title: Senator says NT doesn't 'want to stick to' terms of $4b housing deal
World.content:
The federal and Northern Territory governments are in a deadlock over a multi-billion-dollar project to build thousands of new homes in remote Aboriginal communities, with concerns the project could deliver fewer than half the number originally planned.

Jointly funded in 2024, the NT Remote Housing agreement is aimed at reducing overcrowding and improving housing quality in the Territory's Indigenous communities, town camps and homelands.

PM announces $4 billion NT remote housing package Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has announced the 10-year agreement, which is expected to see up to 270 homes built each year, during a visit to the Northern Territory.

The $4 billion project promised to deliver 2,700 new homes over 10 years, but the NT government has recently asked to renegotiate the agreement.

In federal parliament on Wednesday, Senator Lidia Thorpe tabled documents she said showed $330 million in Commonwealth funding due under the agreement "has not been delivered and the Northern Territory government has provided no progress reports".

"Building is behind schedule, construction targets are being reduced, reporting is missing, funding isn't flowing, and mob are telling you that NT is not working for them," she said.

On Wednesday, Lidia Thorpe tabled documents and shared her concerns over the housing plan for the remote NT. (AAP: Mick Tsikas)

Federal Indigenous Australians minister and senator for the NT, Malarndirri McCarthy, said when the NT government "meets certain criteria, then [it] will receive the funding".

Senator McCarthy told parliament the NT's Country Liberal Party (CLP) government wanted more money from the agreement and that it "wants to reduce the number of homes down to 1,800 or maybe 1,100".

"They don't want to stick to the agreement," she said.

"They want to remove a certain amount of money from it for administration and for the land, in terms of where the houses will be built, in terms of making sure the land is ready."

'Pressures' on the NT

NT Housing Minister Steve Edgington was contacted for comment but did not respond by deadline.

Late last month, Mr Edgington told ABC Radio Alice Springs that 400 houses had so far been built under the agreement, but that he could not detail how much had been spent to build them.

Steve Edgington has previously said the NT government faces a variety of pressures that impact on its ability to deliver on the agreement. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

He argued more money was needed to cover additional costs because "what we're facing at the moment is a whole range of different pressures on the program".

"We've seen significant increases in cost due to the global fuel crisis — around construction, freight, fuel, labour, infrastructure — and all those servicing costs have increased substantially, not just over the last 12 months, but in the last six months," he said at the time.

"Some of the costs are anywhere between $300,000 and around about $600,000, just to bring a block on to have that ready to build a house on.

"So these costs, which include the headworks, the power, water, sewage, all of those things which are essential components to build a home, are escalating out bush at the moment."

Senator Thorpe told the ABC she backed the federal government in rejecting the NT government's proposal to redistribute funds from the agreement for administration and headworks.

She called for Senator McCarthy to dump the NT government from managing the project and to instead directly fund Aboriginal organisations to do the work.

Lidia Thorpe wants the government to directly fund Aboriginal organisations to do the work in remote communities. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

"The Northern Territory government need to basically move over and the minister needs to step in and bypass, which she has the power to do, and fund these organisations directly," she said.

" Then houses can be built immediately. "

'Serious concerns' among committee members

The documents tabled by Senator Thorpe also included a joint statement from the Aboriginal members of the agreement's Joint Steering Committee, dated September 2025.

These Australians are homeless with a house Many Aboriginal people in Tennant Creek live in overcrowded makeshift shelters with no running water or electricity as they wait up to a decade for a home. But experts say the social housing being built is not safe for today's climate, let alone the future.

In it, the members said they held "some serious concerns about the approach of the [NT government], in particular the Department of Housing", and called for the Indigenous Australians minister to "intervene where [the CLP] are falling short and hold them accountable".

The members' concerns included a "lack of clear reporting from the department and a reluctance to share data", along with "repeated comments by the department around the lack of capacity to do anything more than business as usual" on improving repairs and maintenance in the remote NT.

The statement said the Aboriginal committee members had "diminishing confidence that the department has a long-term strategic vision or has the capacity and willingness to change the way they currently do business".

The ABC understands the Joint Steering Committee — which is comprised of representatives from both governments, Aboriginal Housing NT and the four NT land councils — is due to meet next week.

World.title: Breaking: Third Sydney Airport take-off incident investigated by safety body
World.content:
Safety authorities are investigating a third runway incident at Sydney Airport, which involved a Qantas flight crossing the path of a departing Virgin Australia aircraft.

The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said on Wednesday that the incident on Sunday involved Virgin Australia Flight VA555 destined for Perth and Qantas Flight QF728 flying to Ayers Rock Airport.

"At around 10am local time, air traffic control (ATC) cleared the Virgin Australia 737 for a full-length take-off on runway 34L," an ATSB statement said.

"As the crew applied thrust for take-off, they observed the Qantas 737 begin to cross the runway ahead of them from taxiway lima.

"The Qantas crew reported having received a clearance from ATC to cross the runway.

"The Virgin Australia crew reduced thrust and the aircraft came to a stop on the runway."

The ATSB said air traffic controllers cancelled VA555's take-off clearance at the same time its crew noticed the Qantas aircraft ahead.

"Once the Qantas 737 was clear of the runway, the Virgin Australia 737 was re-cleared by ATC to commence take-off," the ATSB said.

It is understood the Qantas plane began to cross the runway about 1,200 metres ahead of where the Virgin Australia flight had started to take off, before its clearance was cancelled four seconds later.

Air Services Australia said the two aircraft were never in close proximity and it was working with the Australian Transport Safety Bureau to investigate the incident.

Spokespeople for Qantas and Virgin Australia told the ABC the airlines would support the ATSB investigation into the incident.

In another incident earlier on Sunday, Jetstar Flight JQ402 was preparing to take off when it was forced to slam on the brakes to avoid colliding with a Qatar Airways 777 that was being towed along the tarmac.

Two weeks earlier, on July 27, a QantasLink flight and a Qantas plane were involved in a near-miss on the tarmac.

World.title: Farmer accused of triple murder would 'spy' and 'linger', court hears
World.content:
A court has heard claims Queensland cattle farmer Darryl Valroy Young, who is accused of murdering three people and attempting to murder a fourth, would spy on a neighbouring property.

Mr Young, 63, is accused of fatally shooting his neighbour Graham Tighe and Mr Tighe's mother and stepfather, Maree Schwarz and Mervyn Schwarz, on August 4, 2022, at Bogie.

Mr Young is charged with the murder of Maree Schwarz and Mervyn Schwarz (pictured). (Supplied)

He is also accused of the attempted murder of Mr Tighe's brother, Ross Tighe.

Mr Young has pleaded not guilty to all charges.

His lawyer said his client never saw the family at the gate of his Bogie cattle station on the morning he was accused of shooting them.

Mr Young is charged with the murder of Graham Tighe (pictured). (Supplied)

Ross Tighe gave evidence on Tuesday and Wednesday and said he and his family members were shot by Mr Young.

'A horror movie'

Mr Tighe told the court that after the shooting he drove while wounded to find help.

Ross Tighe's ex-partner, who cannot be named for legal reasons, today told the court she saw Mr Tighe's wound after the alleged shooting before he was picked up by a rescue helicopter.

The woman, who cried while recounting the events, was questioned by Mr Young's defence lawyer Anthony J Kimmins about how sound her memory was.

"It's like a movie in my head, a horror movie," she told the court.

She said the first time she saw Mr Young was long before the alleged triple murder.

Darryl Valroy Young at the Supreme Court in Townsville. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

She said she had been visiting Graham Tighe's Sutherland Station, which bordered on Mr Young's Shannonvale Station.

She said she was fencing along the adjoining properties but did not speak to Mr Young.

"He was just lingering around on his buggy," the woman said.

" I encountered him a few times on that trip because he lingers around on his buggy spying on everybody. "

She described overhearing a phone call between Graham Tighe and Darryl Young the day before the alleged triple murder.

"Darryl said, 'You can meet me at the border of Shannonvale,' he said, '8am it will be you, your brother, Mervyn and Maree,'" she said.

"He reiterated that about three times before the conversation ended."

Mr Kimmins challenged the woman on whether she actually overheard such a discussion.

"Can I suggest to you that that was never said at all?" Mr Kimmins asked.

"Can I suggest that you weren't even there."

Anthony J Kimmins is representing Mr Young. (ABC News: Chloe Chomicki)

The woman quickly rebuked Mr Young's defence lawyer.

"No, you can't suggest it because that is not the truth," she said.

Accused’s son gives evidence

Mr Young's son, Derek Young, 39, was called to give evidence before jurors today.

He said he asked his father on August 4, 2022, to let wind farm workers into Shannonvale Station who arrived at the property gate about 7:30am.

He said he then left the homestead to tend to cattle for an hour.

Derek Young said he later joined Darryl Young, and Darryl Young's stepmother to meet the wind farm workers where they were installing a radar on a ridge on their property.

The Supreme Court trial is expected to run for three weeks. (ABC News: James Tugwell)

He said the group was told there had been a shooting when one of the wind farm workers called their boss to turn the radar on about 11:30am.

"We had to wait there — all day until we got arrested," Derek Young said.

"There was one wind farm boy doing all the calling to his boss and a police officer.

" The police mediator spoke to us all day. "

Derek Young and Darryl Young's stepmother are not accused of any wrongdoing.

Derek Young said he never saw his father with any blood on him, or with any weapon on the day.

He said he did not notice a change in his father's demeanour throughout the day either.

Darryl Valroy Young watched his son give evidence in court. (ABC News: Carole Howlett)

Derek Young said the group was told to travel together in one vehicle to meet police at the property gate.

He said a wind farm worker drove and the group was arrested.

The trial continues.

World.title: MotoGP track will 'irrevocably' change parklands, Adelaide mayor says
World.content:
Adelaide's lord mayor has warned that the city's parklands will be changed "irrevocably and permanently" by the MotoGP.

The proposed street circuit design will be released in the coming weeks and construction on the track is due to begin in December.

The Australian MotoGP will be held in Adelaide from November 2027 after the South Australian government nabbed the event from Victoria earlier this year.

But there have been concerns about the project, which will require the removal of at least 45 significant trees.

An overhead view of Adelaide's Victoria Park, which will host some of the MotoGP street circuit. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

Adelaide Lord Mayor Jane Lomax-Smith said it was important that the community be given sufficient opportunity to provide feedback.

"I think it's important to recognise that the landscape that we all know and love is going to change irrevocably and permanently," she said.

"Therefore, it's really important that everyone has a chance to look at this design and this project and have their say."

Jane Lomax-Smith has sounded a warning about the impact on the parklands. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

South East City Residents Association treasurer Doug McEvoy said his group was most concerned by environmental impacts from the project.

He spearheaded a letter to the Fédération Internationale de Motocyclisme, the global governing body, arguing that its environmental guidelines were not being upheld.

Dr McEvoy said the group was supportive of major events, including the MotoGP, but "this is the wrong place for a motorcycle race".

"People are actually very attached to the nature in the parks — they want to keep it and they don't want it to be destroyed by more tarmac and noise that's going to take out birds in the breeding season," he said.

Doug McEvoy says saplings are not replacements for significant trees. (ABC News)

Dr McEvoy said it was "naive" to argue that significant trees slated for removal could be replaced by saplings.

"It takes decades for saplings to grow to the point that they can be unique ecosystems in their own right," he said.

A public petition to "stop the chop" — which calls on the SA government to reverse its position on projects including the North Adelaide Golf Course redevelopment and the MotoGP — has attracted more than 28,000 signatures.

Bike group backs city circuit

Motorcycle Alliance of South Australia chair Heath Norris said the city track was crucial to the success of the MotoGP.

He said holding the race in Adelaide was a better option than at The Bend Motorsport Park at Tailem Bend, 100 kilometres from the CBD.

"It's a more central location, more accommodation, easy to get to, more Ubers," Mr Norris said.

"If it's out at The Bend, there's limited transport, limited accommodation.

"Nothing wrong with The Bend, but a more central location means that more people can enjoy it."

Heath Norris says it's better to hold the event in a central location. (ABC News)

Premier Peter Malinauskas said the government was working to release the plans and total cost of the project as soon as possible.

The total number of trees set to be removed will also be revealed.

"The sooner we can get that into the public realm the better, as far as I'm concerned, because we have got tight timelines," Mr Malinauskas said.

In May the designer of the Adelaide street track that hosted the first Australian Grand Prix in 1985, Bob Barnard, estimated it could cost more than $100 million to remodel the course to host the Australian MotoGP.

At the time, Mr Malinauskas said there had not been "any suggestion" of a $100 million bill.

World.title: Gardner breaks silence on affair with teammate, retains vice-captaincy
World.content:
Australia vice-captain Ash Gardner has apologised for the pain caused by her marriage breakdown and thanked Cricket Australia for backing her leadership.

Gardner's affair with Australian teammate Georgia Voll while married to ex-wife Monica Wright created headlines.

Wright publicly questioned the lack of action by CA in the wake of the affair, calling attention to "a clear power imbalance" when a senior member of staff has an affair with a junior.

Wright said Gardner should not be allowed to stay as vice-captain and questioned why CA had said nothing on the matter.

Gardner's marriage breakdown came as the result of an affair with teammate Georgia Voll (pictured). (Getty Images: Jason McCawley)

Cricket Australia CEO Todd Greenberg, speaking on SEN on Thursday, said "additional policies" would be put in place in situations where perceived or real conflicts of interest existed, when relationships between players had been disclosed.

He confirmed CA had been made aware of the relationship between Gardner and Voll before it appeared in the press, but also backed Gardner to stay in her position.

"Ash is a highly regarded leader in our system. The CA board make leadership decisions and have oversight over all leadership decisions," Greenberg said.

"Ash is our vice-captain for a reason, because she's highly regarded, but what we will do is in situations where there are personal relationships is make sure there are additional guardrails, so the perception of conflict or conflict itself — talking about things like selection — are handled appropriately and respectfully."

Todd Greenberg (pictured) says Gardner remains a highly-valued leader within the Australian team. (AAP: James Ross)

"We've got policies in place but we will put additional ones in place given Ash is now vice-captain. If there are relationships that have been disclosed and they have been, then we will make sure that conflict — perceived or real — around selections are removed, so Ash is not involved in those things."

Greenberg said the relationship between Gardner and Voll was "new news" in the media.

"But for those that were in the team and leading the team, we've been well across this for a period of time," he said.

Gardner addressed her affair and the position of the hierarchy in a post on Instagram.

"While my separation from my wife is a personal matter, I understand my current relationship status needed to be addressed by Cricket Australia given my position as vice-captain," Gardner wrote.

"I am grateful that the CA Board has chosen to support my continued leadership. I look forward to playing a strong role as a leader and providing the best possible support for my teammates in the season to come.

"I am grateful for the time Monica and I shared and sorry for the pain this has caused. I wish her nothing but happiness and success in the future.

"I won't be making any further public comment on this matter at this time and ask that the privacy of those involved is respected."

Greenberg made the point "respect" for all concerned was paramount.

"It is a very personal matter for the player, and I think there's a level of respect that needs to go with that," he said.

"Cricket's got very strong respect-at-work policies, so we've got a policy that's been developed over time that can deal with these sorts of things."

AAP

World.title: Quick hits: A 'peanut' jibe, a Starc record and a brain explosion
World.content:
Steve Smith called a Bangladesh bowler a "peanut" for making an appeal, but he could probably have labelled a couple of his batting colleagues as such on a dire batting display for Australia.

Meanwhile, Mitch Starc collected another accolade with yet another top order wicket for the Aussies

As it happened: Bangladesh minnows humble Australia's giants on day one in Darwin

Here are the quick hits from day one of the first Test between Australia and Bangladesh.

1. Weatherald falls in front of hometown crowd

Weatherald was unable to impress in front of his home crowd. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/CA)

Local boy Jake Weatherald began the first Test under significant pressure, having clung onto his opening spot after struggling through his debut series against England.

And there was significant support for the Northern Territorian in Darwin, with the crowd rising and falling as he attempted to get his innings going.

But once again, Weatherald was unable to find his feet at Test level, eventually reaching and swiping and nicking off for an unconvincing 23 off 37 deliveries.

It was Weatherald's 10th sub-50 score from his 11 Test innings, and one that only raised more questions about his viability as a Test match opener

Weatherald, the first Australian men's Test cricketer born and raised in the Northern Territory and now the first Territorian to play Test cricket in Darwin, with three more opportunities to secure a spot on the plane to South Africa in October.

2. Green's pre-lunch brain explosion

Bangladesh was overjoyed to claim Green's wicket with the final ball before lunch. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/Cricket Australia)

With Australia teetering at 3-61, the under-pressure Cam Green decided to take the game on.

Perhaps the Australian most in need of a score, the all-rounder began his innings with a pair of well-timed drives, before hooking Taskin Ahmed for a maximum over backward square leg.

However, Green's counterattack was short lived, with the big man playing one shot too many in the shadows of the first break.

With what turned out to be the final ball of the morning session, Green all but gave his wicket away, meekly chipping one to a grateful Mushfiqur Rahim on the on-side.

Australia headed to lunch at 4-74, Bangladesh couldn't believe their luck, and Green, having come out with such purpose, trudged off for a run-a-ball 13.

3. Smith's triple reprieve

So often the man for a crisis, Steve Smith is no stranger to standing tall as wickets tumble around him.

But Australia's idiosyncratic world beater was anything but convincing as he somehow managed to prod his way to lunch after coming to the crease at 2-52.

Smith should have been out on 2, with his thick edge falling through the fingers of a stooping second slip.

A matter of balls later, Smith was once again nicking towards the cordon — but this time, the ball flew through a gap between second slip and gully, with Bangladesh captain Najmul Hossain Shanto having only just removed a man from behind the wicket.

And it appeared that Smith's luck was well and truly in when he survived a line-ball DRS review.

With Smith swinging hard outside off, Bangladesh went up for caught behind with some confidence. Umpire Kumar Dharmasena was unmoved, and Shanto wasted no time in sending the decision upstairs.

The technology, however, showed no conclusive evidence of an edge, with the ball passing perilously close to Smith's blade but failing to make its mark on ultra edge.

Bangladesh couldn't believe it as Smith was handed his third reprieve of the morning.

4. Smith talks Bangladesh out of a review, lands "peanut" jibe

Smith talked Bangladesh out of a review before late in the second session. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Having burnt two reviews in the first session, Bangladesh had just one DRS Hail Mary to play with for the bulk of the Australian innings.

Late in the second session, seamer Ebadot Hussein was tempted to break the glass for one that he never should have been.

His LBW shout against Smith was clearly far too high, but that didn't stop the Bangladeshi brains trust gathering for a serious discussion in the middle.

Smith couldn't believe it.

"Knee roll you reckon? It was up here you peanut!" Smith could be heard saying through the stump mic, gesturing to his hip area.

"What game are you watching?"

Smith's derision was enough to talk Bangladesh out of the review, but his honesty didn't end up counting for much — the Australian vice-captain eventually top-edging a short ball to be caught for 71.

5. Starc makes history

Australia's Mitchell Starc added another record to his list. (Getty Images: Albert Perez/CA)

The records keep coming for Australia's top-order destroyer, Mitchell Starc.

Fresh from being named his country's Test player of the year last Friday, the 36-year-old carved out another piece of history, becoming the most lethal left arm bowler in the history of the format.

Starc procured a leading edge from opener Shadman Islam to claim the 434th wicket of his Test career, with Nathan Lyon making amends for an earlier dropped chance.

Starc's milestone scalp took him past former Sri Lanka spinner Rangana Herath.

However, that was the only breakthrough of the day in what was a humbling start to the season for Australia.

World.title: Man found guilty of killing his cousin after drug disagreement
World.content:
A judge has found a man who stabbed his cousin multiple times on the New South Wales Mid North Coast in 2023 not guilty of murder but guilty of manslaughter.

Conrad Lardner, 51, was arrested on May 17, 2023, and charged with murdering his 39-year-old cousin David Vale.

Mr Vale was found with stab wounds on Robert Eggins Street in South Kempsey on March 1, 2023.

The judge-alone murder trial began on June 29 at Port Macquarie Supreme Court and ran for four weeks.

The court heard Lardner stabbed Mr Vale twice, with one puncture to the lower side of the chest and another through his rib cage and heart.

Mr Vale died within 15 minutes.

Judge Campbell delivered his verdict today, accepting that Lardner killed Mr Vale but saying there was insufficient evidence to prove intent.

"I accept it is possible he armed himself with the knife, but there is no real evidence that supports the possibility, other than having the opportunity to do so," he said.

Fight over bad drugs

The families of Conrad Lardner outside Port Macquarie Courthouse. (ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager)

During Lardner's cross-examination, he told the court Mr Vale confronted him complaining about the quality of the drugs he was sold.

"I want my f****** money back, what you gave me was shit I went to sleep on it," Lardner told the trial.

"I said, 'There's not a refund,'" Lardner told the court.

Conrad Lardner was found guilty of manslaughter in the judge-alone trial. (Supplied: Facebook)

Justice Stephen Campbell told the court he did not accept the defence's evidence that Mr Vale bought drugs from Lardner on the morning of the stabbing.

"The accused gave evidence when the deceased arrived he was raving on about drugs the accused sold him," Justice Campbell said.

"I do not accept what the accused said happened on the morning or that he never supplied drugs to the deceased ever.

"It seems to follow when the deceased complained about good quality drugs he was referring to a previous supply at some earlier point in time that evidence does not disclose."

It was the Crown case that during the "scuffle" between Mr Vale and Lardner outside the home, Lardner went back into the kitchen and retrieved a knife before stabbing Mr Vale twice.

Justice Campbell said he was satisfied beyond reasonable doubt Lardner's "voluntary act" caused Mr Vale's death.

"The fact the accused stabbed twice with a knife provides some evidence of intent to inflict serious grievous bodily harm," he said.

Defence barrister Dennis Stewart said Lardner acted in self-defence and that he picked up the knife which fell out of Mr Vale's pocket.

Conflicting accounts

Judge Campbell told the court that the 20 witnesses who gave evidence during the trial, including Lardner, were "contradicted, discredited and challenged" by prior statements made to police or witnesses.

"I am satisfied to a necessary degree the deceased had developed a grievance over the accused over the supply of inferior quality drugs which did not give him the desire he wanted," Justice Campbell said.

"It just seems preposterous the deceased would bail him up about defective drugs which had never been supplied by him."

Jessica Howard said her family was glad Lardner was found guilty of manslaughter (ABC Mid North Coast: Nakita Jager)

Jessica Howard, who was David Vale's partner at the time, said she was glad he "got some justice".

"I'm glad the outcome was manslaughter and not not guilty," Ms Howard said.

"I don't really know how I feel because nothing is going to bring David back."

" It affects us everyday, he was a good father and we no longer have him with us anymore. "

Lardner was originally refused bail but he was released on conditional bail on November 11, 2023.

Today, Justice Campbell refused him bail to be sentenced on November 13.

World.title: I’m among the doctors our system rejects. This is why regional healthcare is dying
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessHealthcare Opinion I’m among the doctors our system rejects. This is why regional healthcare is dying Stuart Kostalas Doctor August 13, 2026 — 7:30pm

August 13, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

On March 4 last year, I received an email that, in one sentence, explains how regional health care dies. “Unfortunately, currently the [district] is not in a fiscal position to engage another gastroenterologist,” a senior manager wrote. “We can revisit this on an annual basis.” I am a gastroenterologist in Port Macquarie. I’ve spent nearly 15 years caring for a catchment of a quarter of a million people, and until this year I was head of gastroenterology at Port Macquarie Base Hospital. I had read a similar sentence before. In December 2019, the district’s then medical services director emailed us: “We are in no position to be recruiting a fourth gastroenterologist.” We had asked because three of us could not cover every week without burning out. One week in four each was sustainable; the fourth week had no cover. In April 2020, the hospital’s general manager conceded in writing that this was “a risk to patient safety”. The risk was documented. The fourth gastroenterologist was never funded. Regional Australians are older and sicker, yet this is where specialist care is thinnest. iStock In November 2024, the Royal Australasian College of Physicians, which accredits hospitals to train specialists, surveyed our department. The public gastroenterology service relied on three visiting specialists whose sessions totalled 0.6 of one full-time position, “barely sufficient for the supervision of a full-time trainee”.



The district’s answer opened this article. In June 2025, the college spelled out the risk: “If one of the current supervisors leaves the public system, this position would not fulfil accreditation requirements.” Its other conditions were an inventory of poverty; we could not even offer the trainee a desk. Stuart Kostalas Gavin Moroney Photography Then the district did the one thing the college had warned against. In December 2025, it wrote that under a new staffing model my contract “would no longer be required”. On January 21, 2026, I was given three months’ notice of termination. On April 1, 2026, accreditation lapsed; my termination took effect three weeks later. A public service that cannot survive the loss of one part-time specialist is not a service. It is a coincidence with a roster. The poverty is real: a ministry review has the district cutting about 160 positions. But the college accredits hospitals, not spreadsheets. We are told the regions cannot attract specialists. This is not true. In 2017, I recruited an outstanding hepatobiliary interventional endoscopist, trained in Australia and at a Canadian liver transplant centre, the specialist you want when a scan shows a pancreatic mass or you turn yellow. He moved to town and worked eight years without a public hospital contract.



His endoscopic ultrasound service, the test that confirms pancreatic cancer and shows whether it can still be cured, was available here only to the privately insured, while public patients with suspected cancer travelled nearly three hours down the highway. In mid-2025, he stopped waiting and moved back to a major city. The endoscopic ultrasound service left with him. Related Article Healthcare Instead of sending city doctors to rural hospitals, this uni is changing course When I objected in writing to an executive’s sneer at a recruit over vaccination paperwork – “One wonders why he’s so reluctant” – the acting district director of medical services replied: “I want you to refrain from this kind of public feedback to your manager, please.” A reply-all, apparently, is “public feedback”. My emails and letters to the district’s chief executive have gone unanswered since early 2025. Even my termination letter instructs me not to discuss this matter with anyone. Consider this article the exit interview nobody scheduled. And count what this town has lost. The training post that produced its next generation of specialists. The ultrasound service that detected pancreatic cancer early, when intervention can still cure it or buy years. The early cancer resections performed by its terminated head of department. What remains is a waiting list and a highway.



And need runs opposite to access: regional Australians are older and sicker than their city counterparts, more likely to have bowel cancer found late and less likely to survive it, yet this is where specialist care is thinnest. Related Article Hospitals in crisis Inquiry condemns NSW Health as hospital staff live with a ‘culture of fear’ The fixes are unglamorous. Fund four properly appointed public gastroenterologists, one more than the college’s bare floor. The next time a specialist moves to town and offers, employ them. Set rosters with the specialists who fill them. And when a head of department writes to the chief executive about a collapsing service, answer. “We can revisit this on an annual basis,” the district wrote in March 2025. The year passed. The district has repeated the same sentence since 2019. The college finally replied regarding the gastroenterology training: “Port Macquarie Base Hospital does not currently meet the minimum requirements for accreditation … Accordingly, accreditation lapsed on 1 April 2026.” Professor Stuart Kostalas is a gastroenterologist, director of endoscopy and chair of the medical advisory committee at Port Macquarie Private Hospital, a former head of the department of gastroenterology at Port Macquarie Base Hospital, and a conjoint professor of medicine at UNSW. Get a weekly wrap of views that will challenge, champion and inform your own.

World.title: ‘It’s terrible’: Top Sydney private school in negotiations to buy entire street
World.content:
NationalNSWEducation ‘It’s terrible’: Top Sydney private school in negotiations to buy entire street Christopher Harris August 13, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A north shore private school wants to buy an entire public road so it can expand its senior campus. North Sydney Council initially rebuffed overtures from Redlands School to purchase Monford Place in Cremorne back in 2021. Cleaning business owner Lais Ferraz says selling Monford Place to the school would make life harder. Sitthixay Ditthavong The council is more receptive to the idea after the cost of the North Sydney pool rebuild jumped from $58 million to more than $122 million and it was constrained from raising rates by as much as it hoped to meet costs. The council voted on Monday night to sell the cul-de-sac for “no less” than the independent valuation price, which has not been disclosed.



The council last year investigated selling a portion Edward Street to Shore School in North Sydney. It exposes long-running tension between the council and private schools that use parks for play time yet do not pay rates; North Sydney Council estimates it is missing out on more than $1 million in revenue from schools. “It is a very short piece of cul-de-sac. It is entirely surrounded by the school. Its main use is parking for the teachers, that’s why the council was open to exploring the sale,” North Sydney Mayor Zoe Baker said. Not everyone sees it that way. Dominik Przywara, the owner of Strings Embassy, which provides lessons for and rents out string instruments, said his customers used the street’s 18 parking spaces.



“We have a big problem here of parking and density … this street is very, very busy.” Dominik Przywara, who runs the String Embassy on Military Road. Sitthixay Ditthavong He did not know about the plan to sell the street but said because Military Road is a clearway after 3pm, the 18 car parks in the street were valued by him and his customers who came for lessons. “The council is charging businesses a lot of money, and small businesses should be supported here, especially in this area … we have a huge rotation of businesses. A lot of businesses are bankrupt.” Cleaning business owner Lais Ferraz parked in the street every day and said it was useful for her staff.



“It’s terrible. This area is super busy with the commercial side, with restaurants and everything,” she said. “For the council, it’s money for them. But for the people running a business, living here, it’s not good.” Glen Curyer said the council should come clean with how much it planned to sell the street for. Sitthixay Ditthavong Neutral Bay resident Glen Curyer, chair of its local precinct committee, said if the council was selling a street used by residents it must disclose the price. “The street is quite beneficial in the evening even though people from Redlands were parking there during the day,” he said, noting its proximity to a nearby restaurant strip.



He said the fact a school was buying an entire street stoked long-held resentment with how North Sydney area was a focal point for “new and established private schools”. Editor's pick Opinion

City life I swam in the newly reopened North Sydney pool. Was the 1986-day wait worth it? Cindy Yin Urban affairs reporter “We’re near transport, you can ship the students here if you need to, you can drop them off on the way to work,” he said. He said school students, supervised by teachers, commandeered local parks and used them as playgrounds which effectively meant residents, who pay rates, could not use them during the day. “That gets up everyone’s nose,” he said.



The potential sell-off of roads comes a year after Baker wrote to local schools asking them to voluntarily pay rates. They politely declined, citing legislation that states schools must not operate for profit. In a statement, Redlands said it was committed to ongoing consultation with council and neighbours, noting Monford Place is a no-through lane surrounded by school-owned properties. “With future generations in mind, we are working towards a vision that would create opportunities to further enrich learning, wellbeing and co-curricular experiences at Redlands as well as contributing positively to our wider community.” A Shore spokeswoman said with respect to Edward Street, it had previously explored opportunities.



“Any future activity would be subject to appropriate planning, consultation and regulatory processes. Shore is not currently in a position to comment on any future plans,” she said. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Iranian researchers blocked at universities taking hardline approach
World.content:
NationalVictoriaEducation Iranian researchers blocked at universities taking hardline approach Jackson Graham August 13, 2026 — 7:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two Melbourne universities are not accepting applications from Iranian students to study research degrees such as PhDs, as they take a hardline approach to complying with federal government sanctions. The tightening of enrolments has led Australian-based Iranian academics to call for the universities to reconsider the policies, which they say have unfairly prevented students from adding to fields such as medicine, food science and architecture. Deakin University and Swinburne University are not taking new enrolments from higher degree by research students – including master’s and PhD students – from sanctioned countries such as Iran. University of Melbourne political science researcher Afsaneh Seifinaji says Deakin and Swinburne universities are taking an overly strict approach to advice over research students from Iran. Penny Stephens “This decision follows advice from government and the university’s broader compliance and risk obligations in relation to certain Australian sanctions,” a Deakin University spokesperson said. “There are both legal and regulatory considerations.”



A Swinburne spokesperson said the university was following government advice and legal requirements related to sanctions and research security. “We regularly assess and update our procedures in light of an evolving and complex regulatory landscape,” the spokesperson said. Iran, which has been in a conflict with the US and Israel since February, is governed by a regime whose nuclear program has caused unease among the international community. Australia has sanctions against Iran through the UN Security Council and imposes its own autonomous sanctions on it. The tightening of enrolments of researchers with Iranian citizenship comes after the federal government updated advice last month for universities to enhance their due diligence to ensure they do not breach sanctions by providing banned services to that country, or dealing with specific entities or individuals within it. Penalties for the universities breaching the sanctions can be up to $3.64 million, or greater for breaches worth large sums of money. Whether a researcher’s activity could be a breach can depend on their nationality, recent travel history, prior education and involvement in fields “that are sensitive or dual use in nature, such as nuclear technology, advanced weaponry, or cybersecurity”, the Australian Sanctions Office advice states.



However, the office also clarifies it “does not consider a blanket restriction on enrolling all such persons to be the only way to mitigate risk”. Deakin University says it is not proceeding with the enrolments of a new higher degree by research candidates from certain sanctioned countries. Vicky Hughson University of Melbourne political science researcher Afsaneh Seifinaji has been in contact with several Iranian researchers who have been unable to enrol at Deakin and Swinburne after applying to study fields such as food science, endometriosis in women and environmentally sustainable architecture. “Iranian students are some of the really hardworking and top students among international students in Australia. I don’t think this is fair because of an ongoing conflict. I think this is too conservative [of the universities],” Seifinaji said. “It is understandable that Australia takes a conservative approach of not admitting certain [researchers] – for example, a nuclear scientist or some sort of research that can be used in weapons manufacturing.



Related Article Exclusive

University Of Sydney University of Sydney bans collaboration with rogue states “But I believe that if you are not conducting highly sensitive research, you should not be included in this. A lot of people wanted to have the opportunity to conduct study in a better country all their lives, and that is now on pause for who knows how many years.” She is also aware of students who have been awarded PhD scholarships at one of the universities but are now unable to gain enrolment due to the blanket ban. In May, Monash University arts faculty staff received an email, seen by this masthead, saying the university was “putting a temporary pause on processing enrolment offers to potential [higher degree by research] candidates from Iran”. However, it has since lifted the pause. “Students from sanctioned countries can apply for admission as PhD students at Monash, and may enrol if admitted, subject to standard screening and visa processes,” a Monash University spokesperson said.



Other universities such as RMIT are also taking a more nuanced approach, assessing research students on a case- by-case basis. “RMIT has introduced enhanced due diligence checks on prospective students from sanctioned countries, aligned with Australia’s foreign policy settings and relevant laws,” a spokesperson said. The University of Melbourne is also not restricting enrolments based on student citizenship. Vice-chancellor of global, culture and engagement Michael Wesley said the responsibility to adhere with the government’s expectations was being taken seriously, and that the university was alert to the risks of foreign interference, and “devotes considerable resources to identifying and mitigating these risks”.
