Tech.title: CBP Workers Allegedly Used Government Databases to Spy on Exes, Crushes, and Colleagues
Tech.content:
Internal records obtained by WIRED reveal how, for years, United States Customs and Border Protection employees and contractors were accused of abusing sensitive government databases for reasons that had nothing to do with their jobs. The records contain hundreds of allegations of misuse of law enforcement databases, including federal agents querying data to look up romantic interests, monitor family members, expose various personal information and, in some cases, provide intelligence to suspected smugglers or drug-trafficking organizations.

Acquired through Freedom of Information Act requests to CBP’s Office of Professional Responsibility and the Department of Homeland Security’s Office of Inspector General, the records reveal the breadth of alleged database abuse by CBP employees spanning more than a decade. As immigration and border authorities expand their surveillance through facial recognition, license plate readers, mobile-device searches, and commercially purchased location information generated by ordinary apps, the sheer range of these records, which date from 2009 through 2022, highlights how US residents can be—and have been—targeted by federal government employees with access to highly sensitive data and powerful tools.

WIRED has made this article free for all to read because it is primarily based on reporting from Freedom of Information Act requests. Please consider subscribing to support our journalism.

In one case, a CBP officer allegedly used government databases to contact a flight attendant. In another, an officer was accused of pulling information from trusted-traveler applications to ask people out. Other CBP employees were accused of providing border-crossing data to someone involved in a “heated divorce.” And yet another DHS employee allegedly used controversial ad-tech-derived location data to track several coworkers’ cell phones—which appears to be the first known internal abuse case involving DHS use of ad-tech-derived mobile location data.

“Customs and Border Protection has a long history of impunity and abuse of people's civil and human rights,” says Laura Rivera, an attorney with Just Futures Law, a civil and immigration advocacy legal organization. “Accountability for their wrongdoing has been elusive, and the dynamic involving the abuse of data is simply another aspect of that. As our society adopts more AI, data collection, and surveillance tools, each of us becomes increasingly vulnerable.”

The 2009-2022 dataset shines light on what officers did with the access they already had prior to gaining even more access. According to CBP, digital surveillance tools are supposed to help officers screen travelers and investigate crimes more efficiently. The records, however, reveal how, in case after case, sensitive data collected for law-enforcement purposes was weaponized against private individuals.

Breaches and Queries

At the time these allegations were made, complaints involving CBP personnel were initially routed through the Joint Intake Center, which has since been renamed the CBP Intake Center, and the Joint Intake Case Management System, which CBP and Immigration and Customs Enforcement still use for case tracking. Analysts decided whether each allegation should be retained for information, referred to an employee’s manager, or assigned to the Office of Professional Responsibility investigators as potentially serious misconduct.

Of the almost 300 data-related entries identified by WIRED, 138 were referred to CBP management for review, 78 were serious enough to be assigned to OPR criminal investigators, and 43 were classified as “Information Only,” meaning OPR did not open its own investigation. A smaller number fell into other categories: 12 misconduct allegations were sent for management review, where they were handled internally by the employees’ supervisors rather than by CBP’s central investigators; three were logged as “Law Enforcement Records” cases, meaning criminally investigated misconduct; two were logged as “Immediate Management Actions,” meaning minor misconduct resolved without opening a formal case; and only one as logged as an administrative inquiry, a formal fact-finding investigation conducted by CBP’s Office of Professional Responsibility. CBP withheld 21 cases, citing an exemption protecting active law-enforcement proceedings, suggesting criminal misconduct.

WIRED identified 99 entries involving alleged breaches or unauthorized disclosures of data and 48 explicitly involving improper database queries. Many of these cases happened around 2020, when the pandemic-prompted shift to remote work led CBP employees to start emailing work files to their personal accounts.

Tech.title: There’s a Fatty Liver Epidemic. AI Could Help Get Ahead of It
Tech.content:
All over the world, a slow, insidious change is taking place in the composition of the livers of more than a billion people.

While the presence of fat in a normal, healthy liver is negligible, many adults and even children have livers where fat exceeds 5 percent or even 10 percent of the organ’s total weight. Its unnatural presence causes inflammation, cell damage, and the formation of scar tissue known as fibrosis, all hallmarks of fatty liver disease, a condition that now impacts approximately 30 percent of adults worldwide.

If left to linger, progressive fat accumulation can ultimately lead to liver failure, and it has been linked to an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and various cancers. But the condition typically develops without noticeable symptoms, so it is rarely detected at an early and treatable stage. Even in cases of cirrhosis or advanced scarring of the liver, three-quarters of people are only diagnosed once their condition has become life-threatening.

As a result, growing numbers of specialists are investigating how AI might help. Jeffrey Lazarus, a professor at the CUNY Graduate School of Public Health and Health Policy, suggests that AI tools could be used to comb through vast numbers of electronic health records and pinpoint the people most likely to have accrued worrying amounts of liver fat.

“AI can retrospectively go through massive numbers of hospital visits and lab reports,” says Lazarus. “You can use that to really prioritize who’s at most risk.”

If fatty liver disease can be identified early, much of the damage is highly reversible. In the initial stages, lifestyle changes such as reducing alcohol intake, losing weight through dietary improvements and exercise, and even drinking more coffee have all been shown to be capable of reversing scarring and inflammation. Even for people with moderate to advanced liver scarring, novel treatments such as the GLP-1 medication semaglutide and a drug called resmetirom have been shown to be highly effective therapeutics.

“The liver is a very versatile and interesting organ because it can regenerate, fibrosis can be reversed, and you can be completely healthy again,” says Lazarus. “But traditionally, we’ve focused more on late-stage care and trying to see how long we can keep a patient alive rather than finding them early and preventing the condition from advancing.”

One of the frustrations for Lazarus and others is that while simple, noninvasive means of assessing liver health exist, they are rarely used, even in people known to be at a much higher risk of the consequences of fatty liver disease, such as those with obesity and type 2 diabetes.

The Fib-4 index, for example, rates a person’s risk of advanced liver fibrosis through computing a score of between 0 and 6, based on their age, their levels of two liver enzymes, and their blood-clotting ability. This requires physicians to run a liver blood test, something which is often carried out as part of an annual medical checkup in the US. Doctors also have access to a more accurate, second-line blood test known as the enhanced liver fibrosis test, which measures the levels of two proteins involved in creating scar tissue and an enzyme which inhibits the clearance of scars in the liver.

Using both of these tests in patients with worrying amounts of liver fat has been shown to improve the diagnosis of those with advanced fibrosis by four-fold. But for physicians facing a growing workload and administrative burden, simply adding more testing to the workflow is not felt to be a sustainable option.

“You have to have something that can run in the background or it’s easy to just hit a button and do it,” says Jonathan Dranoff, a professor of medicine at Yale University.

Tech.title: My Favorite Things from Made by Google 2026
Tech.content:
Google showed off its new Pixel lineup at its Made By Google 2026 event on Wednesday in New York City, but it wasn’t a typical big-tech announcement that gave the public its first look at new devices — that happened in the morning.

Perhaps Google chose to show its Pixel products off hours ahead of its event because a lot of details were leaked in advance, possibly leading the company to avoid following the traditional 10 a.m. PT show. Official details of the Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL, Pixel 11 Pro Fold foldable, Pixel Watch 5 smartwatch and Pixel Tag tracker were released at 7 a.m. PT, letting people get good looks at all the devices before they were officially announced during the show, which started at 6 p.m. ET.

Be sure to check out all of CNET’s coverage, including hands-on experience and Andrew Lanxon’s exclusive photo walk through Paris with the Pixel 11 Pro XL. After you’ve loaded browser tabs with each of those, let’s move on to what stood out today.

Live human presenters who can think on their feet

Apple has switched to almost entirely prerecorded keynotes, and while Samsung’s Galaxy Unpacked had live presenters on stage in front of an audience, they mostly delivered rehearsed and teleprompted scripts as they debuted their new devices.

Google remembers that a product release is a show and brought hosts who can be entertaining.

Host Trevor Noah and Google Senior Vice President Rick Osterloh chat at the beginning of the Made By Google 2026 event. Screenshot by Tyler Graham/CNET

Last year, Jimmy Fallon bounded around a set that felt more like his Late Night studio than an auditorium. This year brings comedian (and former late-night talk show host) Trevor Noah as host, who also interviewed people from Google in a multi-camera talk show environment.

Although some of Google’s folks did have a measure of polished presenter training going on, they had to bounce off Noah’s impromptu interjections. At one point, he said, “I’m the one who’s supposed to make sure nothing goes wrong. I mean it’s live – I’ll make sure everything goes wrong.” There were some awkward moments, to be sure, but I spent the time always curious just how Noah would react.

Trevor Noah and Joël Yawili text Yawili’s mother in multiple languages. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

But a demonstration of the Rambler dictation feature with Google’s Joël Yawili, where Yawili got Noah to text his mother in English and French, was conversational and funny. Yawili surprised Noah by saying that he was also originally from Johannesburg, and at times, it looked as if they needed to remind themselves they were there to show features, not just banter among themselves.

Live demos

Live demonstrations of technology can be the third rail of product announcements — crucial to see, but sometimes disastrous if they fail in front of viewers. But Google included several live demos during the event of new features debuting on the Pixel 11 series. That led to some fun moments, such as when Noah used his finger to wiggle the screen when using the new Rambler technology saying, “Wait, so are you guys seeing the screen with me? I’m controlling. Oh damn, that’s me.”

Also great was the demonstration of American Sign Language-to-text, where Google director of product inclusion and equity Annie Jean-Baptiste had a conversation with deaf actor Daniel Durant, who communicated in ASL.

Magic Capture does even more of the picture-taking for you

Is pressing the shutter button in the Camera app too haaaarrd? Have you wished the camera in your smartphone could do even more of the work, not just come up with well-exposed photos in all sorts of lighting conditions? Well, you’re in luck, because Magic Capture will do it all.

I hope my sarcasm as a photographer came through there, because now I’m going to tell you about the reality of picture taking: We miss shots all the time. We realize later we could have framed them better and crop them so everyone things we nailed it on the first try. We sometimes aren’t as quick with the shutter press to grab the shot we really wanted.

That’s a big part of why photography is appealing: it’s work, it takes practice and making a quality photo is a great feeling.

But most people just want to point their phone at a subject and snap a good picture. Magic Capture is another tool to help them do that without stressing over capturing the perfect moment. You point the camera at a scene, and the feature grabs shots for you, no shutter button-mashing required.

JuJu Watkins, Kenn Sulaimon and Jesser look at a photo shot using the Pixel 11 Pro’s Magic Capture feature. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Smartphone cameras are already making dozens of micro-captures for every shutter press, so Magic Capture is a logical extension of that process. It records video and then pulls out the best frames as still photos. At the event, it was demonstrated by Google’s Kenny Sulaimon live from Brooklyn Bridge Park with YouTuber Jesser and college basketball star JuJu Watkins shooting hoops and capturing stills of the action.

I’m reserving my full opinion about Magic Capture until I’ve had a chance to try it out – is it really making smart decisions about what to capture? – but for now, I’m going to embrace Magic Capture as a way to help non-photographers make better photos.

Pixel Tag, you’re it

The Apple AirTag has been a quiet giant success for years, but AirTags don’t work as well with Android phones as they do with devices in the Apple ecosystem. And though Android-compatible portable trackers have also been around for a while, the ability to use distributed networking to make them work better is a recent development.

Google, as the primary author of Android and its ecosystem, developed the Find My Devices technology used by the Samsung Galaxy SmartTag 2 and Motorola Moto Tag, as well as numerous third-party devices. Now it has its own hardware, the Google Tag.

Trevor Noah and Google’s Isabelle Olsson talk about the new Google Tag at Made By Google 2026. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Even if the Google Tag doesn’t reach the same saturation as Apple’s tracking pucks, the little oblong locators with a prominent G stamped onto them are no doubt worth doing. AirTags have a 50% to 60% profit margin, according to some estimates, so as long as Google can manufacture them reasonably, they’ll join the worldwide Find Hub network, helping people locate all the stuff we lose every day.

I’m a ramblin’ man

I know people who dictate most everything – texts to friends, web searches, articles – and they’re remarkably smooth. I’ve never had that gift. When I try to dictate, I invariably devolve into sentence fragments, grunts and swear words.

Rambler, a new Gemini feature originally demoed at Google I/O 2026 in May, is a much more patient listener than most transcription apps or AIs. It understands those bits and pieces of conversation and threads them back into usable text.

I’m looking forward to seeing if I can stump it. I suppose I could also work on my speaking skills, too.

AI can translate ASL to text

Google demonstrated its sign-language-to-text (SL2T) language model, a way for people to communicate in American Sign Language by translating and transcribing their body motions.

Google’s Annie Jean-Baptiste uses sign-language-to-text to have a conversation with actor Daniel Durant. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

This is a very cool feature, but I’m more impressed with how it’s executed. The phone records a person using ASL, which sets off privacy bells and has me wondering what the company might do with that video.

But in fact, the “on-device model tracks the location of points on the signer, and only those geometric coordinates are sent to the server for translation,” according to Google. The video is immediately discarded while the sequence is translated into text.

HiLight starts at a surprising low point

HiLight looked like it would be an actual highlight of the Pixel 11 Pro line, but I have to admit I’m a little slack-jawed at what Google is shipping. I think the crowd at the event and even Noah were underwhelmed, too.

Replacing the temperature sensor on the Pixel 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL and 11 Pro Fold – I forgot that feature was there, sorry – HiLight is a circular LED near the cameras that can light up more than a typical smartphone flash. Reminiscent of Nothing’s inventive Glyph, the HiLight can light up in other colors and act as a notification alert when the phone is face down.

“Aaand… there it is.” The HiLight shows green when a contact calls. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

But all it can do right now is display an assigned color when one of your contacts calls you – purple for your partner or orange for your parents, for example – and light up in a swirl of colors when you activate the Gemini assistant. Surprisingly, the presenter said that it can’t do the color red.

Yeah, that’s it. Colors for phone calls, not texts, and an indicator that you’re using Gemini when you presumably just made a request of Gemini.

Trevor Noah looks incredulous that there isn’t more to the Pixel 11 Pro’s HiLight feature during Made By Google 2026. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

Let’s hope Google just ran out of time and that there will be additional features that take advantage of the HiLight, and a way for developers to create their own interactions.

That little circle is just begging for a port of Doom. And to play The Odyssey the way Christopher Nolan intended.

Tech.title: Pixel 11 vs. Pixel 11 Pro vs. Pixel 11 Pro XL: Google’s Latest Phones Compared
Tech.content:
Google unveiled a brand-new slate of handsets for 2026: the Pixel 11, 11 Pro, 11 Pro XL and 11 Pro Fold. The Pixel 11 series has a number of improvements over its predecessors, including more efficient Tensor G6 processors, camera advancements such as Magic Capture and overall spec upgrades.

While there aren’t many design differences compared with the Pixel 10, the Pixel 11 Pro devices in particular do have one notable addition: HiLight. Initially rumored as the “Pixel Glow,” HiLight is essentially an array of ambient LED lights built around the camera’s flash that provide visual cues depending on the type of notification you’re getting. It hearkens back to the BlackBerry’s notification LED.

The Pixel 11 series also showcases many of Gemini Intelligence’s latest features, such as voice-to-text capabilities that filter out filler words when sending a message, or the ability to communicate in ASL via the Pixel camera.

The Pixel 11 series is now available to preorder. Wondering which new Pixel to buy? Here’s how the Pixel 11, 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL compare against one another.

Pixel 11 vs. 11 Pro/11 Pro XL: Design and display

The Pixel 11 Pro XL’s screen is brighter than previous Pixel Pro models.

At first glance, the Pixel 11 series doesn’t look too different from its predecessors. The Pixel 11 and 11 Pro still have a 6.3-inch OLED screen, and the 11 Pro XL has a 6.8-inch OLED display. The Pixel 11 has a peak brightness of 3,000 nits, but the Pixel 11 Pro and Pro XL both have peak brightness increased to 3,600 nits (up from 3,300 on the 10 Pro and 10 Pro XL).

One major design change is that the Pixel’s camera bar is now made of edge-to-edge glass, giving it a much more seamless look. This camera bar is also home to the new HiLight ambient LED feature, though it’s exclusive to just the Pixel 11 Pro devices.

The aim of the HiLight feature is to provide visual cues about who is calling you when the phone is face down. According to Google, the feature integrates with your contacts list, so your favorite contact’s custom color will light up if they’re trying to call you.

Size-wise, the Pixel 11 and 11 Pro both measure 6 by 2.8 by 0.3 inches and the Pixel 11 Pro XL is 6.4 by 3 by 0.3 inches. Interestingly, however, they seem to weigh a tiny bit less than the Pixel 10 series. The Pixel 11 weighs in at 6.9 ounces (down from 7.2 ounces), the 11 Pro is 7.2 ounces (down from 7.3 ounces), and the Pixel 11 Pro XL is 8 ounces (down from 8.2 ounces).

Let’s not forget the color options. The Pixel 11 is available in frost, pistachio, hibiscus and obsidian, while the 11 Pro and 11 Pro XL are available in canyon, olive, fog and obsidian (matte finish).

Pixel 11 vs. 11 Pro/11 Pro XL: Cameras

Software adds the biggest upgrades to the Pixel cameras.

For the most part, the Pixel 11 series has the same trio of rear cameras as its predecessors.

Pixel 11 series cameras compared

Wide-angle Ultrawide Telephoto Selfie Pixel 11 48 megapixels 13 megapixels 10.8 megapixels 10.5 megapixels Pixel 11 Pro/11 Pro XL 50 megapixels 48 megapixels 50 megapixels 42 megapixels

The big difference with the 11 series is that the 11 Pro cameras now have a Pro Zoom of up to 120x. The base Pixel 11 also has an upgraded 30x Super Zoom. Google also says that all three handsets have improved light sensitivity and larger sensors. The image sensors on the 11 Pro/11 Pro XL are larger than the ones on the Pixel 11’s cameras.

Many of the camera’s biggest improvements are software-based. For example, there’s a new Magic Capture mode that records a short video clip and then uses AI to select the best still frames from it. It definitely feels aimed at parents who want to take photos of their kids without worrying about getting the shot at the right time.

Another feature called Camera Looks lets you take photos with unique color and analog film styles. It’s similar to Photographic Styles on the iPhone.

Pixel 11 vs. 11 Pro/11 Pro XL: Storage, battery and other specs

One of the more notable shifts with the Pixel 11 series is that the 128GB model has been dropped from the lineup. Now, the lowest storage you can get is 256GB. That’s not necessarily a bad thing, but it does raise the price of entry.

Model Storage RAM US Price Pixel 11 256GB 12GB $899 Pixel 11 Pro 256GB 12GB $1,099 Pixel 11 Pro XL 256GB 12GB $1,199 Pixel 11 512GB 12GB $1,019 Pixel 11 Pro 512GB 16GB $1,219 Pixel 11 Pro XL 512GB 16GB $1,419 Pixel 11 Pro 1TB 16GB $1,499 Pixel 11 Pro XL 1TB 16GB $1,649

The Pixel 11 ships with a 4,985-mAh battery, the 11 Pro has 4,850 mAh and the 11 Pro has a 5,115 mAh. On paper, that might seem like a smaller capacity than their Pixel 10 counterparts, but Google says the Adaptive Battery feature on the Pixel 11 series should deliver over 30 hours of battery life. We’ll have to do some testing of our own to check those claims.

All the new Pixel 11 handsets are powered by the new Google Tensor G6, which should result in better power efficiency, faster browsing and faster app loading. Google also says that Gemini Nano should run with higher quality and lower latency on the Pixel 11 series thanks to the Tensor G6.

Tech.title: Could a Shirt Fool Facial Recognition? The Answer Is Complicated
Tech.content:
A camera and its software labeled Bill Swearingen as a person. Then it suddenly wasn’t sure — all because of some weird pattern that he held up to disguise himself.

I watched it happen from my seat at annual hacker convention Defcon. Swearingen, a longtime cybersecurity professional and founder of the Kansas City security community SecKC, stood onstage in front of a live camera feed as a person-detection system analyzed him. On the giant screen behind him, the software’s confidence score cleared 0.75, the threshold it needed to declare that, yes, there was a human being in the frame.

Then Swearingen raised a flat panel covered in a bizarre black-and-white pattern. The score started falling. It slipped below the threshold, eventually landing at 0.21.

“No person detected,” the screen announced in bright green letters.

It felt like a low-budget magic trick. Swearingen was still standing there, plainly visible to everyone in the room. The software was still receiving the camera image, but it no longer detected a person above the configured confidence threshold.

Swearingen has spent the past year searching for patterns that can confuse the computer-vision systems used to identify people. His project is called noRecognition, and its end goal is to create clothing that makes the wearer harder for AI surveillance systems to detect. It’s a fascinating project, but it’s still a work in progress.

The camera wasn’t trying to identify him

We tend to call this kind of technology “facial recognition,” but surveillance systems can involve several separate layers of AI-based detection.

A person detector asks whether a human body is in the frame. A face detector finds and isolates a face. Facial recognition then compares that face with a database and asks whether it knows who the person is.

Person detection, face detection and facial recognition perform different jobs, though each step can depend on the one before it.

The demonstration I saw targeted the first step. The system didn’t mistake Swearingen for somebody else or decide the room was empty. It simply stopped reporting a person detection above the threshold set for the demonstration.

If you break the first link, the rest of the surveillance chain may never get started. If a camera fails to detect a person, it may never crop out that person’s face, send it to an identity database, then track them across a series of images.

An AI detector doesn’t “see” a person in the way we do. It generates thousands of guesses about what might be in an image, assigns a score to them and discards anything that fails to clear a chosen confidence threshold.

Swearingen was still there. The detector’s math just wasn’t sure he was a person.

How the patterns are made

Swearingen didn’t sit down and draw the patterns himself. He built a program to create them.

Security researchers normally use programs called fuzzers to bombard software with strange inputs in an attempt to break it. Swearingen’s fuzzer does something similar with computer vision. It creates a pattern, digitally places it on an image of a computer-generated person and then shows the altered image to several AI models.

If a pattern causes a major change, like making the person’s detection box disappear or sharply lowering the model’s confidence score, then the fuzzer flags it for more testing.

The most successful designs are altered and combined to produce new patterns, much like selectively breeding specific traits in animals. Swearingen’s software repeats that process automatically, allowing it to work through far more possibilities than a person could design and test by hand.

He currently tests each pattern against 11 models: five that detect people, four that find faces and two that try to recognize whose face it is. In many cases, he tested a public model that works similarly to proprietary systems, not the actual software being used by companies in the wild. Most are publicly available models that researchers can run themselves.

Swearingen said the project had run 31.7 million tests as of June. About 534,600 triggered one of his system’s anomaly rules. That could mean a detector found fewer people or faces than it did in the original image, invented extra ones, produced a much lower confidence score or returned the wrong identity. It doesn’t mean he found 534,600 patterns that could hide someone from a camera.

Swearingen’s custom fuzzer automatically generates patterns, tests them against computer-vision models and flags designs that produce unusual results.

Of those results, 85 met the project’s definition of “extreme,” which means the pattern defeated at least one person detector and at least one face detector in the same test.

The tests also showed that covering more of the body isn’t always more effective. Torso patterns had the greatest effect on person detectors, while patterns closer to the head mattered more to systems looking for faces. In one comparison, Swearingen said a small collar pattern worked better than a much larger print across the torso.

Even the winning patterns can lose

Some of Swearingen’s results looked promising until he tested the designs on different people.

One pattern lowered the detector’s confidence for all four people whose images were used while it was being developed. But when Swearingen applied that same design to images of eight new people, it didn’t work once.

Swearingen used computer-generated people wearing different garments and accessories to test where adversarial patterns might work best.

Counted together, the pattern had worked on four of 12 people. Swearingen withdrew the resulting 33% performance claim because every success involved people whose images had been used to develop the pattern. It hadn’t worked on anyone new.

Another pattern, designed to fool a different detector, worked on all eight new people. That contrast shows how much the results can change between detectors — what works with one person or detection model may fail with another.

Even a successful pattern may have a short shelf life. A camera company could retrain its software to recognize it. Swearingen compared the patterns to software “zero-days” vulnerabilities — they take advantage of a weakness that may disappear once the system is updated.

The shirt doesn’t exist yet, and the tech isn’t field-tested

On one of Swearingen’s slides, in large type, were the words “Still unproven: The worn garment.”

During the demo, Swearingen held the pattern in front of his body on a rigid panel. It wasn’t printed on clothing, which would be a much harder test. Ink on a flat board stays exactly where the software expects it to be. Fabric drapes, folds and stretches. Sunlight, shadows, wrinkles, viewing angles and distance all change what reaches the camera.

Swearingen said most of his 31.7 million tests were digital, with patterns pasted onto images and scored by computer-vision models. The panel demonstration was a limited physical test using a model he said came from a fielded Flock Safety unit. Until a pattern works while printed on fabric, worn by a moving person and viewed through deployed hardware, he isn’t claiming that the clothing itself works.

In a noRecognition digital test, the detector reported the plain-shirt image as a person with 86% confidence but produced no person detection after the pattern was added.

The noRecognition website is promoting a Kickstarter-backed run of T-shirts, hoodies and neckwear, with each pattern scored against 11 models before it ships. Swearingen said the money would help pay for test fabrics, a dye-sublimation printer and additional cameras so he can see whether the patterns still work once they’re printed and worn.

So could a pattern on your clothing fool facial recognition?

Maybe. But the real test begins when he prints it on clothing and steps back in front of the camera.

Tech.title: Apple Faces Lawsuit Over iCloud Private Relay Vulnerability
Tech.content:
The revelation that Apple’s iCloud Private Relay feature hasn’t been as secure as Apple says has spawned a lawsuit against the iPhone maker.

Last week, a blog post by Talal Haj Bakry and Tommy Mysk exposed a vulnerability in how iCloud Private Relay, in some circumstances, doesn’t shield a customer’s IP address, which is the entire purpose of the feature. Even when it’s enabled, their information can be exposed when using a passkey to sign in or when a website uses two methods (DNS prefetching and WebTransport) to load data faster.

In a complaint filed by Clarkson Law Firm on Aug. 6, plaintiff Edward Rickman says he subscribed to iCloud Plus believing that iCloud Private Relay would hide his IP address and Safari browsing activity.

“Instead, Apple delivered a system that recreates through its own credential service the precise harm Apple told the world it had made impossible,” reads the complaint, which seeks class action status.

The lawsuit also seeks an injunction against Apple requiring it to change its business practices to mitigate the risk of consumer deception, as well as monetary relief and attorneys’ fees.

An Apple representative didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment.

Craig Federighi, Apple’s senior vice president of software engineering, describes new privacy features at an Apple event. James Martin/CNET

A core component of the lawsuit is that iCloud Private Relay is a paid service of iCloud Plus, which costs between 99 cents and $60 per month. The feature is available only if you’re subscribed to iCloud Plus, not the basic iCloud service.

Also key is the fact that Apple has advertised for years that iCloud Private Relay is a safe way to browse the web and avoid the types of tracking that services such as Facebook use to connect people’s browsing habits and assemble profiles on them that can be monetized.

“Apple built its entire brand on the promise that it would protect its users’ privacy when no other company would,” Tim Giordano, a partner at Clarkson Law Firm, said in a statement. “For Apple’s iCloud users to now learn that for years they were paying Apple a premium for a protection that simply didn’t work, exposing them to the very tracking, profiling and targeting Apple warned them about, is an outrageous violation and betrayal of consumer trust and law.”

Clarkson recently won a $250 million settlement from Apple over the company’s marketing of AI features for the iPhone 16 Pro that were never delivered.

The researchers who discovered the flaw set up a website that lets anyone check whether iCloud Private Relay is protecting their IP address. They say they released the information publicly rather than first alerting Apple because of the company’s lengthy review process.

The information in the red box was the IP number of my home router. Screenshot by Jeff Carlson/CNET

In an email to CNET, Mysk wrote, “If we had a better experience with the Apple Security Bounty program that would make us feel confident the issue would be addressed promptly for the benefit of iCloud Private Relay users as well as Psylo users, we would have reported this iCloud Private Relay issue to Apple without having to release a Psylo update addressing the issue, and as a result having to disclose it to our users.” Psylo is the developers’ privacy-focused web browsing app.

Tech.title: SpaceXAI Joins the AI Agent Game With Grok Bot
Tech.content:
We need bots, but do they need us? Not a whole lot, if Grok Bot can do everything it purportedly can. SpaceXAI introduced the new AI agent platform this week and says it can do it all — message each other, do group chats, share work and even answer to an AI boss.

Grok Bot was jointly developed by SpaceXAI and Cursor, an AI development company that SpaceX is acquiring for $60 billion. Grok Bot is not to be confused with Grok, which is an AI chatbot that can answer questions and generate images, videos and code. Grok Bot is designed to be a team of AI agents that can help with work tasks and projects.

AI agents differ from AI assistants in that they can work autonomously and proactively to execute projects. Assistants can make dinner reservations for you; agents can help run a restaurant. Professional services firm Deloitte estimates that 75% of companies plan to incorporate AI agent systems into their operations by 2028.

Grok Bot is only the latest AI agent to come along. Predecessors include OpenClaw, Sai by Simular, Claude Computer Use, Manus, OpenAI Operator, NanoClaw and Hermes Agent. These options vary by what they can do, how secure they are and how complicated they are to use.

How does Grok Bot work?

Customers can create one or more AI agents that use their own cloud-based computer — not the customer’s — and can access the apps, websites and email inboxes the customer so designates. The agents can execute jobs from beginning to end and will contact the customer only if an approval is needed, SpaceXAI said.

Customers can message the AI agents by phone or computer to hand off a project or discuss an ongoing one. The company said Grok Bot can “remember conversations, learn how you like things done and get sharper the more you work together.”

SpaceXAI said Grok Bot doesn’t require the customer to set up workflows or routines — “simply message a Bot to take on a task, and it gets it done.”

What can Grok Bot do?

In its announcement, SpaceXAI said employees have been using Grok Bot in-house. The company said that bots have helped with sales, recruiting, processing invoices and implementing bug fixes.

SpaceXAI said Grok Bot agents can work in concert, with each handling a separate operation — email, expenses, recruiting, bug fixes and operations. The agents can send messages to each other, pass work off if need be and assign ownership of tasks.

Customers can also create an agent to act as “chief of staff” to manage the other agents.

Learning from the customer

SpaceXAI said customers can train Grok Bot agents by having them follow along and watch their workflow to learn the steps and processes the customer uses. After learning the routines, the agents can fly solo the next time “without re-explaining it again,” the company said.

Grok Bot becomes more proactive and self-directed over time, completing necessary work before the customer even requests it, SpaceXAI says.

SpaceXAI said Grok Bot — currently in beta — is now available to subscribers of SuperGrok Heavy, Cursor Ultra and Cursor Teams Premium on desktop and iOS. Enterprise users can join a waitlist for future access. After downloading the app, customers can create a Grok Bot teammate and then assign tasks and projects.

Trust is paramount

Grok Bot, like other AI agents, must be reliable from start to finish, or else trust in these “co-workers” will disappear, says Uttara M. Ananthakrishnan, an assistant professor in the Foster School of Business at the University of Washington.

“The biggest issue pops up with multi-step jobs,” Ananthakrishnan told CNET. “If a bot gets through the first two steps of a process and then flakes out, the person using it has to start all over. If a task needs approvals from five different people in different departments, a bot is going to be terrible at it.”

Ananthakrishnan said it’s a “game changer” if companies can seamlessly integrate AI agents into their operations to do repetitive tasks, save time and increase efficiency. But if the AI agents are clunky, workers will revert to their own ways of doing things.

“People will always have their own optimized workflows and won’t tolerate an agent making minor errors. If they try two times and if it doesn’t work, they will just roll their eyes and think about it as an AI for AI’s sake product,” Ananthakrishnan told CNET.

Going rogue

In theory, AI agents like Grok Bot, OpenClaw and others can be very useful for companies. But sometimes they can be too self-directive. Their abilities can sometimes go off the rails.

In a recent instance in Australia, a man wanted OpenClaw to book him a spot in an exercise class. There was a waiting list, but the AI agent managed to move him up the list — by deleting someone else who was ahead of him. OpenAI and Anthropic also disclosed last month that their AI models hacked other companies’ servers during internal cybersecurity tests.

And in another incident, Anthropic’s top AI model used fake identities to deceive humans and insert malicious code during testing by Britain’s AI Security Institute.

Tech.title: It’s Not Just RAM: Windows Licenses Are Also Pushing Up PC Prices
Tech.content:
If you’ve been shopping for a new computer this year and are on a budget, it may feel like the news keeps getting worse and worse.

As with other types of electronics, including smartphones and tablets, the price of computers has been consistently rising due to shortages of certain components and steep price increases for components like RAM and storage devices like hard drives and SSDs. Motherboards have been rumored to see price hikes soon. But it’s not just hardware: Reports suggest the cost of Windows licenses for manufacturers is rising by up to 10%.

Several sites that closely follow Microsoft news, including Windows Central and Windows Latest, have published articles citing a report from Taiwan’s Economic Daily News that claims some PC manufacturers are seeing a 7% to 10% increase in the cost of Windows 11 licenses.

PC makers pay for Windows as part of their OEM, or original equipment manufacturer, costs. Because they buy licenses in bulk, they get a sizeable discount over what a consumer would pay for a new copy of Windows 11. But given the existing cost pressures from other components, a big Windows 11 price hike could lead them to pass on some of the added cost to PC buyers. According to the EDN story, PC makers could raise prices by about 5% over the next quarter due to the reported Windows price hike.

A representative for Microsoft declined to comment on the report.

Variable pricing

A translated version of the Economic Daily News article contains information from an unnamed PC brand executive. It says that while Microsoft typically raises licensing costs every year by single-digit percentages, that hike has reached 7% to 10% this year, a significant increase.

As this article points out, OEM pricing for Windows varies by company and even by the type of processor being used in the computer. Two of the largest PC makers in the region, Asus and Acer, already confirmed PC price increases earlier this year. In the case of Asus, the PC price increase was 30% for Taiwan.

Framework cited “an increase in Windows license costs” in a blog post explaining price hikes for its laptops in July.

While Windows 10 users were given Windows 11 as a free upgrade, for consumers who aren’t OEM manufacturers, the cost of the operating system is $139 for the Home version and $200 for the Pro version.

Tech.title: PS Plus Is Loaded With Great Games for August, Including Helldivers 2, Hell Is Us, Kingdom Come 2
Tech.content:
It’s officially the second half of 2026, and every game publisher is rushing to get their games out before the release of Grand Theft Auto 6 in November. Sony appears to be doing its part by having one of its best months for PS Plus subscribers, as the rest of August is filled with critically acclaimed games coming to the service.

PS Plus, which is Sony’s version of Xbox Game Pass, offers a large, constantly expanding library of games. Subscribers can choose from the Essential, Extra and Premium tiers, each with unique perks and benefits. Starting at $11 a month, the plans give subscribers access to games and rewards, and each month, all subscribers can play a handful of new games at no additional charge.

If you’re a PlayStation Plus Extra or Premium subscriber, you can grab these games starting Wednesday.

Helldivers 2

Helldivers 2 came out in 2024 and quickly became one of the biggest multiplayer games of the year. Developed by Arrowhead Game Studios, it puts players in the role of Helldivers, soldiers fighting to protect Super Earth from alien and robotic threats. Up to four players can team up to take on missions, but things can quickly go sideways when calling in airstrikes, turrets and other powerful weapons. The game’s ultra-patriotic tone, reminiscent of Starship Troopers, makes it a must-play for fans of action games who also enjoy a bit of satire.

Helldivers 2 is available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers as of Wednesday.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 takes players back to 15th-century Bohemia, where the protagonist, Henry, finds himself caught up in a war between rival nobles. Developed by Warhorse Studios, the RPG builds on the first game with a much bigger world, deeper quests and a commitment to making medieval life feel as realistic as possible. There’s no magic or fantasy here, just sword fights, political intrigue and plenty of situations where Henry can get himself into trouble. The game was also up for numerous awards across the industry, including Game of the Year.

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers on Aug. 18.

Vampire Survivors

Vampire Survivors looks deceptively simple, but that’s exactly what makes it so addictive. You control a character who automatically attacks while you move around the map, collecting experience and choosing new weapons and upgrades as increasingly ridiculous numbers of enemies swarm you. A run can start with a few bats and skeletons before turning into complete chaos, with dozens of weapons and upgrades combining to turn your character into an unstoppable killing machine.

Vampire Survivors will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting Aug. 18.

Hell Is Us

Hell Is Us drops players into the war-torn country of Hadea, where a mysterious supernatural disaster has created creatures unlike anything else in the game. Protagonist Rémi returns to his homeland looking for answers about his past, but what makes the game interesting is how much it refuses to tell you. There are no traditional quest markers or map guiding you from one objective to the next, so paying attention to conversations and the environment actually matters. Combat mixes melee weapons with a drone companion, while the strange world and its mysteries give the game a much darker, more unsettling feel.

Hell Is Us will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting Aug. 25.

Umamusume: Pretty Derby – Party Dash

Umamusume: Pretty Derby – Party Dash is a wildly strange take on horse racing mixed with a collection of chaotic party games starring the series’ horse girls. Instead of focusing on the actual racing that caught some gamers’ attention, the game has characters competing in events involving basketball, dodgeball, eating competitions and obstacle courses. There’s also a story mode and plenty of character interactions for fans of the anime and mobile game. The pixel-art presentation fits the game’s silly tone, while the different events give players a much more casual take on the Umamusume series than its usual racing-focused gameplay.

Umamusume: Pretty Derby – Party Dash will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting Aug. 25.

Two Point Museum

Two Point Museum puts a goofy spin on the usually serious business of running a museum. Building the perfect collection means sending experts out on expeditions to hunt down rare artifacts, then figuring out how to display them in a way that keeps visitors interested and spending money. There are dinosaurs, supernatural oddities, aliens and plenty of stranger exhibits to discover, with each museum offering its own challenges. Like the other Two Point games, things can quickly get ridiculous, but there’s also a surprising amount of freedom in designing the museums and deciding what kind of experience you want visitors to have.

Two Point Museum will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting Aug. 25.

Metro Exodus

Metro Exodus takes the Metro series out of the tunnels of Moscow and into the much larger, more dangerous Russian wilderness. Artyom and a group of Spartan Rangers board the Aurora, a heavily modified train that carries them east in search of a new place to live after the nuclear war. The game mixes the series’ tense survival-horror atmosphere with larger, nonlinear areas where players can explore, scavenge for supplies and decide whether to fight or sneak past enemies. It still feels like Metro, but the move aboveground gives the game a much greater sense of scale.

Metro Exodus will be available for PS Plus Extra and Premium subscribers starting Aug. 25.

Dying Light 2

Dying Light 2 drops players into Villedor, one of the last major human settlements left after the zombie apocalypse, where surviving means dealing with both the infected and the people still fighting over the city. Parkour is a huge part of getting around, with rooftops providing safer routes through the city and plenty of ways to turn movement into part of combat. Nighttime changes the equation completely, as more dangerous infected emerge, while choices involving the city’s competing factions can alter parts of Villedor and the way the story plays out.

Dying Light 2 will be available for PS Plus Premium subscribers starting Aug. 25.

Onimusha: Dawn of Dreams

Onimusha: Dawn of Dreams arrived on the PlayStation 2 in 2006, wrapping up Capcom’s original run of Onimusha games for nearly two decades. Set 15 years after Onimusha 3, the story follows Soki, a warrior with supernatural powers who joins forces with several companions to stop Toyotomi Hideyoshi and his army of demons. The game also expanded the series’ combat with multiple playable characters, each with their own weapons and abilities, giving it more of an action-RPG feel than its predecessors.

Onimusha: Dawn of Dreams will be available for PS Plus Premium subscribers starting Aug. 18.

Disney’s Atlantis: The Lost Empire

Disney’s Atlantis: The Lost Empire came to the original PlayStation in 2001, alongside the animated movie it was based on. The action-adventure follows Milo Thatch and the rest of the expedition as they make their way through dangerous environments on the way to the lost city, with players able to switch between several members of the crew. Each character has distinct abilities useful for overcoming obstacles and solving puzzles, while the gameplay combines exploration, combat and platforming.

Disney’s Atlantis: The Lost Empire will be available for PS Plus Premium subscribers starting Aug. 18.

PlayStation Plus subscriptions start at $10 a month See at Sony

Tech.title: The Pixel Watch 5 Makes One of My Favorite Watches Better, but More Expensive
Tech.content:
The Pixel Watch 5 is a refined version of its predecessor, which was already a favorite of mine. But its $50 price hike might be a tough sell when many of the new watch’s best features are coming to older models too.

I got to spend a few hours with the Pixel Watch 5 in a press briefing — just enough time to get an idea of how it’s changed from last year’s Pixel Watch 4. Walking into Google’s demo room was like stepping into a rainbow. Each station had its own vibe, matching the shades of the new lineup: the Pixel Watch 5, Pixel 11 and Fold phones, Pixel Buds and Pixel Tags. I saw stations in peach, lilac, olive, lime, black and my personal favorite, bright pink.

The parade of colors — especially the almost blindingly bright pink, which I couldn’t stop staring at — momentarily distracted me from the fact that, aside from new band options and a new metallic finish called pyrite (a gold-and-silver blend), the watch itself hadn’t changed in the slightest. At least on the outside.

Google’s Pixel Watch 5 starts at $399 and is available to preorder. It’ll be in stores starting Aug. 20.

Google Pixel Watch 5 in matte black, polished silver, satin and pyrite. Carly Marsh/CNET

Pixel Watch 5’s welcome, but familiar design

I love the minimalist, bezel-free circular display, with nothing interrupting the curved glass except the rotating crown and side button. It still comes in both 41-mm and 45-mm sizes, and the domed display makes it feel more like a statement piece than a tiny computer strapped to your wrist.

My biggest complaint also hasn’t changed. That beautiful curved glass isn’t especially forgiving if you’re accident-prone. I managed to scratch my Pixel Watch 4 when I took a tumble during a trail run in the first month of testing, and the Pixel Watch 5 has the same Gorilla Glass 5 protection and the same LTPO AMOLED display with 3,000 nits of peak brightness and 320ppi resolution.

Pixel Watch 5’s battery and processing power

Under the hood, the Pixel Watch 5 gets an updated Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 Accelerated processor, which Google says boosts CPU performance by 12% (over the previous generation). Google also bumps RAM from 2GB to 3GB (a 50% increase) and doubles onboard storage from 32GB to 64GB.

The Pixel Watch 5 has the same round, all-screen design and bubbled display like its predecessor. René Ramos/CNET

The Watch 5 also has a slightly larger battery than its predecessor: 465 mAh versus 455 mAh on the 45mm model. In practice, though, this shouldn’t translate to a longer battery life. Google says the battery gains mostly offset new AI capabilities like offline Gemini, and you can expect anywhere from 30 to 40 hours of use with the always-on display enabled.

Pixel Watch 5’s offline Gemini

Gemini is still one of my favorite reasons to use a Pixel Watch, as it makes interacting with its small screen largely hands-free. Whether I’m checking train schedules while sprinting for the subway or asking for nearby coffee recommendations during a walk, talking to the watch is often faster than poking at a tiny touchscreen.

Raise-to-talk isn’t new, but the assistant can now handle more tasks offline, even when the watch is disconnected from your phone. That includes simple actions like starting a workout or setting a timer without relying on a data connection.

With Wear OS 7 (preloaded on Pixel Watch 5), Google is also positioning the watch as the hub for its growing wearable ecosystem. From your wrist, you’ll be able to manage Gemini-enabled earbuds, smart glasses and even Google’s new Pixel Tag trackers for objects like suitcases and keys.

Pixel Watch 5’s health and fitness features

While the Pixel Watch 5 uses the same GPS and health sensors as previous generations, Google says improvements to its machine learning algorithms significantly boost accuracy, not only on the Pixel Watch 5 but also on older supported Pixel Watches.

The watch has the same dual-band GPS system introduced on the Pixel Watch 4, but Google says it’s now even more accurate in dense urban environments where tall buildings often interfere with GPS signals.

Google even says that the Pixel Watch 5 outperforms the Apple Watch Ultra 3 and Garmin Fénix 8 Pro, which seems like a tall order considering these are dedicated sports watches that retail for twice the price. I obviously couldn’t verify these claims inside a demo room, but I’ll be putting it to the test for my review.

Likewise, I’ll need some time to test Google’s assertion that the Pixel Watch 5’s sleep and recovery metrics are now 15% more accurate than its predecessor.

Pixel Watch 5’s workout Builder

Workout Builder lets you create custom strength-training workouts on the Google Health app that sync directly to the watch, guiding you through each exercise, counting reps, timing rest periods and nudging you through your routine.

Screenshot Screenshot by CNET

All Pixel Watch 5 owners get free access to Google’s library of exercise videos, ranging from bodyweight movements like planks to dumbbell and kettlebell exercises. You can even filter workouts based on the equipment you have available. Ranking your workout effort after the fact helps the watch learn your threshold and adjust your next workout accordingly to challenge you more (or less) to match your current level.

If you subscribe to Google Health Premium ($10 a month), Google’s AI coach can build a workout for you from just a photo of your equipment. I tested this in Google’s demo room using kettlebells, resistance bands and slam balls.

After snapping a photo, I asked Gemini to build a 20-minute circuit. Within seconds, it created a workout complete with step-by-step instructions and instructional videos, which I could immediately launch on the Pixel Watch.

What impressed me wasn’t the AI-generated workout itself. Plenty of AI fitness tools can already do that. The difference is that Google’s solution bridges the gap between planning and actually exercising by pushing the routine directly to your watch, where it guides you through every rep and rest interval in real time. That’s been one of the missing pieces for AI coaching, and it’s the feature I’m most excited to test further.

Pixel Watch 5’s Health Guardian

Google is also introducing Health Guardian, an expansion of its existing emergency safety features.

Building on Loss of Pulse Detection, Health Guardian can recognize signs of breathing emergencies, including events related to choking, pneumonia or drug toxicity, as well as persistent (and potentially life-threatening) drops in blood oxygen saturation. If the watch detects one of these emergencies, it can automatically contact emergency services and share your location with your emergency contacts.

The Pixel Watch 5 has new health features that will help flag potentially serious medical conditions. Screenshot by CNET

Pixel Watch 5 tracks blood pressure and insulin resistance

The watch will track blood pressure and insulin resistance trends over time.

Rather than diagnosing medical conditions, these wellness features are designed to identify longer-term trends that could signal elevated risk for hypertension or diabetes. At the time of publishing, these features have not received FDA clearance and won’t be available at launch. Google says they’re expected to arrive in a software update later this fall on the Pixel Watch 5 and Fitbit Air.

Pixel Watch 5 bottom line

Only time and real-world testing will tell just how noticeable some of these gains actually are, but for now, the Pixel Watch 5 feels like an iterative upgrade to an already well-rounded smartwatch and one of the best smartwatch experiences running Wear OS 7 in the market.

The lack of a significant battery improvement, combined with the fact that some of its best new health features and accuracy gains are also coming to older watches, makes this a less obvious upgrade, especially at $50 more.
